The session begins.

Dawn finds its way through the gaps in the shutters and lays thin gold lines across the floorboards. Somewhere down the street a hammer strikes iron, then another joins it. Beregost's forges are waking. Over the rooftops, the bells of the Morninglord's temple roll out their slow greeting to the sun.

The cat is already up. It sits on the windowsill with its tail curled around its paws, watching the street below with keen interest. Now and then it turns to look at you, as if wondering why you are still in bed.

Your purse lies where you left it, heavy with about three hundred and fifty gold from that last hand. The road to Baldur's Gate runs north past the window. Nobody expects you anywhere today.

From below come the smell of frying bacon and the scrape of benches. Under that is a sound you would know anywhere: cards being shuffled and slapped down on wood, and a rough laugh. "Raise you two silver, and may Tymora weep for you!"

Then three brisk knocks at your door. "Master Worgen?" It is a woman's voice, the innkeeper's. "Breakfast's on, if you want it. And I need to know whether you're keeping the room another night, or whether I let it to the caravan folk who came in late."

The cat's ears twitch toward the door. The latch waits.

The latch lifts and the door swings in. Hulda Brask stands on the landing with a ring of keys on one hip and a dish towel over her shoulder. She looks him over from his bare feet to his face, the way she might look over a ham.

"Breakfast, then. And the room goes to the caravan," she says. "Good. Their master's been at me since midnight."

Behind James the cat jumps down from the sill and pads past his ankles to the doorway. Hulda doesn't so much as glance at it.

"North? Aye, they're going north. Four wagons of Beregost iron for the Gate. Master's a man called Pell Ostrand. Came up from Nashkel way, got in late, half his oxen lame and his temper worse." She shifts the keys to her other hand. "He's short a man as well. One of his guards took his pay at the Nashkel fair and stayed there. So if you want company, I'd say he wants it more."

From the common room comes another slap of cards on wood and a groan. Someone shouts, "That's three hands! You're marking them, Dace!"

Hulda's mouth tightens. "As for company that doesn't play cards..." She tips her head toward the stairs. "That's his guards down there. You'll have to fish for it."

She's already half turned toward the next door when she adds, "Ostrand's the one in the green coat by the hearth, not playing. Bacon's on the table now, and it won't wait. Settle your reckoning with me before you leave."

Her steps go off down the corridor. Below, the shuffling starts up again.

James dresses by the thin light from the shutters: studded leather, the old regimental cloak, the rod at his belt. The deck goes in last. He pushes it down under the bedroll and rations until his fingers touch canvas. The cat watches him do it. It says nothing.

The common room is warm, loud and full of bacon smoke. Four men sit at the long table nearest the stairs, with coins in small heaps beside their plates. The one dealing is lean and sandy-haired, with quick hands and a grin he can't keep off his face. A big man across from him has stopped eating to watch those hands. James goes the long way round, past the kitchen hatch. Behind him the cards go down again with a slap.

The man in the green coat sits alone by the hearth with a trencher he has hardly touched. He's somewhere past forty. He has road dust in the creases of his neck and a ledger open on his knee. Through the back door beyond him, two men in the yard hold a grey ox by the halter while a farrier crouches at its hind foot.

He looks up at his name. First at James, then at the cat sitting on the boards by James's boot, then back at James.

"Ostrand. Aye." He shuts the ledger on his thumb. "Hulda talks fast." He nods at the bench across from him. "Sit, then. If you're eating, eat. I've no time to watch a man chew."

A girl from the kitchen puts down a plate of bacon, black bread and a fried egg without being asked. Ostrand waits until she's gone.

"Terms are a gold a day, and you eat what my men eat. Paid at the Gate, not before. The last man I paid early is drinking it in Nashkel." He jerks his chin at the yard. "Four days to the city if the oxen hold, five if they don't. We leave when that farrier's done, and not an hour later."

He looks James over without hurrying. He takes in the light crossbow, the rapier, the empty hands.

"You say you've soldiered. Where? And what do you actually fight with? That sword doesn't look like it gets much use."

Ostrand hears him out without interrupting. At the word "spells" his eyes go to the rod at James's belt, then to the cat, which has sat down on the boards with its tail around its paws as if it owns the hearth. He doesn't look happy about it, but he doesn't look surprised either.

"Zaranda's lot. Hm." He picks up a strip of bacon at last and takes a bite. "Spells. My men won't like it. Iron doesn't care." He chews and swallows. "Healing's worth more to me than the rest. Last time a man got cut on the road, the nearest priest was two days off."

He's quiet for a moment and looks at the fire instead of at James.

"Trouble. Not trouble, exactly. Two days back, the far side of the Nashkel road, we found a wagon in the ditch. A good wagon, nearly new. The harness was cut clean, like with a knife, not torn. No team, no driver, no guards. No blood that I saw." He turns the ledger over on his knee without opening it. "The load was still on it. Salt, twenty barrels, lids nailed down. Bandits don't leave salt. We didn't stop long. I told the Fist post here last night. The sergeant wrote it in his book and asked me if I wanted a drink."

He sets the bacon down.

"North of here should be quieter. It's the Friendly Arm stretch, plenty of traffic. But I'd rather have one man too many than one too few."

He tips his head at the card table, where the big man is still watching Dace deal.

"Hagen. The big one. He's run my guards six years. On the road you do what he says about watches and where you stand. Everything else comes to me." He thinks about it. "He'll ask what you told me. Tell him the same, and don't put on a show for him. He hates shows."

At the long table Dace lays down a card with a flourish and rakes in a little heap of silver. The man to his left swears. Hagen says nothing. He has stopped watching Dace's hands and is watching James now.

James wipes the last of the egg up with the black bread, leaves the plate and crosses to the long table. The cat stays by the hearth and watches him go, as if the matter doesn't concern it.

Dace is shuffling again. The cards ripple through his fingers with a soft purr, and he looks up with that grin. "Morning. Room for one more, friend. Stakes are low and the company's lower."

The man on his left, red-faced, with egg on his beard, snorts into his cup. Hagen says nothing to either of them.

He hears James out with his forearms on the table. He doesn't look at James's face much. He looks at James's hands: the right one loose at his side, the left near the rod at his belt. When James nods toward the yard, Hagen's eyes follow the nod as far as the door and come back.

He takes his time. Dace finishes the shuffle and squares the deck with a tap. Nobody deals.

"Last wagon," Hagen says at last. "On the box with Orrin. He drives, you watch. The road behind, both ditches. Anything comes up on us from the back, it's yours first." He turns his cup a quarter turn on the wood. "Nights, you take the second watch. With me. I want to see you awake."

That seems to be all of it. Then his eyes go to the deck under Dace's hand, back to James's hands, and stay there.

"You came the long way round this table. Kept your eyes off it the whole time." It isn't quite an accusation. "You play?"

Dace's grin gets a little wider. He waits as well.

Hagen holds his eyes. For a long moment he says nothing. Dace's thumb rests on the top card and doesn't move.

"Good," Hagen says, and nothing more. He turns his cup back the quarter turn he gave it earlier.

Dace lets out a breath through his nose, half a laugh. "Shame. You've got the hands for it." He cuts the deck one-handed and squares it again. "Offer stands, if the Lady ever lets you off."

The red-faced guard reaches for the pot of small beer. "He's the clever one, then," he mutters to nobody in particular. "Deal, Dace. I want my silver back."

As James turns away, Hagen pushes back his bench and stands. He goes to the hearth, bends and says a few words to Ostrand. James can't hear them. Ostrand listens, grunts and opens his ledger again. The cards slap down behind them.

Hulda is at the kitchen hatch, counting loaves into a basket for the road. She doesn't stop when James comes up; she just tips her head to show she's listening. When he asks, she answers without having to work it out.

"Five silver the room, two the breakfast. Seven." She holds out a floury palm. "Mind, that's with the bacon."

James puts a gold piece in her hand. She looks at it once, turns it over out of habit, and counts three silver back onto the counter from a pouch at her belt.

"There. Square." She drops the gold into her apron. Her eyes go past him to the hearth, where Ostrand is writing something with his tongue between his teeth, and then back to him. "Riding with Ostrand, then. You'll want to fill that waterskin at the yard pump before they hitch up, not after. There's a queue at the pump once the oxen are watered."

The cat has come over from the hearth and is sitting by James's boot again, looking up at the basket of loaves with open interest. Hulda does see it this time. She breaks the heel off a loaf and drops it on the boards without comment, then goes back to her counting.

Through the back door the farrier is still crouched over the grey ox's foot. One of the drovers has gone to fetch a second ox from the stalls. By the look of the yard, it'll be a few hours before anything moves.

Hulda doesn't look up from the loaves. "Aye. Mind the pump handle, it sticks on the upstroke." She counts two more loaves into the basket and that's the end of it.

The yard smells of dung, wet straw and hot iron. The farrier has the grey ox's hoof between his knees and is tapping nails in with small, careful blows. The ox stands it with the patience of the very old. The pump is free for now. The handle sticks on the upstroke, just as Hulda said, and after a few hard pulls cold water comes up rusty, then clear. James fills the waterskin to the neck. Across the yard a drover is leading a second ox out of the stalls, a huge red animal that stops every few steps to think it over.

The cat doesn't wait for him. By the time James has stoppered the skin it is sitting on the tailboard of the last wagon, between two tarred canvas bundles. Under the canvas the iron bars are stacked flat and tight.

Orrin is down at the front of that wagon, checking a yoke pin with his thumb. He's a short, broad man of sixty or so, bow-legged, with a face like a walnut and a straw in the corner of his mouth. He hears James out without turning round, works the pin back into its hole and only then straightens up and squints at him.

"Eyes. Good. Mine aren't what they were." He looks past James's shoulder to the tailboard. "That yours, the cat?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. He slaps the near ox on the flank, a dun animal with one horn cracked off short. The ox ignores him entirely.

"This is Bishop. Bishop thinks he sets the pace. He walks in front, he swings his head, he makes a noise at the other teams." He moves to the off side. The second ox is smaller and dull brown, and it's chewing slowly with its eyes half shut. "This is Mutton. Mutton sets the pace. When Mutton stops, we stop, and Bishop finds out about it afterwards."

He shifts the straw to the other side of his mouth.

"Ostrand's lot up front, they've got the grey. That's the slow one. Lame as a churchwarden last night. If the farrier's any good, we'll make the Arm road by dark tomorrow." He pats Mutton's neck, and Mutton goes on chewing. "If he isn't, we won't."

He bends to look at a hoof, then glances up again, sideways, at James.

"Mind, Bishop's not all show. Two days back, south of here, he wouldn't go past a wagon in the ditch. Planted his feet and blew. I had to get down and lead him past by the nose, and he was shaking." He spits out the straw. "Thirty years I've driven oxen. Dead horse by the road, they don't care. Blood, they don't care much. That wagon had neither."

He picks a fresh straw out of the bale on the box and puts it in his mouth.

"You'll want to stow your pack under the seat. Left side. Right side's where my jug goes."

Orrin squints at the cat on the tailboard. The cat looks back at him without blinking.

"Under discussion," he says. "Aye. My wife said that about me for twenty years." He leaves it there.

James pushes the pack under the left side of the box, against a coil of spare rope. Under the right side a stone jug lies wedged in straw, corked with a rag.

At Ostrand's name Orrin goes back to Mutton's yoke and runs his thumb along the wood where it rests on the neck. He doesn't answer straight away.

"Smell, aye," he says at last. "Not rot. Not blood. Like the air when lightning comes down close. Sharp, up the nose. Four dry days we'd had, not a cloud." He presses the yoke and watches the ox's skin to see if it flinches. It doesn't. "I thought it was me. Then Bishop got a noseful and planted his feet."

He comes round the front of the team, slowly, on his bad legs.

"Marks I can't tell you. My eyes stop about the second wagon. Hagen walked round it while Ostrand was cursing. Ask him." He stops beside Bishop and lays a hand flat on the ox's broken horn. Bishop swings his head and grumbles. "One thing I did see, because I was down in the mud leading this fool by the nose. Soft ground there, both sides of the road. That wagon had a team on it once, you could see where they'd stood. Deep prints, two oxen, been there a while, shuffling." He pats the horn. "No prints going away. Not up the road, not down it, not into the grass. Harness cut, and the beasts just... weren't."

He says it in the same flat voice he used about the yoke pins.

"Settle? Not for a mile, near enough. He sweated the whole mile, and the wind was cold." He takes his hand off Bishop. "Then he was himself again. Shouting at the grey."

Across the yard the farrier sets the grey's hoof down and straightens up with a hand on his back. The ox takes a careful step on the new shoe, then another. The drover has the red ox up to the second wagon now. It has stopped beside the shaft to think things over again.

Orrin is bent over Mutton's near forefoot. He doesn't look up.

"He'll let you know," he says. "Loud. Then he'll lie down in the road and you'll know it twice."

He lets the hoof go. Mutton puts it back down without opening his eyes.

Hagen isn't in the common room. James finds him at the yard gate by the lead wagon, the one with the grey ox, running a hand along the trace chains link by link. The noise of the card table doesn't reach this far, only the hammers from the street and the grey ox's slow breathing. Hagen lets James finish. His hand stops on the chain and stays there.

He says nothing for long enough that a drover crosses the whole yard behind them with a bucket.

"Not a knife," he says at last. "I've cut harness. A knife frays the leather and leaves a tail. These ends were smooth. Flat across, like a joiner took a plane to them. Hard at the very end, too. Like leather that's been held too close to a fire." He takes his hand off the chain. "There was no fire. No ash, no scorch on the shafts."

He looks at James's hands, not his face.

"Boots as well. Four men, by the marks. Standing in the mud by the wagon, shifting about. The same as the oxen. Then nothing. Nobody ran. Nobody was dragged." He waits. "Orrin's right about the smell. It was gone by noon."

He reaches into his belt pouch and brings out something closed in his fist. He holds the fist a moment before he opens it.

On his palm lies a disc of dark, dull metal, thinner than a coin and not quite round, as if somebody had flattened a lead shot with one blow of a hammer. A sign is scratched into one face: a ring with a single straight line cut across it, like the bar across a door. The other face is blank. In the yard's morning warmth a faint mist has formed on the metal where his skin touched it and is already fading. The thing is cold. Hagen's hand has been around it, and it is still colder than it has any right to be.

"In the mud. Where the near ox stood. Pressed in, sign up." He doesn't offer it to James, and he doesn't close his hand either. "Didn't show Ostrand. He'd have thrown it in a ditch, or sold it."

His eyes go from the disc to the rod at James's belt.

"You know it?"

 (Out of game: that action did happen in the last turn without a roll. James found Hagen by the lead wagon at the yard gate, away from the card table, and asked him; Hagen answered and showed him the disc. Asking a willing witness a question doesn't need a roll.)

James leans in over Hagen's open palm, close enough to feel the cold coming off the metal on his cheek. He keeps his hands at his sides. The cat comes up the yard and sits by the wheel of the lead wagon. Its whiskers go forward, then flatten.

The barred ring is scratched, not stamped. The line is a little deeper at one end, as if whoever cut it pressed harder as they finished. The edge is rough where the hammer spread it. No maker's mark, no letters. Just the sign and the cold.

James thinks back over the years: company mages on the southern roads, a hedge-wizard's tower in Tethyr the scouts cleared once, the talk around a hundred campfires.

It comes together in pieces.

First the smell. James has smelled it before, in the second year of the war, in a stone farmhouse outside Darromar. A Tethyrian pretender's battle-mage was cornered there. He spoke six words and wasn't there any more. The air where he had stood went sharp and thin, exactly like the moment after lightning strikes close. The company wizard told the scouts afterwards that it was what conjuration leaves behind when it moves something from one place to another all at once. There was no storm, only a hole that had been made and closed.

Then the harness. A spell like that takes what lies inside its reach and leaves the rest behind. Whatever crosses the edge gets cut where the edge falls. That doesn't fray the leather the way a blade does. It leaves a clean face, like a cut through cheese with a hot wire. James has heard sellswords' talk of half a sword found in a doorway, and of a man who got his hand back but not his ring. He believed half of it at the time. The traces were on the oxen's side of the line, and the shafts were on the wagon's side.

Last, the disc itself. Magic that pours through a thing and leaves it often leaves it cold. It is the way a kettle cools once it's off the fire, but backwards, as if something drew the warmth out on its way through. A thing that has been used as a focus, or a mark for a spell to find, can stay cold for days afterwards. This one is still cold two days later, and that says a great deal of power went through it.

The sign tells him nothing. It isn't a wizard's school mark, a temple glyph or a guild token that James has ever seen. It is a ring with a bar across it, cut by hand into a slug of soft metal. Somebody made it for their own use.

He straightens up. The mist on the disc has faded again where Hagen's thumb isn't touching it.

Hagen hasn't moved. His hand stays open and flat, as James asked. His eyes have gone from the disc to James's hands, and from his hands to his face, which isn't where Hagen usually looks.

Over by the lead wagon the cat stands up, walks a slow half circle round the two men without coming closer, and sits down again on the far side.

Hagen looks down at the disc in his palm. The mist has faded from it again.

"Two days," he says. "On my belt. Beside the iron. Under my bedroll at the Arm road camp."

He doesn't say anything else about that, but his thumb comes off the metal as if it had turned hot.

The lane bends round a copse of ash, and High Hedge is there.

The name is honest. It is a hedge, holly and yew grown together and clipped square, half again as tall as a man on horseback and so dense the light doesn't get through. It runs off to either side farther than the lane shows. Above it rise the slate roof of a house and, behind that, a squat stone tower with a single window high up. A thin thread of smoke comes from the tower, not the house.

The lane ends at a gate of black iron bars set into the green, with a chain hanging beside it and a small bronze bell at the top of the chain. Nailed to the gatepost at eye height is a board. The paint on it is old but the letters were touched up not long ago:

They stand side by side, shoulder to shoulder, and watch the two men in the lane. Their noses go up when Hagen stops, and both heads turn together toward his left hand.

Hagen steps through the gate. He sets the bundle down in the centre of the ring, straightens and steps back two long paces. He wipes his left hand down his breeches twice.

Thalantyr doesn't touch the bundle. He snaps a twig off the yew beside the gate and crouches stiffly, one hand on his knee. With the twig he flicks back the sacking, then the knot of the kerchief, then its folds, until the disc lies bare on the slate with the sign facing up.

For a long while he just looks at it.

Then his stained fingers move in a short, practised pattern and he murmurs a few words under his breath. James knows the shape of that spell from a dozen company wizards: the simple sight that shows magic for what it is. Whatever Thalantyr sees, he keeps it off his face.

While he watches, the silvery line in the slate begins to frost. It starts at the point nearest the disc and creeps round the circle both ways, slowly, until the two ends meet. The air above the stone smells faintly sharp. It's nothing like the wagon would have smelled, but it's the same kind of smell.

"Hm," says Thalantyr.

He stands up, which takes a moment, and tosses the twig into the hedge.

He glances at Hagen, then back at James.

"Mutton never lost a wagon," he says. "Never got a man killed. Never once had an idea." He thinks about it. "Better than most I've seen, then."

After that he talks the way the road goes. A word now and then, mostly about the oxen, and long stretches of nothing. He seems to like it that way.

The Trade Way runs north through stubble fields and then rough pasture, with sheep scattered over it like dropped laundry. The dust rises off the wheels in front, and by noon it has settled into the folds of James's cloak. Behind them the road stays wide, pale and dull. The farm cart turns off at a gate within the first hour. The dog lasts longer, then gives up and trots home.

About midday a courier in Fist red comes up from the south at a canter. He passes the last wagon close enough for James to smell the horse, then the whole line, and doesn't look at any of them. A little later a party of six pilgrims comes the other way. They wear Lathander's rose-and-gold, and they walk with staves and sing something about the dawn, a little out of tune. One of them raises a hand to Orrin, and Orrin raises a finger off the reins. Bishop shouts at them, and they don't sing any louder.

The ditches give James nothing. There are nettles and dock leaves, a heron that lifts off a wet patch and flaps away, and once a hare that sits up, looks at the wagon and decides against it. Through the cat's eyes the road behind looks the same, only lower and sharper. The cat doesn't move from its post on the canvas all afternoon, except once. When the line halts at a stream ford to water the teams, it goes down the wheel into the long grass and comes back a few minutes later licking its mouth. It climbs back to its place facing south as if it had never left.

The sun is going down red over the country toward the sea when Ostrand lifts his hand at the front of the line. The camp place is one the caravans clearly know: a flat bit of turf west of the road with a beech hedge for a windbreak, a ring of fire-blackened stones, and a spring trickling out of a bank into a stone trough somebody set there long ago. The wagons come round into a loose square with the oxen inside it. Orrin climbs down from the box in stages, like a man going down a ladder, and goes straight to Mutton's yoke.

The cat lets him. It sits on the tailboard facing south, and when James reaches up it pushes its head into his fingers, once and hard, the way cats do when they've decided to allow something. It allows it for a few breaths. Then it pulls away and turns back to the dark, ears forward, tail hanging down over the edge of the board.

The crossbow lies along the bedroll by his right hand with the bolt case beside it. The rod is under the fold of his cloak where his left hand can find it. The wheel at his back is still warm from the day's sun.

Behind him the cards purr and slap. Bram groans once and the drover laughs. After a while Dace says, "That's me square, then," in the voice of a man who isn't. Then the fire settles, and a pot gets scraped. Hagen's blankets rustle somewhere across the square. The oxen shift and breathe in the middle of the wagons, slow and heavy. Mutton chews in his sleep. Bishop grumbles at nothing. The beech hedge ticks in a small wind off the sea, and the spring keeps running into its trough.

James sleeps.

A hand on his shoulder wakes him. It doesn't shake him. It just rests there, heavy, until his eyes open.

Hagen is crouched by the wheel with the fire low and red behind him. The sky has cleared, and the stars are thick over the hedge. The air smells of dew and dead ash, and it's cold now. Hagen takes his hand away as soon as he sees James is awake. He doesn't say "midnight." He doesn't need to.

Over by the fire Dace is handing over his watch to nobody in particular, standing up and stretching.

"Quiet," he says, through a yawn. "Fox along the hedge, twice. Cart went by about the tenth hour, southbound, didn't stop." He jerks a thumb at Bram, who has already rolled himself into his blanket like a sausage in a crust. "And he ate the bread we were saving for breakfast. So that's the worst of it."

"I was hungry," says the blanket.

Hagen doesn't look at either of them. He waits until Dace has gone to his own bedroll, then speaks low, to James.

"Hedge side's yours. Road's mine. We walk the square once an hour, opposite ways, meet at the trough." He looks at the cat on the tailboard, then at James's hands as they come out of the blanket. "Fire stays low. Don't look into it."

He straightens up and goes toward the road side of the camp without waiting. His shape is a darker piece of the dark against the stars.

The cat hasn't moved all night, by the look of it. It still faces south, down the pale line of the Way.

 (Out of game: all three happened last turn, and none needed a roll.)
1) James laid the crossbow along his bedroll by his right hand, with the bolt case beside it, and put the rod under the fold of his cloak where his left hand could reach it. Putting your own gear within reach can't fail.
2) The cat allowed the scratch. It pushed its head into his fingers for a few breaths, then went back to watching south. Your familiar was willing, so there was nothing to roll.
3) James fell asleep by the wheel and slept until Hagen woke him at midnight. Nothing disturbed the camp, so sleep wasn't in doubt.

· Time passes: 5 hours
· Journal: “Company on the road north” updated

Place: Caravan camp on the Trade Way · Time: Day 2 · night

James gets up without a sound. The Boots of Elvenkind make nothing of the turf. The cold gets in under his cloak at once, and he pulls it close at the throat. He takes the crossbow from beside the bedroll and settles the bolt case on his hip. The rod sits snug at his belt under the cloak's fold.

The cat on the tailboard doesn't turn when he asks it, mind to mind, to warn him of anyone coming. All he gets back is the feel of something already doing its job, a little put out at being told. Its ears stay pointed south.

He keeps away from the fire. Hagen is right about it: even banked low it pulls at the eye, and one look into the coals would cost him the dark for a long count. He works along the inside of the square in the wagons' shadow, then out to the gap between the last wagon and the hedge.

The beech hedge is a black wall against the stars, about the height of a man and a half. Its dead leaves keep their rattle in the small wind off the sea, so the whole length of it ticks and whispers, and he has to listen past that. He hears the spring running into its trough. In the square the oxen breathe heavily, and Mutton grinds his teeth in his sleep. An owl calls once, a long way off over the fields to the east, and is quiet.

Past the end of the hedge the turf runs west, flat and grey under the starlight, to a dark line he takes for a ditch. Nothing stands on it.

Halfway along, the cat's senses brush against his own. A sharp musky reek reaches him through the cat's nose before he would ever have smelled it himself. When he looks with the cat's eyes the dark goes grey and clear. At the far end of the hedge, maybe a hundred and twenty feet off, a fox comes out of the roots and stops with one forepaw raised. It looks at the wagons and at the man in the cloak, and it decides against all of it. Then it's gone back into the hedge bottom, and the ticking leaves cover the sound of it. Dace's fox, the third time.

James finishes the circuit along the spring bank and comes round to the trough. The stone is wet and furred with moss, and the water spills over its lip into the grass.

Hagen is already there, a big dark shape with his back to the fire. He has his hands on the rim of the trough, and they're the only part of him that's moving. He's working the cold out of his fingers. He lets James come all the way up before he does anything else.

He says nothing for a while. The spring runs. Out on the road side the Way is a pale stripe going off north and south, empty.

Then he looks past James, over the wagons, at the small shape on the last tailboard, which is still facing south.

"What's it watching?"

messages.text:
“Breakfast, yes. Another night, no—best I get north before I grow respectable.”

I get out of bed and open the door, keeping my eyes off the deck beside my purse.

“Any of those caravan folk bound for Baldur’s Gate? I’d welcome company on the road. Preferably company that doesn’t play cards.”

I dress and gather my gear, burying the deck at the bottom of my pack, then head downstairs with the cat.

Giving the card table a wide berth, I approach the man in the green coat. “Master Ostrand? James Worgen. Hulda tells me you’re heading north and short a guard. I’m bound for the Gate, and I’ve soldiered and guarded caravans before. Mind if we discuss the road and your terms over breakfast?”

“Tethyr. Infantry under Queen Zaranda, then scouts. Caravan work with adventuring companies after that.”

I settle onto the bench. “The sword doesn’t get much use. I fight with spells—better at range than shoulder to shoulder. I can also scout and do a little healing when someone’s luck runs out.”

I break off a piece of bread. “A gold a day and food, paid at the Gate, suits me. What trouble have you had on the road, and who commands the guards?”

“Agreed. I’ll speak to Hagen and settle with Hulda before we leave.”

I finish my breakfast, then walk over to Hagen, keeping my eyes on him rather than the cards.

“James Worgen. Ostrand’s hired me for the run to the Gate. Former Tethyrian infantry and scouts; these days I fight with spells at range, and can manage some healing. He says you give the orders on watch and in trouble.”

I nod toward the yard. “Where do you want me when we move out?”

“Used to. Won my last hand, and the price was never playing another.” I meet Hagen’s eyes. “I mean to keep that bargain.”

“Last wagon with Orrin, rear and ditches. Second watch with you. Understood.”

I nod to the table. “Enjoy your game, gentlemen. I’ve a bill to settle.” I go find Hulda and ask what I owe for the room and breakfast.

“Thank you, Hulda. For the warning and the bacon.”

I head into the yard with the cat and fill my waterskin before the oxen get their turn, then look for Orrin by the last wagon.

“James Worgen—your extra pair of eyes as far as the Gate. Hagen’s put me on the box with you.” I glance at the teams being readied. “Which of these beasts sets our pace, and which merely thinks it does?”

“The cat travels with me. Whether that makes it mine is under discussion.”

I stow my pack under the left side of the seat. “Ostrand mentioned that wagon. Said the salt was untouched and the harness cut.”

I glance at Bishop, then back to Orrin. “When you led him past, did you notice anything else—a smell, a sound, marks on the wagon? And did he settle once you were clear of it?”

“If Bishop objects to anything on this road, let me know. I’ll take him seriously.”

I leave Orrin to the team and seek out Hagen, away from the card table if possible.

“Orrin says there were hoofprints where the missing team stood, but none leading away, and a sharp smell like a lightning strike. He said you walked around the wagon. What did you find?”

“Let me look. Keep it in your hand for now.”

I lean close enough to study the barred ring without touching the disc, searching my memory for the sign and anything that might link its unnatural cold to the smell of lightning and those cleanly severed traces.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“I don’t know the sign. But the rest fits conjuration—magic that moves things from one place to another. The smell, the clean cuts, no tracks leaving. Those people and oxen may have been taken somewhere, rather than killed there.”

I nod toward his palm. “That could have been a marker for the spell to find, or a focus used to cast it. Still cold after two days means powerful magic. I can’t tell whether it’s spent.”

I lower my voice. “Ostrand needs to know before we carry it north with everyone. Will you show him while I explain?”

“Likely a focus or marker for powerful conjuration. I don’t recognise the sign.”

I keep my voice quiet and matter-of-fact. “The smell at the wagon, the cut harness and the tracks ending where men and oxen stood fit magic moving them somewhere else. This was found in those tracks. Its cold suggests a great deal of magic passed through it.”

“I can’t tell you whether it’s spent, or whether carrying it puts us at risk. I recommend we leave it here with someone qualified to examine it—not throw it away for another traveller to find. Is there a wizard in Beregost you trust?”

“High Hedge, then. A conjurer’s our best chance of a useful answer. Thank you, Hagen.”

I turn to Ostrand. “We’ll leave now. If we miss the hitching, we’ll catch you on the Way.”

I retrieve my pack from Orrin’s wagon and beckon the cat to follow, then set off west with Hagen. “Keep it wrapped and separate from your other things. I don’t know that it helps, but let’s avoid handling it more than we must.”
I ring the bell once, then step back from the gate and wait, keeping my hands plainly visible and giving the hounds their space.

“James Worgen. This is Hagen. He found a small metal disc beside an abandoned wagon south of Beregost two days ago. It bears a scratched ring with a bar across it, and it’s still unnaturally cold.”

“Four men and two oxen left prints where they stood, but none leaving. The harness ends were cut smooth and hardened, without scorching nearby. There was a sharp smell like lightning. The cargo remained.”

“I suspect conjuration, and that the disc was a focus or marker. I don’t know whether it’s spent or dangerous to carry. We were told conjuration is your field, so we’ve come for an expert examination, not to sell it. What would you charge—and where should Hagen safely put it down?”

“Twenty-five gold, and it stays here. Agreed.”

I count out the coins. “Send your findings to James Worgen, care of the Friendly Arm Inn. We should reach it after tomorrow’s travel; I’ll ask the innkeeper for your message.”

I glance at the frosted circle. “If you discover where those people were taken, or anything that might help find them alive, please include it. Hagen reported the wagon to the Fist here, so they have its location.”

“Is there anything else you need from us before we leave?”

“Thank you. We’ll look for your letter.”

I step back into the lane with Hagen and shut the gate securely behind us, then start back toward the inn with the cat.

“Four sets of boots,” I say once we’re on the road. “Whoever planted it may have been travelling with them. Did you see any sign of someone kneeling by that spot, or were the prints too churned up to tell?”

“Thalantyr says carrying it won’t summon anything—the spell’s finished. He’s examining it and will send his findings to the Friendly Arm.”

I stow my pack under the left side of Orrin’s seat again and climb onto the box, leaving him room to work.

“The wizard kept it. You and Bishop can both rest easy on that account.” I settle my crossbow within reach and look over our view of the rear and the ditches, ready to leave.

“I’ve marched behind worse commanders than Mutton.”

I settle into the journey, keeping my attention on the road behind us and both ditches. I leave the cat to watch from its perch and keep conversation light enough not to distract either Orrin or me from our work.

“Midnight. Understood.”

I check that my crossbow and rod are within reach, then settle into my bedroll with my back to the card game. I rub the cat behind the ears if it permits.

“Wake me if something needs waking for,” I murmur, and try to get some sleep before my watch.

I rise quietly, pull my cloak close, and take up my crossbow with the rod secure at my belt.

Through our familiar bond, I ask the cat to alert me if it notices anyone approaching, then take the hedge side as ordered. I keep clear of the firelight and listen as well as look, watching the hedge and the ground beyond the wagons as I begin my first circuit.

What worked best was the grounded atmosphere. Orrin and his oxen, Hulda’s brisk manner, Hagen watching my hands—those details made the caravan feel like people at work rather than a quest waiting for me. Their voices were distinct, and the humour fit the setting. I also appreciated that ordinary conversation and preparation didn’t require rolls, and that we could move through an uneventful day without manufacturing a fight.

The abandoned wagon was a good mystery. The physical clues gave me something to reason about, and consulting Thalantyr felt like a sensible choice with a real cost in gold and time. I had room to decide how James handled it.

What broke immersion most was the repeated out-of-game accounting of my previous actions. Explaining that walking, talking, packing, or petting a willing cat needed no roll wasn’t necessary, especially when I hadn’t questioned it. Those passages sometimes resembled debugging notes rather than play.

There were also mechanical inconsistencies:
- The Arcana roll used +4 even though the sheet says +3. It changed a failure into a success.
- The opening records changed some supplied character details, notably rapier proficiency and Healing Light’s per-use limit. Actual 2014 Celestial rules support the four-die limit, but discrepancies with the campaign sheet should be settled explicitly.
- The cat received apparent night vision, and James sometimes used its senses without my choosing to do so. That matters because sharing its senses blinds and deafens James to his own surroundings.

What I missed was a little more initiative from the world beyond the mystery and the card temptation. The cards were effective initially, but repeated shuffling and invitations risked making James’s weakness feel like a button being pressed. Likewise, the cat’s constant southward attention became ominous without giving me much actionable information. If those were deliberate clues, I wanted a clearer opportunity to investigate them.

Overall, I enjoyed the quiet, practical start and would continue. Keep the strong NPCs, meaningful choices, and restrained pacing; tighten the rules bookkeeping, leave James’s sensory choices to me, and drop the unsolicited explanations of why routine actions didn’t need rolls.

Yes—when Ostrand gave us a few hours before departure, I wanted to visit the Song of the Morning. James had just sworn off another invitation to cards, and a quiet visit to a temple felt like a chance to explore what serving Tymora means to him outside a crisis.

I followed the disc instead because it seemed potentially dangerous to everyone travelling with us, and the departure deadline made that feel more urgent. That was a reasonable consequence of the situation, not something you blocked—but it meant James’s first free morning became an investigation before I’d explored much of his personal life.

turns.reply:
The latch lifts and the door swings in. Hulda Brask stands on the landing with a ring of keys on one hip and a dish towel over her shoulder. She looks him over from his bare feet to his face, the way she might look over a ham.

"Breakfast, then. And the room goes to the caravan," she says. "Good. Their master's been at me since midnight."

Behind James the cat jumps down from the sill and pads past his ankles to the doorway. Hulda doesn't so much as glance at it.

"North? Aye, they're going north. Four wagons of Beregost iron for the Gate. Master's a man called Pell Ostrand. Came up from Nashkel way, got in late, half his oxen lame and his temper worse." She shifts the keys to her other hand. "He's short a man as well. One of his guards took his pay at the Nashkel fair and stayed there. So if you want company, I'd say he wants it more."

From the common room comes another slap of cards on wood and a groan. Someone shouts, "That's three hands! You're marking them, Dace!"

Hulda's mouth tightens. "As for company that doesn't play cards..." She tips her head toward the stairs. "That's his guards down there. You'll have to fish for it."

She's already half turned toward the next door when she adds, "Ostrand's the one in the green coat by the hearth, not playing. Bacon's on the table now, and it won't wait. Settle your reckoning with me before you leave."

Her steps go off down the corridor. Below, the shuffling starts up again.

turns.reply:
James dresses by the thin light from the shutters: studded leather, the old regimental cloak, the rod at his belt. The deck goes in last. He pushes it down under the bedroll and rations until his fingers touch canvas. The cat watches him do it. It says nothing.

The common room is warm, loud and full of bacon smoke. Four men sit at the long table nearest the stairs, with coins in small heaps beside their plates. The one dealing is lean and sandy-haired, with quick hands and a grin he can't keep off his face. A big man across from him has stopped eating to watch those hands. James goes the long way round, past the kitchen hatch. Behind him the cards go down again with a slap.

The man in the green coat sits alone by the hearth with a trencher he has hardly touched. He's somewhere past forty. He has road dust in the creases of his neck and a ledger open on his knee. Through the back door beyond him, two men in the yard hold a grey ox by the halter while a farrier crouches at its hind foot.

He looks up at his name. First at James, then at the cat sitting on the boards by James's boot, then back at James.

"Ostrand. Aye." He shuts the ledger on his thumb. "Hulda talks fast." He nods at the bench across from him. "Sit, then. If you're eating, eat. I've no time to watch a man chew."

A girl from the kitchen puts down a plate of bacon, black bread and a fried egg without being asked. Ostrand waits until she's gone.

"Terms are a gold a day, and you eat what my men eat. Paid at the Gate, not before. The last man I paid early is drinking it in Nashkel." He jerks his chin at the yard. "Four days to the city if the oxen hold, five if they don't. We leave when that farrier's done, and not an hour later."

He looks James over without hurrying. He takes in the light crossbow, the rapier, the empty hands.

"You say you've soldiered. Where? And what do you actually fight with? That sword doesn't look like it gets much use."

Bandits don't leave salt. We didn't stop long. I told the Fist post here last night. The sergeant wrote it in his book and asked me if I wanted a drink."

He sets the bacon down.

"North of here should be quieter. It's the Friendly Arm stretch, plenty of traffic. But I'd rather have one man too many than one too few."

He tips his head at the card table, where the big man is still watching Dace deal.

"Hagen. The big one. He's run my guards six years. On the road you do what he says about watches and where you stand. Everything else comes to me." He thinks about it. "He'll ask what you told me. Tell him the same, and don't put on a show for him. He hates shows."

At the long table Dace lays down a card with a flourish and rakes in a little heap of silver. The man to his left swears. Hagen says nothing. He has stopped watching Dace's hands and is watching James now.

Dace is shuffling again. The cards ripple through his fingers with a soft purr, and he looks up with that grin. "Morning. Room for one more, friend. Stakes are low and the company's lower."

The man on his left, red-faced, with egg on his beard, snorts into his cup. Hagen says nothing to either of them.

"You came the long way round this table. Kept your eyes off it the whole time." It isn't quite an accusation. "You play?"

Dace's grin gets a little wider. He waits as well.

turns.reply:
Hagen holds his eyes. For a long moment he says nothing. Dace's thumb rests on the top card and doesn't move.

"Good," Hagen says, and nothing more. He turns his cup back the quarter turn he gave it earlier.

Dace lets out a breath through his nose, half a laugh. "Shame. You've got the hands for it." He cuts the deck one-handed and squares it again. "Offer stands, if the Lady ever lets you off."

The red-faced guard reaches for the pot of small beer. "He's the clever one, then," he mutters to nobody in particular. "Deal, Dace. I want my silver back."

As James turns away, Hagen pushes back his bench and stands. He goes to the hearth, bends and says a few words to Ostrand. James can't hear them. Ostrand listens, grunts and opens his ledger again. The cards slap down behind them.

Hulda is at the kitchen hatch, counting loaves into a basket for the road. She doesn't stop when James comes up; she just tips her head to show she's listening. When he asks, she answers without having to work it out.

"Five silver the room, two the breakfast. Seven." She holds out a floury palm. "Mind, that's with the bacon."

James puts a gold piece in her hand. She looks at it once, turns it over out of habit, and counts three silver back onto the counter from a pouch at her belt.

"There. Square." She drops the gold into her apron. Her eyes go past him to the hearth, where Ostrand is writing something with his tongue between his teeth, and then back to him. "Riding with Ostrand, then. You'll want to fill that waterskin at the yard pump before they hitch up, not after. There's a queue at the pump once the oxen are watered."

The cat has come over from the hearth and is sitting by James's boot again, looking up at the basket of loaves with open interest. Hulda does see it this time. She breaks the heel off a loaf and drops it on the boards without comment, then goes back to her counting.

He hears James out without turning round, works the pin back into its hole and only then straightens up and squints at him.

"This is Bishop. Bishop thinks he sets the pace. He walks in front, he swings his head, he makes a noise at the other teams." He moves to the off side. The second ox is smaller and dull brown, and it's chewing slowly with its eyes half shut. "This is Mutton. Mutton sets the pace. When Mutton stops, we stop, and Bishop finds out about it afterwards."

He shifts the straw to the other side of his mouth.

"Ostrand's lot up front, they've got the grey. That's the slow one. Lame as a churchwarden last night. If the farrier's any good, we'll make the Arm road by dark tomorrow." He pats Mutton's neck, and Mutton goes on chewing. "If he isn't, we won't."

He bends to look at a hoof, then glances up again, sideways, at James.

"Mind, Bishop's not all show. Two days back, south of here, he wouldn't go past a wagon in the ditch. Planted his feet and blew. I had to get down and lead him past by the nose, and he was shaking." He spits out the straw. "Thirty years I've driven oxen. Dead horse by the road, they don't care. Blood, they don't care much. That wagon had neither."

He picks a fresh straw out of the bale on the box and puts it in his mouth.

"You'll want to stow your pack under the seat. Left side. Right side's where my jug goes."

James leans in over Hagen's open palm, close enough to feel the cold coming off the metal on his cheek. He keeps his hands at his sides. The cat comes up the yard and sits by the wheel of the lead wagon. Its whiskers go forward, then flatten.

The barred ring is scratched, not stamped. The line is a little deeper at one end, as if whoever cut it pressed harder as they finished. The edge is rough where the hammer spread it. No maker's mark, no letters. Just the sign and the cold.

James thinks back over the years: company mages on the southern roads, a hedge-wizard's tower in Tethyr the scouts cleared once, the talk around a hundred campfires.

It comes together in pieces.

First the smell. James has smelled it before, in the second year of the war, in a stone farmhouse outside Darromar. A Tethyrian pretender's battle-mage was cornered there. He spoke six words and wasn't there any more. The air where he had stood went sharp and thin, exactly like the moment after lightning strikes close. The company wizard told the scouts afterwards that it was what conjuration leaves behind when it moves something from one place to another all at once. There was no storm, only a hole that had been made and closed.

Then the harness. A spell like that takes what lies inside its reach and leaves the rest behind. Whatever crosses the edge gets cut where the edge falls. That doesn't fray the leather the way a blade does. It leaves a clean face, like a cut through cheese with a hot wire. James has heard sellswords' talk of half a sword found in a doorway, and of a man who got his hand back but not his ring. He believed half of it at the time. The traces were on the oxen's side of the line, and the shafts were on the wagon's side.

Last, the disc itself. Magic that pours through a thing and leaves it often leaves it cold. It is the way a kettle cools once it's off the fire, but backwards, as if something drew the warmth out on its way through. A thing that has been used as a focus, or a mark for a spell to find, can stay cold for days afterwards. This one is still cold two days later, and that says a great deal of power went through it.

The sign tells him nothing. It isn't a wizard's school mark, a temple glyph or a guild token that James has ever seen. It is a ring with a bar across it, cut by hand into a slug of soft metal. Somebody made it for their own use.

He straightens up. The mist on the disc has faded again where Hagen's thumb isn't touching it.

Hagen hasn't moved. His hand stays open and flat, as James asked. His eyes have gone from the disc to James's hands, and from his hands to his face, which isn't where Hagen usually looks.

Over by the lead wagon the cat stands up, walks a slow half circle round the two men without coming closer, and sits down again on the far side.

At the last wagon Orrin is checking Bishop's hoof. He doesn't straighten up while James pulls the pack out from under the left side of the box.

"Walking to the wizard," he says to the hoof. "Two miles out, two miles back. Bishop'll be sorry he missed it."

James whistles once, low. The cat jumps down from the wheel of the lead wagon and follows, but not close. It keeps James between itself and Hagen the whole way out of the yard and stays well to his left, the way a cat walks around a puddle.

Hagen hears James out about the disc. At the gate he stops, takes the kerchief from his neck and wraps the thing in it, two turns and a knot. Then he pulls a scrap of sacking off the gatepost and wraps that around the kerchief. He doesn't put it in his pouch or under his belt. He carries it in his left hand, out from his side, the way a man carries a dead rat by the tail.

"Not near the iron," he says. "Not near me, if I can help it."

They go out past the last forges. Beregost thins to fences, then to fields of stubble with crows in them. The lane west is cart-wide, with grass down the middle, and it runs between hawthorn and ditch. The morning is warm and still. After a quarter mile Hagen's knuckles have gone pale around the sacking, and a damp patch has spread through the cloth where the cold is coming out.

He doesn't talk. Half a mile on he glances once at the cat, which is trotting along the far verge with its tail up and its ears turned back toward him.

"It knew," he says. "In the yard. Before I opened my hand."

That's all he says, and he doesn't make it a question.

The lane bends round a copse of ash, and High Hedge is there.

The name is honest. It is a hedge, holly and yew grown together and clipped square, half again as tall as a man on horseback and so dense the light doesn't get through. It runs off to either side farther than the lane shows. Above it rise the slate roof of a house and, behind that, a squat stone tower with a single window high up. A thin thread of smoke comes from the tower, not the house.

The lane ends at a gate of black iron bars set into the green, with a chain hanging beside it and a small bronze bell at the top of the chain. Nailed to the gatepost at eye height is a board. The paint on it is old but the letters were touched up not long ago:

RING. WAIT.

Behind the bars, on the gravel, two dogs are already standing. They're big grey long-legged hounds, rough-coated, and they didn't come running. James never heard them arrive. They aren't barking. They stand side by side, shoulder to shoulder, and watch the two men in the lane. Their noses go up when Hagen stops, and both heads turn together toward his left hand.

On the far verge the cat has sat down in the grass and gone very still.

The bell hangs at the end of its chain.

The man who comes round the side of the house is old and tall. He's stooped at the shoulders like someone who has spent years ducking under low lintels. He wears a long grey robe with the sleeves pushed up past the elbow, and a leather apron over it, scorched in a dozen small places. His beard is white and cut short. His forearms are thin and corded, and one of them is stained to the wrist with something dark blue. He's wiping his hands on a rag as he walks, and he doesn't stop until he reaches the hounds.

"Sit."

He doesn't raise his voice. Both dogs sit at once, shoulder to shoulder. Their heads stay turned toward Hagen's left hand.

The old man notices that. He looks at the hounds, then follows their gaze to the sacking, and his eyes stay there a moment longer than they stayed on either man. Then he looks at James: the rod at his belt, the open hands, the regimental cloak. He doesn't seem to think much of any of it. Last of all he glances past them at the patch of grass where the cat is trying not to exist.

"Well. You rang, and you waited. That puts you ahead of half of Beregost." He tucks the rag into his apron. He makes no move toward the gate. "I am Thalantyr. You'll have been told that already, along with a good deal of nonsense about my dogs."

“Four men and two oxen left prints where they stood, but none leaving. The harness ends were cut smooth and hardened, without scorching nearby. There was a sharp smell like lightning. The cargo remained.”

“I suspect conjuration, and that the disc was a focus or marker. I don’t know whether it’s spent or dangerous to carry. We were told conjuration is your field, so we’ve come for an expert examination, not to sell it. What would you charge—and where should Hagen safely put it down?”

Thalantyr hears him out without moving. His eyes stay on the sacking the whole time. At "prints where they stood, but none leaving," one of his eyebrows goes up a little. At "harness ends cut smooth and hardened" it comes down again, as if that settled something.

"Expert examination." He says it the way a smith might repeat a farmer's word for a horseshoe. "Half of Beregost thinks I eat dogs and the other half thinks I'll turn iron into gold if they ask nicely enough. It's a change to have a man use the right word."

He takes a key from a pocket under the apron and unlocks the gate. It swings inward without a sound. The hounds stay where they are, sitting shoulder to shoulder, but they shift to keep their noses on Hagen's left hand.

"Put it there."

Just inside the gate, to the left of the gravel path, a slab of grey slate about three feet across is set flush with the ground. A ring is cut into its face and filled with something dull and silvery. Moss grows up to the edges of the slab but not onto it. It has been there a long time, and things have been set down on it before. The stone is worn smooth in the middle.

Hagen steps through the gate. He sets the bundle down in the centre of the ring, straightens and steps back two long paces. He wipes his left hand down his breeches twice.

Thalantyr doesn't touch the bundle. He snaps a twig off the yew beside the gate and crouches stiffly, one hand on his knee. With the twig he flicks back the sacking, then the knot of the kerchief, then its folds, until the disc lies bare on the slate with the sign facing up.

For a long while he just looks at it.

Then his stained fingers move in a short, practised pattern and he murmurs a few words under his breath. James knows the shape of that spell from a dozen company wizards: the simple sight that shows magic for what it is. Whatever Thalantyr sees, he keeps it off his face.

While he watches, the silvery line in the slate begins to frost. It starts at the point nearest the disc and creeps round the circle both ways, slowly, until the two ends meet. The air above the stone smells faintly sharp. It's nothing like the wagon would have smelled, but it's the same kind of smell.

"Hm," says Thalantyr.

He stands up, which takes a moment, and tosses the twig into the hedge.

"It isn't a focus. A focus goes home in the caster's pocket. This was made to be left behind." He tucks his hands into the sleeves of his robe. "You'd call it a peg. You drive it into the ground so the spell knows where to take hold. It's crude work. It's also strong work. Those two don't usually go together."

He glances at Hagen, then back at James.

"Spent? The spell it served is done. The peg is still holding on to the place it was pressed into, and it's no longer in that place, so it's holding on to very little. Carrying it about in your neckcloth won't call anything down on you. It was foolish all the same."

He looks down at the scratched sign again.

"That isn't a school's mark, or any temple's I know. Somebody cut it for their own use." A pause. "And this isn't lead."

He doesn't say what it is instead. He takes the rag out of his apron and wipes his fingers, though he hasn't touched anything.

"My terms. I want a day with it in the tower, and some materials I'd rather not waste on Beregost's curiosity. Twenty-five gold. Afterwards it stays with me. I don't hand back things like this to men who carry them in kerchiefs." His mouth tightens very slightly at one corner. "Your caravan master will be pleased about that, I expect. The ones who send things here usually want them gone."

Behind James, out in the lane, the cat has crept a few feet nearer through the grass and stopped. The hounds haven't moved.

"Which leaves the one question that's yours to answer," Thalantyr says. "You'll be on the Way north by noon, I take it. Where do I send what I find?"

I glance at the frosted circle. “If you discover where those people were taken, or anything that might help find them alive, please include it. Hagen reported the wagon to the Fist here, so they have its location.”

“Is there anything else you need from us before we leave?”
turns.reply:
James counts the coins out of his purse: twenty-five gold pieces, in five stacks of five. Thalantyr holds out his stained palm for them. He doesn't count them. He weighs them once in his hand, the way Hulda turned the gold piece over, and drops them into a pocket under his apron.

"The Friendly Arm. Very well." He says the name as if he were writing it in a ledger. "A carter takes my letters north when he goes, and he goes most days. If there's anything worth writing, it will be waiting for you there. If there isn't, I'll write that too, so you needn't stand at the innkeeper's elbow wondering."

At the mention of the Fist, Hagen stirs. He doesn't take his eyes off the slab.

"Pell told them. Not me." A pause. "Sergeant wrote it in his book."

Thalantyr's mouth tightens at one corner. It's the nearest thing to an opinion of the Flaming Fist he gives.

"As for finding them alive." He looks down at the disc and the frosted silver ring around it, not at James. "I can tell you what this is made of, and perhaps where it was made, and something about the hand that made it. Where four men and two oxen are standing this morning is another question entirely. I won't sell you an answer I may not have. Don't expect one."

He turns his head toward Hagen. It's the first time he has looked at the big man for longer than a moment.

"You said pressed in, sign up. Dropped, or pushed?"

Hagen takes his time, as he always does.

"Pushed. Flat. Mud closed round the edge like you'd pressed a thumb in."

"And the prints around it. How many sets?"

"Four."

"Four," Thalantyr says. He lets the word sit. "Four men taken, four sets of boots. And somebody knelt in the mud and pushed this in flat, sign up, where the near ox stood."

He doesn't say anything more about it. He takes the rag out of his apron and wipes his fingers on it again, and tucks it back.

"No. I need nothing else from you." He nods at the gate. "Shut that behind you. The dogs know their way out, and I'd rather they didn't use it."

The hounds still sit shoulder to shoulder on the gravel with their noses on the slab. Out in the lane the cat has come up out of the grass. It sits on the verge in plain sight now, with its tail around its feet, watching the gate.

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“Thank you. We’ll look for your letter.”

I step back into the lane with Hagen and shut the gate securely behind us, then start back toward the inn with the cat.

“Four sets of boots,” I say once we’re on the road. “Whoever planted it may have been travelling with them. Did you see any sign of someone kneeling by that spot, or were the prints too churned up to tell?”
turns.reply:
The gate swings shut on its silent hinges. James checks the latch with his hand until he feels it seat. Behind the bars the hounds still sit shoulder to shoulder with their noses on the slab. Thalantyr is already walking back round the side of the house with the rag in his hand, and he doesn't look back.

The cat waits until the gate is shut. Then it gets up off the verge and comes into the lane. It walks on James's left as before, but closer, and once it crosses in front of Hagen's boots without seeming to notice him.

They're past the ash copse before James asks. Hagen walks a dozen paces without answering. His left hand is empty now, and he keeps opening and closing it at his side as if it still feels the cold.

"Didn't look for knees," he says. "Looked for where they went."

Another few paces.

"Near ox stood in soft ground, and an ox shifts his feet. That patch was all hoof. A man could kneel in that and you'd not know it from the rest." He frowns at the lane ahead. "Boots, I can tell you. Three sets back by the tailboard and along the off side, where guards stand when a wagon stops. One set up by the near ox's head."

He doesn't say what that means, so James's own years on the road say it for him. A guard watches the road. On a wagon, the man who stands at the near ox's head is the one holding the team, the drover or the driver. A drover works his team from the near side.

Hagen has got there too. It shows in the way his jaw sets.

"If it was him," he says, "he didn't drop it. He stood there with it. Held the ox and waited." He says it flat, the way he said "four" at the gate. "Then he went with the rest."

He leaves it at that. The lane runs on between the hawthorn and the ditch. The crows in the stubble lift and settle again as they pass.

About three quarters of an hour after the gate, the first forge hammers reach them over the fields. Then come the fences, then the street, and then the yard of the Lantern and Anvil. It's a different place now. The grey stands yoked at the lead wagon on its new shoe. The red ox has given up thinking and stands at the second shaft. Drovers are running trace chains and calling to each other. Dace is up on the second wagon, lashing down canvas with his quick hands, and the red-faced guard is handing him rope.

Orrin sits on the box of the last wagon with a fresh straw in his mouth, his eyes half shut, like Mutton's. He opens one of them when he sees them come in.

Ostrand is at the gate with his ledger. He looks at Hagen's empty hands first and at James second.

"Gone?"

"Gone," says Hagen.

"Sold?"

"Paid him to keep it," Hagen says, and leaves the rest to James.

Ostrand looks at James for a moment. Then he grunts, writes something in the ledger, and jerks his chin at the last wagon.

"Good. We roll when the red one's chained. Not long." He's already turning away. "Get your pack on that box."

place.name: Yard of the Lantern and Anvil

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“Thalantyr says carrying it won’t summon anything—the spell’s finished. He’s examining it and will send his findings to the Friendly Arm.”

I stow my pack under the left side of Orrin’s seat again and climb onto the box, leaving him room to work.

“The wizard kept it. You and Bishop can both rest easy on that account.” I settle my crossbow within reach and look over our view of the rear and the ditches, ready to leave.
turns.reply:
Ostrand is still at the gate with his ledger when James passes him. He hears it out as he goes and doesn't look up from the page.

"Won't summon anything." He writes something short. "Good. I wasn't afraid of summoning. I was afraid of Hagen sleeping on it." He turns the page. "His problem now. The wizard's, I mean."

James pushes the pack under the left side of the box again, against the coil of rope, and climbs up. Orrin shifts over a few inches to make room. He doesn't stop working the reins through his fingers, checking the leather by touch the way he checked the yoke pin.

At the news about the wizard he grunts.

"Bishop doesn't rest easy," he says. "He'd be bored if he did." He looks down at the dun ox, who is swinging his head at the red ox two wagons ahead and grumbling. "Mind, I'll sleep better. That's one of us."

James sets the crossbow across his knees with the bolt case at his hip. From the box the view is good. He can see the tailboard and the stacked canvas behind him, the yard gate and the street past it, and both edges of the lane where the wheels will run. The cat doesn't wait to be asked. It goes up the back wheel and onto the canvas, walks the length of the iron, and settles on top of the load just behind James's shoulder, facing backward. Its ears point south.

The hitching takes most of what's left of the hour. The red ox finally lets them chain it, after one more long pause to think about it. Dace jumps down from the second wagon, coils the spare rope and gives James a nod and a grin as he passes. The red-faced guard climbs up beside the third driver with a loaf from Hulda's basket under his arm. Hagen walks the line from front to back, once. He checks a trace chain on the grey, says a word to Dace that wipes the grin off for a moment, and stops at the last wagon. He looks up at James on the box and at the crossbow across his knees. He looks at the cat on the canvas. He says nothing, nods once, and walks back to the lead wagon.

A little after half past ten Ostrand climbs onto the first box and lifts his hand. The grey leans into the yoke on its new shoe. One by one the wagons go, iron creaking against iron under the canvas. Orrin clicks his tongue. Mutton opens his eyes and steps off, and Bishop has to follow and pretend it was his idea.

They roll out of the Lantern and Anvil's yard into the street. The forges are going hard now, and the heat comes out of the open doors as they pass. A smith's boy runs alongside the wagons for a while to look at the oxen. Up the hill to the right, the Song of the Morning catches the full sun on its roof. Then Beregost thins to fences again, the fences to fields, and the Trade Way opens out north. It's wide, rutted and pale with dust, and there's grass on both verges.

Behind them the road runs back toward the town, empty except for a farm cart a long way off and a dog trotting along the ditch on business of its own. The ditches on both sides are shallow, with nettles and dock leaves in them. Nothing moves in them that shouldn't.

Orrin puts a fresh straw in his mouth and settles into the jolt of the box like a man settling into a chair he's sat in for thirty years.

"Mutton's pace," he says. "Get used to it. You'll be seeing that dog for a while yet."

 (Out of game: there was nothing to roll there. James was only telling Ostrand and Orrin what Thalantyr had already said, and Thalantyr's findings can't be looked at until his letter reaches the Friendly Arm. The caravan gets there tomorrow evening at the earliest.)

place.name: Trade Way north of Beregost

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“I’ve marched behind worse commanders than Mutton.”

I settle into the journey, keeping my attention on the road behind us and both ditches. I leave the cat to watch from its perch and keep conversation light enough not to distract either Orrin or me from our work.
turns.reply:
Orrin works the straw over to the other side of his mouth and looks at Mutton's slow brown rump for a while.

"Mutton never lost a wagon," he says. "Never got a man killed. Never once had an idea." He thinks about it. "Better than most I've seen, then."

After that he talks the way the road goes. A word now and then, mostly about the oxen, and long stretches of nothing. He seems to like it that way.

The Trade Way runs north through stubble fields and then rough pasture, with sheep scattered over it like dropped laundry. The dust rises off the wheels in front, and by noon it has settled into the folds of James's cloak. Behind them the road stays wide, pale and dull. The farm cart turns off at a gate within the first hour. The dog lasts longer, then gives up and trots home.

About midday a courier in Fist red comes up from the south at a canter. He passes the last wagon close enough for James to smell the horse, then the whole line, and doesn't look at any of them. A little later a party of six pilgrims comes the other way. They wear Lathander's rose-and-gold, and they walk with staves and sing something about the dawn, a little out of tune. One of them raises a hand to Orrin, and Orrin raises a finger off the reins. Bishop shouts at them, and they don't sing any louder.

The ditches give James nothing. There are nettles and dock leaves, a heron that lifts off a wet patch and flaps away, and once a hare that sits up, looks at the wagon and decides against it. Through the cat's eyes the road behind looks the same, only lower and sharper. The cat doesn't move from its post on the canvas all afternoon, except once. When the line halts at a stream ford to water the teams, it goes down the wheel into the long grass and comes back a few minutes later licking its mouth. It climbs back to its place facing south as if it had never left.

The sun is going down red over the country toward the sea when Ostrand lifts his hand at the front of the line. The camp place is one the caravans clearly know: a flat bit of turf west of the road with a beech hedge for a windbreak, a ring of fire-blackened stones, and a spring trickling out of a bank into a stone trough somebody set there long ago. The wagons come round into a loose square with the oxen inside it. Orrin climbs down from the box in stages, like a man going down a ladder, and goes straight to Mutton's yoke.

Supper is the same for everyone, as Ostrand promised. It's barley and bacon out of one pot, with the last of Hulda's loaves. The red-faced guard eats two bowls and starts on a third. Ostrand eats with his ledger open on his knee and writes in it between spoonfuls.

When the bowls are wiped, Dace takes his deck out by the fire. He doesn't deal. He just shuffles, the cards purring through his fingers in the firelight, and looks at nobody in particular. The red-faced guard and one of the drovers drift over to him anyway.

Hagen comes round the square once more, checking each wagon's chocks with his boot. He stops by the last wagon, where James has laid out his bedroll against the wheel.

"Dace and Bram have first watch," he says. He tips his head at the red-faced guard. That's Bram, then. "I'll wake you at midnight. You and me till the fourth hour."

He looks at the cat, which has moved from the canvas to the top of the tailboard and is facing south into the dark.

"Sleep, if you can," he says, and goes to his own blankets.

By the fire the cards keep purring.

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“Midnight. Understood.”

I check that my crossbow and rod are within reach, then settle into my bedroll with my back to the card game. I rub the cat behind the ears if it permits.

“Wake me if something needs waking for,” I murmur, and try to get some sleep before my watch.
turns.reply:
The cat lets him. It sits on the tailboard facing south, and when James reaches up it pushes its head into his fingers, once and hard, the way cats do when they've decided to allow something. It allows it for a few breaths. Then it pulls away and turns back to the dark, ears forward, tail hanging down over the edge of the board.

The crossbow lies along the bedroll by his right hand with the bolt case beside it. The rod is under the fold of his cloak where his left hand can find it. The wheel at his back is still warm from the day's sun.

Behind him the cards purr and slap. Bram groans once and the drover laughs. After a while Dace says, "That's me square, then," in the voice of a man who isn't. Then the fire settles, and a pot gets scraped. Hagen's blankets rustle somewhere across the square. The oxen shift and breathe in the middle of the wagons, slow and heavy. Mutton chews in his sleep. Bishop grumbles at nothing. The beech hedge ticks in a small wind off the sea, and the spring keeps running into its trough.

James sleeps.

A hand on his shoulder wakes him. It doesn't shake him. It just rests there, heavy, until his eyes open.

Hagen is crouched by the wheel with the fire low and red behind him. The sky has cleared, and the stars are thick over the hedge. The air smells of dew and dead ash, and it's cold now. Hagen takes his hand away as soon as he sees James is awake. He doesn't say "midnight." He doesn't need to.

Over by the fire Dace is handing over his watch to nobody in particular, standing up and stretching.

"Quiet," he says, through a yawn. "Fox along the hedge, twice. Cart went by about the tenth hour, southbound, didn't stop." He jerks a thumb at Bram, who has already rolled himself into his blanket like a sausage in a crust. "And he ate the bread we were saving for breakfast. So that's the worst of it."

"I was hungry," says the blanket.

Hagen doesn't look at either of them. He waits until Dace has gone to his own bedroll, then speaks low, to James.

"Hedge side's yours. Road's mine. We walk the square once an hour, opposite ways, meet at the trough." He looks at the cat on the tailboard, then at James's hands as they come out of the blanket. "Fire stays low. Don't look into it."

He straightens up and goes toward the road side of the camp without waiting. His shape is a darker piece of the dark against the stars.

The cat hasn't moved all night, by the look of it. It still faces south, down the pale line of the Way.

 (Out of game: all three happened last turn, and none needed a roll.)
1) James laid the crossbow along his bedroll by his right hand, with the bolt case beside it, and put the rod under the fold of his cloak where his left hand could reach it. Putting your own gear within reach can't fail.
2) The cat allowed the scratch. It pushed its head into his fingers for a few breaths, then went back to watching south. Your familiar was willing, so there was nothing to roll.
3) James fell asleep by the wheel and slept until Hagen woke him at midnight. Nothing disturbed the camp, so sleep wasn't in doubt.
