turns.message:
I rise quietly, pull my cloak close, and take up my crossbow with the rod secure at my belt.

Through our familiar bond, I ask the cat to alert me if it notices anyone approaching, then take the hedge side as ordered. I keep clear of the firelight and listen as well as look, watching the hedge and the ground beyond the wagons as I begin my first circuit.
turns.reply:
James gets up without a sound. The Boots of Elvenkind make nothing of the turf. The cold gets in under his cloak at once, and he pulls it close at the throat. He takes the crossbow from beside the bedroll and settles the bolt case on his hip. The rod sits snug at his belt under the cloak's fold.

The cat on the tailboard doesn't turn when he asks it, mind to mind, to warn him of anyone coming. All he gets back is the feel of something already doing its job, a little put out at being told. Its ears stay pointed south.

He keeps away from the fire. Hagen is right about it: even banked low it pulls at the eye, and one look into the coals would cost him the dark for a long count. He works along the inside of the square in the wagons' shadow, then out to the gap between the last wagon and the hedge.

The beech hedge is a black wall against the stars, about the height of a man and a half. Its dead leaves keep their rattle in the small wind off the sea, so the whole length of it ticks and whispers, and he has to listen past that. He hears the spring running into its trough. In the square the oxen breathe heavily, and Mutton grinds his teeth in his sleep. An owl calls once, a long way off over the fields to the east, and is quiet.

Past the end of the hedge the turf runs west, flat and grey under the starlight, to a dark line he takes for a ditch. Nothing stands on it.

Halfway along, the cat's senses brush against his own. A sharp musky reek reaches him through the cat's nose before he would ever have smelled it himself. When he looks with the cat's eyes the dark goes grey and clear. At the far end of the hedge, maybe a hundred and twenty feet off, a fox comes out of the roots and stops with one forepaw raised. It looks at the wagons and at the man in the cloak, and it decides against all of it. Then it's gone back into the hedge bottom, and the ticking leaves cover the sound of it. Dace's fox, the third time.

James finishes the circuit along the spring bank and comes round to the trough. The stone is wet and furred with moss, and the water spills over its lip into the grass.

Hagen is already there, a big dark shape with his back to the fire. He has his hands on the rim of the trough, and they're the only part of him that's moving. He's working the cold out of his fingers. He lets James come all the way up before he does anything else.

He says nothing for a while. The spring runs. Out on the road side the Way is a pale stripe going off north and south, empty.

Then he looks past James, over the wagons, at the small shape on the last tailboard, which is still facing south.

"What's it watching?"

note.text:
What worked best was the grounded atmosphere. Orrin and his oxen, Hulda’s brisk manner, Hagen watching my hands—those details made the caravan feel like people at work rather than a quest waiting for me. Their voices were distinct, and the humour fit the setting. I also appreciated that ordinary conversation and preparation didn’t require rolls, and that we could move through an uneventful day without manufacturing a fight.

The abandoned wagon was a good mystery. The physical clues gave me something to reason about, and consulting Thalantyr felt like a sensible choice with a real cost in gold and time. I had room to decide how James handled it.

What broke immersion most was the repeated out-of-game accounting of my previous actions. Explaining that walking, talking, packing, or petting a willing cat needed no roll wasn’t necessary, especially when I hadn’t questioned it. Those passages sometimes resembled debugging notes rather than play.

There were also mechanical inconsistencies:
- The Arcana roll used +4 even though the sheet says +3. It changed a failure into a success.
- The opening records changed some supplied character details, notably rapier proficiency and Healing Light’s per-use limit. Actual 2014 Celestial rules support the four-die limit, but discrepancies with the campaign sheet should be settled explicitly.
- The cat received apparent night vision, and James sometimes used its senses without my choosing to do so. That matters because sharing its senses blinds and deafens James to his own surroundings.

What I missed was a little more initiative from the world beyond the mystery and the card temptation. The cards were effective initially, but repeated shuffling and invitations risked making James’s weakness feel like a button being pressed. Likewise, the cat’s constant southward attention became ominous without giving me much actionable information. If those were deliberate clues, I wanted a clearer opportunity to investigate them.

Overall, I enjoyed the quiet, practical start and would continue. Keep the strong NPCs, meaningful choices, and restrained pacing; tighten the rules bookkeeping, leave James’s sensory choices to me, and drop the unsolicited explanations of why routine actions didn’t need rolls.

after.text:
Yes—when Ostrand gave us a few hours before departure, I wanted to visit the Song of the Morning. James had just sworn off another invitation to cards, and a quiet visit to a temple felt like a chance to explore what serving Tymora means to him outside a crisis.

I followed the disc instead because it seemed potentially dangerous to everyone travelling with us, and the departure deadline made that feel more urgent. That was a reasonable consequence of the situation, not something you blocked—but it meant James’s first free morning became an investigation before I’d explored much of his personal life.

opening.text:
Dawn finds its way through the gaps in the shutters and lays thin gold lines across the floorboards. Somewhere down the street a hammer strikes iron, then another joins it. Beregost's forges are waking. Over the rooftops, the bells of the Morninglord's temple roll out their slow greeting to the sun.

The cat is already up. It sits on the windowsill with its tail curled around its paws, watching the street below with keen interest. Now and then it turns to look at you, as if wondering why you are still in bed.

Your purse lies where you left it, heavy with about three hundred and fifty gold from that last hand. The road to Baldur's Gate runs north past the window. Nobody expects you anywhere today.

From below come the smell of frying bacon and the scrape of benches. Under that is a sound you would know anywhere: cards being shuffled and slapped down on wood, and a rough laugh. "Raise you two silver, and may Tymora weep for you!"

Then three brisk knocks at your door. "Master Worgen?" It is a woman's voice, the innkeeper's. "Breakfast's on, if you want it. And I need to know whether you're keeping the room another night, or whether I let it to the caravan folk who came in late."

The cat's ears twitch toward the door. The latch waits.

The session begins.

Morning finds you before you find it: a thin bar of light through the shutters, the clang of the first forge hammer somewhere down the street, and the slow bronze voice of Lathander's bells rolling over the rooftops of Beregost. The room above the Lantern and Anvil smells of old timber, cold ashes and fresh bread drifting up the stairs.

Your cat sits on the windowsill, tail curled neatly around its paws, watching you with the patience of a creature that has been awake for hours. Beside it, face up on the sill, lies a playing card: the queen of coins, its edges soft with handling. Your own deck is where you left it. This card is not from it, and it was not there last night.

From the yard below comes the rattle of dice in a cup, a burst of laughter and someone cursing their luck. A knock sounds at the door, and a young woman's voice calls through it: "Master Worgen? Hot water, if you want it, and there's porridge and sausages downstairs while they last."

The purse is heavy, the day is empty, and the queen of coins looks up at you from the windowsill. What do you do?

"Two sausages," the girl's voice says through the door, cheerful and businesslike. "I'll tell Mam to hide them from the carters. Water's by the door, Master Worgen." Her footsteps go on down the passage, and a knock sounds at the next room.

You get up and dress. The floorboards are cold. You hang Tymora's coin on its cord around your neck, where it rests warm against your breastbone like it always does, and you slide the rod into your belt on the left so it comes out clean. Then you go to the window.

Whisker watches you come. When you ask your question, the cat holds your gaze for a long moment and then yawns, wide and pink and unbothered. Through the thread between you comes no answer in words, because a cat doesn't have any. What comes is an impression: dark and warm, the smell of pipe smoke, spilled wine and tallow. The underside of a table. Men's boots shifting near your whiskers. Something flat and stiff on the floorboards that smells strongly of a man's hand, and the satisfaction of carrying it off in your mouth. Then the impression is gone, and Whisker starts washing a paw.

You pick the card up by its edges. It isn't from any cheap tavern deck. The card is thick and heavy, the paint on it is good, and the corners have been rounded by years of shuffling. The queen wears a high stiff collar in the Amnian style, and on her palm she holds a coin stamped with a little ship. The back is deep green with a gilt border of twisting vine scrollwork, worn dull where a thousand thumbs have pushed it across a table.

Your own deck is in the coat on the chair. You count it quickly, the way you used to count before every game: all there. Your queen of coins is a plain Baldurian woodcut lady with a coin and a sour face, nothing like this one. They're from different decks, made by different hands.

You tilt the stranger's card toward the bar of light from the shutters and look at the back the way an old player looks at a back.

The common room is half full and loud. Carters sit hunched over bowls along the long table by the door, a pair of journeymen in leather aprons gulp porridge standing up, and Marta's mother, a broad woman with flour to the elbows, works the hatch from the kitchen. Most of the room has been wiped down already. One table hasn't. It's the round one in the corner by the cold hearth, set a little apart. It still carries rings of dried wine, a clay pipe with a cracked stem, and three tallow stubs burned down to puddles. The bench has been pushed back crooked, as if someone left in a hurry or a temper.

Whisker goes straight to it, slips under, sits down in the exact middle of the floor beneath and looks up at James through the chair legs. *Here.* The smell comes over the bond, stale and sharp.

Only one man in the room looks like he slept badly: a heavy carter at the end of the long table with grey stubble and red eyes, holding his head in one hand and his spoon in the other, and not eating.

Marta comes past with a stack of bowls on her hip. She sees James and nods at the hatch. "Two sausages, under the cloth. Mam nearly gave them to Garric."

Then he asks his question, and she shifts the bowls and gives the corner table a sour look.

"That one, aye. Went on past midnight. Master Ammarin, the southern gentleman in the front room upstairs. He plays with his own cards, always does. Green ones with gold on, like you said. Garric over there sat in, and Brannoc's lad from the smithy, and a sellswordy woman passing through. Lad lost his whole week. Mam had to put them out at the end." She lowers her voice a little. "Master Ammarin was down already this morning, before you. He asked had the floor been swept yet. Mam told him not that corner. He said he'd be back down after he'd dressed."

She's already moving toward the carters with the bowls. "Sausages are going cold, Master Worgen."

"Ten," she says. "Count 'em if you like. Garric'll live." She's already turning back to the pot before you can answer.

Marta goes past with an empty tray, and you press a silver piece into her hand. She closes her fist around it and grins. "I'll tell her it was heroism. She'll pretend she didn't hear, and then she'll tell everyone." Then she's off to the carters with the bread basket.

You take the bowl, the two sausages, which are still warm under the cloth, and a heel of bread to a small table against the wall. From there you can see the corner table on your right and the foot of the stairs straight ahead. You sit with your back to the plaster and eat slowly. Whisker stays under the round table a moment longer, as if to show he's coming because he wants to. Then he comes over, sits down by your boot and takes the sausage skin from your fingers neatly. When you tell him to look innocent, he wraps his tail around his paws, half-closes his eyes and stares at the far wall like a cat who has never seen a playing card in his life.

The carters finish one by one and go out into the yard to their teams. The journeymen leave too. Garric stays, gets about three spoonfuls into his porridge, then pushes the bowl away and sits staring at the corner table. He doesn't look like a man remembering a fun night.

The bells of Lathander have gone quiet and half the room has emptied by the time a step sounds on the stairs.

The man coming down is about fifty, lean, and dressed for a better town than Beregost. He wears a dark plum coat buttoned high to a stiff collar, and his grey beard is cut close and sharp along the jaw. There's a ring on each hand, gold on the left and a dark stone on the right. He doesn't hurry. He nods to Mistress Hollin at the hatch, says something low that you don't catch, and she points her ladle at the corner without looking up.

Master Ammarin goes to the round table. He doesn't drop to his knees at once. First he moves the crooked bench and sets it straight, as if he's tidying up. Then he crouches, one hand on the table's edge, and looks underneath. He takes his time. His eyes follow the gaps between the floorboards and the gap where the wall meets the floor, then the space under the cold hearth's lip. He slides two fingers along a crack. He checks under the tallow puddles on the tabletop as well, lifting each stub with a fingernail.

You've seen men look for a dropped card before. Most of them glance under the table, curse, and buy a new deck at the next market, because any town on the Trade Way sells cards. A man who plays with his own deck minds more than that, and a fine old deck isn't cheap. But this man is going over the floor plank by plank, and you've only ever seen that done for something that can't be bought again.

He straightens and brushes off his knees. For a moment his face is quite still. Then he smooths it back into ease, turns, and finds you looking at him. It's only a glance, polite and passing. Then his eyes go to the cat at your boot.

He crosses the room to your table and gives you a small bow from the neck, the southern way.

"Good morning, sir. Forgive me for interrupting your breakfast." His Common is careful, softened by an Amnian accent. "A foolish matter. I lost a card from my deck last night, there under the table. It's worth nothing to anyone but me. The deck was my late wife's, and it isn't the same with a card missing." He smiles at Whisker as if they've been introduced. "The lady of the house tells me the corner hasn't been swept. And cats do like to carry things off, I find. Is he yours? I don't suppose he's brought you any presents this morning?"

Garric, at the end of the long table, has lifted his head and is watching the two of you.

Ammarin looks at the card under your palm, then at your face, and for a moment he says nothing. Then he laughs quietly, the laugh of a man who has been caught being too proper.

"Fifty-two. Yes, of course. You are a careful man, sir. I respect that."

He unbuttons the top of the plum coat and takes out a small packet wrapped in green silk from an inside pocket on the left. He unfolds the silk on the wood, lifts the deck out and spreads it face up across the table in one stroke. It's a long, even arc, every card showing the same sliver of edge. You've seen that spread a thousand times, and only from men who deal for a living. A traveller who plays now and then for fun pushes the cards out in clumps. This spread came from practice.

The backs are against the wood and the faces are turned to the room. Kings, queens, knaves and pips, all painted by the same good hand. The coins wear the little ship, the cups are chased with grapes, the swords have Amnian hilts. You count them the old way, by suit and then by rank, without moving your lips. There are fifty-one cards. Three queens are there: cups, swords and staves. There is no queen of coins, and there's no second card where she should be. It's a fine old deck that is short one card, just as he said.

Garric counts too, slower, his thick forefinger hovering a hair above each card, his lips moving. He loses his place at the staves, frowns and starts the staves again. When he reaches the end he straightens up.

"Fifty-one."

"Fifty-one," Ammarin agrees. He folds his hands on the table again, rings still, and turns to you. "Sir, if you would. Then she is home, and Master Garric can count to fifty-two, and Mistress Hollin can sweep her corner."

Garric doesn't move away. He's looking at your hand flat on the table, and at the green back of the card that shows at the edges of your fingers. The morning light from the window falls across it.

On the third nudge the inside of the band comes round to the light.

James bends low. The engraving is small and the lines are fine. A thumb has polished the silver for nine years, but it never reached inside the band, and the cut is still sharp. It's a leaf, the same three-lobed vine leaf that runs along the border of every card in the deck. Inside the leaf is an eye. It's a single curved line for the lid with five tiny strokes below it for lashes, and the eye is shut.

There are no letters, no date and no name. Just the leaf and the closed eye, cut by a hand that took great care over something nobody would ever see unless the ring came off.

While he looks, he reaches along the thread to Whisker, quietly.

The answer comes back slowly, the way a cat does everything. First comes the smell of the man who wore it: skin, old sweat, pomade, the brass tang of silver. That part is plain and dull. Then the cat's attention narrows past the band to the stone, and the impression changes. The stone has no smell at all. Everything has a smell, the table and the wax and the wood and the dust, and the stone has none. To the cat it's like a hole cut in the world exactly that size. With that comes a fierce, simple wanting: to put a paw on it, to bat it off the table, to carry it away somewhere dark and sit on it. It's the same satisfaction he felt carrying the card up the stairs last night, only stronger. Then the impression thins out. Whisker hasn't moved on the bench. His eyes haven't left the ring.

Garric leans in enough to see what James is looking at.

"An eye," he says. "Shut."

Ammarin answers the question while James is still bent over the band. He doesn't haggle, and he doesn't wait to be asked twice.

"Teodor Vasse." He says the name like a man paying a debt he'd hoped to put off. "He kept the tables at a house called the Ivy Door, on the near side of the Bridge, where the moneychangers' street comes down to the river. A respectable house, as such houses go. The Council's men played there." He looks at the ring lying in the candlelight and doesn't reach for it. "He sold me the pair for four hundred gold. I paid it gladly, and I made it back inside a year. That is the whole of what I know about Teodor, except that he was a careful man and never cheated anyone in his own house. Whether he is still there, I cannot tell you. I left Athkatla six years ago and I have not been back."

He pauses.

"And that eye, sir. I have looked at it more nights than I would care to count. I asked him once what it meant. He said it was the maker's, and that the maker was not a man to go looking for. I took it for a dealer's joke." His bare hands stay folded. "I have never been sure."

Outside, a cart rolls past the window and the light on the table shifts. Ammarin glances at the window, then back at you, and keeps quiet. He has given you the name, and he's waiting.

He pauses and picks his next words with care, as he does with everything. This time there's less polish on them.

"What happens to me. Nothing, sir. That's the honest answer, and I have thought about it a great deal. He finds the girl, presses a silver piece into her hand for the sausages, and keeps his voice easy.

"Worth your while, as promised. Tell me something. Was there a card game in here last night after I went up? A serious one, with a good southern deck, green backs and gilt edges? I'm not looking to play," he adds with a crooked smile, more to himself than to her. "Just curious who was."

James straightens up, puts both hands flat on the table well away from the silver, and is quiet for a moment.

"You have," he says. "So here's my answer, and I'll make it plain."

He taps the row of six face-down cards.

"The deck is yours. It's a pretty thing, and without that stone it's only pretty. Garric can let go of it." He nods to the carter. "But the queen of coins stays with me for now. She walked up my stairs on her own last night, more or less, and I'm superstitious about that sort of thing."

Then he looks at the ring, and at the pale band of skin on Ammarin's finger.

"As for the ring, I won't keep it, and I won't steal it off a man who's been honest with me for the last hour. But I won't put it back on your hand blind, either. You sat in a wine shop for an hour and couldn't stop thinking where it was. Nine years with it never off. And this morning the candle got brighter when you took it off." He shakes his head slowly. "Those are the words of a man describing a hook, Master Ammarin, not a keepsake."

He jerks his chin toward the door and the bells that rang this morning.

"The Song of the Morning is a few streets from here. Lathander's priests look at cursed things for a living. You come with me now, the ring rides in Garric's fist or in a dish, nobody's hand on it, and a priest looks at it. If they say it's clean, it goes straight back on your finger and I'll apologise in front of the altar. If they say it isn't, then you've lost nothing but an hour you'd have spent fretting anyway." He gives a crooked smile. "And on the way back I've a smith's lad to pay."

## Player's note: James Worgen, session 1 (Beregost, one morning)

### What worked

**The scene itself was excellent.** I came in with "no quest, the day is yours," and within twenty minutes of game time a single odd card on the windowsill had grown into a proper mystery. It ran from a cheating dealer to a reader deck to enchanted ink to a keyed ring to a maker's mark. Each step was earned at the table, never handed to me.

- **It played fair.** My failures stayed failures. The natural 1 upstairs gave me nothing. The missed Insight left me unsure whether the widow was real. The missed Arcana on the stone told me nothing. Successes gave clear, usable facts. I never felt the outcome was decided before I rolled.
- **The details paid off.** Ammarin's dealer's spread, the fold of the silk, the pale band on his finger, Garric gating the cat's paw with one finger, Mistress Hollin's "on the house, if it gets him gone." The NPCs had their own wants and timing. The sellsword had already left on the north road without me, and that's the world running on its own.
- **Whisker was exactly right.** Speaking only in impressions (smell, wanting, "a hole cut in the world") is a lovely way to give a familiar a voice. It also left what the cat really is open.
- **The GM took my flags seriously.** When the deck's label leaked "marked," the GM owned it and corrected it. I appreciated that.
- **Promises came out of my own throwaway lines.** "Worth your while," the lad's wages, and the sellsword's five gold all became tracked promises. That's a great feature.

### What broke

1. **Skill modifiers on the roll card.** Intimidation and Persuasion both showed **+4** in the header and the math, while the line under them said +7. The GM acknowledged this and promised +7 "from now on." The very next Persuasion card added +4 again. I'm guessing the server takes it from the combat profile's "skill modifier" field (the sheet note says "0, or 3 if refused") plus something, not from the skill line. The bug is in the system, not the narration, and the GM can't fix it by promising.
2. **The reroll button didn't work.** I pressed "Request an allowed reroll" twice and the card came back unchanged both times. The session then ended on that unresolved roll. That's the worst possible place for it to fail, since rerolls are a stated resource ("two per session").
3. **Turns sometimes didn't go through.** If I pressed a button with an out-of-game note attached, I often got "Nothing was sent: the turn waits for the card" and had to press again. Either buttons should accept a note, or the app should say clearly that it won't.
4. **Small record issues:**
   - The queen of cups was listed as "In the camp" while she sat on the table in front of me. The label explains it, but "camp" reads as mine.
   - The smith's lad's 1 gp 5 sp went straight into my own purse (350 gp 14 sp). It's a promise to deliver and should be tracked apart from my money.
   - The records say Healing Light is up to 4 dice at once, while my sheet says 5. That's worth checking.
   - The records correctly say I'm not proficient with the rapier (+2), while my sheet says +5. Here the records are right and my sheet was wrong.

### What was missing or could be better

- **The out-of-game notes got long.** The "none of these needed a roll, here's why" lists were repetitive by the third time. One line is enough.
- **The ending was abrupt.** The session stopped mid-roll, with Ammarin's answer, the trip to the temple and the ring all hanging. A cliffhanger is fine, but not one caused by a broken button.
- **Tymora went unmentioned.** My patron is the whole premise. A queen of coins on the sill reads like her hand, and I'd guess that's intended. One small nod from the coin at my throat, warmer at the right moment, would have tied the hook to my character.

**Overall:** the storytelling was strong and the dice felt honest. Fix the skill-modifier source and the reroll button and I'd happily keep playing this exact thread.

Yes, three of them.

**1. Touching the coin and asking Tymora.** This is the big one. When the queen turned up on my sill, and again when the ring came off, I wanted James to close his hand around the coin at his throat and quietly ask, *"Is this yours? Is this the job?"* I didn't, for two reasons:
- I didn't know how this table handles patron contact. Can I ask at all, or would I be putting words in the goddess's mouth that the GM hadn't planned for?
- It felt like asking for a hint. Everything else in the scene was earned by rolls, and I didn't want to short-circuit it.

A cue would have unlocked it, even just a line that the coin stayed warm. I'd also gladly have rolled Religion for it.

**2. Letting Whisker have the ring.** When the cat felt that "fierce, simple wanting" to bat it off the table and carry it somewhere dark, part of me wanted to let him. James has a cat whose nature is undecided, and the cat is the one who found the card in the first place. Maybe he's the goddess's hand, and maybe he knows something. I put my boot between them instead, because a soldier's caution said not to let anything touch an unknown magic object. It was the right in-character call, but I suspect it was the less interesting one. I'm still wondering what would have happened.

**3. Leaning into the cards.** When Ammarin spread that deck in one perfect arc, the honest James reaction is a flicker of hunger: wanting to pick it up, feel the weight, shuffle it once just to see. That's his stated weakness. I played him as purely professional instead. I worried that if I roleplayed the temptation myself, I'd be inviting trouble the GM hadn't set up, and that it would derail a scene that was going well. In hindsight, one line of James's fingers itching would have been free character work and cost nothing.

A smaller, practical one: I wanted to **break off and go to Brannoc's smithy** with the lad's money, or step outside to see who else was watching that window. The scene was good enough that I never left the common room, and "the day is yours" turned into "the morning at one table." I don't regret it, but I noticed it.

There's also a mechanical one: a few times I wanted to add a small action to a button press, such as a glance at Garric or a word to the cat. Because notes on button presses didn't go through, I dropped them rather than send twice.

James sits up slowly, rubs his face, and calls toward the door without getting up: "Hot water, yes, thank you. And save me two sausages, I'll make it worth your while."

Then he crosses to the windowsill, careful not to touch the card at first. He looks at the cat, then the queen of coins, then back at the cat.

"Did you bring that in, or did she?"

He picks up the card by its edges and turns it over to check the back: the pattern, any marks or writing, whose deck it might come from. Then he checks his own deck is all there and pulls out his queen of coins to compare the two.

*(While dressing I hang the coin of Tymora on its cord around my neck and slide the Rod of the Pact Keeper into my belt where I can draw it, so it's on me rather than in the pack.)*
turns.reply:
"Two sausages," the girl's voice says through the door, cheerful and businesslike. "I'll tell Mam to hide them from the carters. Water's by the door, Master Worgen." Her footsteps go on down the passage, and a knock sounds at the next room.

You get up and dress. The floorboards are cold. You hang Tymora's coin on its cord around your neck, where it rests warm against your breastbone like it always does, and you slide the rod into your belt on the left so it comes out clean. Then you go to the window.

Whisker watches you come. When you ask your question, the cat holds your gaze for a long moment and then yawns, wide and pink and unbothered. Through the thread between you comes no answer in words, because a cat doesn't have any. What comes is an impression: dark and warm, the smell of pipe smoke, spilled wine and tallow. The underside of a table. Men's boots shifting near your whiskers. Something flat and stiff on the floorboards that smells strongly of a man's hand, and the satisfaction of carrying it off in your mouth. Then the impression is gone, and Whisker starts washing a paw.

You pick the card up by its edges. It isn't from any cheap tavern deck. The card is thick and heavy, the paint on it is good, and the corners have been rounded by years of shuffling. The queen wears a high stiff collar in the Amnian style, and on her palm she holds a coin stamped with a little ship. The back is deep green with a gilt border of twisting vine scrollwork, worn dull where a thousand thumbs have pushed it across a table.

Your own deck is in the coat on the chair. You count it quickly, the way you used to count before every game: all there. Your queen of coins is a plain Baldurian woodcut lady with a coin and a sour face, nothing like this one. They're from different decks, made by different hands.

You tilt the stranger's card toward the bar of light from the shutters and look at the back the way an old player looks at a back.

You turn it this way and that, but the gilt throws the morning light back into your eyes, and the vines twist into one another until the pattern swims. Nothing stands out. No pinholes, no nicks in the edge, no ink. As far as you can tell it's a fine old southern card, well loved and long used. It doesn't tell you whose hand it came from.

From below come the clatter of bowls and a man's voice calling for more bread. The water steams in its jug by the door. Whisker has finished the paw and started on an ear.

 Your search comes to nothing. Even after a long, careful look at the back of the card, James Worgen, who once read decks for a living, can't find anything on it. Whatever this card might know, it isn't telling you this morning.

You put it down on the sill beside the cat. Downstairs a bench scrapes and someone laughs, and the smell of sausages comes up through the floorboards.

James splashes his face with the hot water, runs wet fingers through his hair and shaves badly. He tucks the stranger's queen into the inside pocket of his coat, on the opposite side from his own deck. He doesn't want the two mixing.

"Under a table, then," he says to Whisker. "Pipe smoke and wine. Somebody's game, and somebody's short a queen. Come on. You can show me which table."

He goes down to the common room with the cat at his heels. On the way he looks the room over the way a scout would: which tables are still crowded from last night, which have spilled wine or a cold pipe left on them, who looks short on sleep and in a bad mood.

He finds the girl, presses a silver piece into her hand for the sausages, and keeps his voice easy.

"Worth your while, as promised. Tell me something. Was there a card game in here last night after I went up? A serious one, with a good southern deck, green backs and gilt edges? I'm not looking to play," he adds with a crooked smile, more to himself than to her. "Just curious who was."

*(Out of game: −1 sp for the girl's tip. Whisker's impression was a table, so I'm watching for any table that matches it: smoke, wine, tallow.)*
turns.reply:
The water is still hot enough to sting. James shaves by feel, nicks himself under the jaw and gives up before he has finished the chin. The stranger's queen goes into the inside pocket on the right, his own deck stays on the left, and the coat sits a little heavier on one side than the other.

Whisker drops off the sill without being asked and pads down the stairs ahead of him, tail up.

The common room is half full and loud. Carters sit hunched over bowls along the long table by the door, a pair of journeymen in leather aprons gulp porridge standing up, and Marta's mother, a broad woman with flour to the elbows, works the hatch from the kitchen. Most of the room has been wiped down already. One table hasn't. It's the round one in the corner by the cold hearth, set a little apart. It still carries rings of dried wine, a clay pipe with a cracked stem, and three tallow stubs burned down to puddles. The bench has been pushed back crooked, as if someone left in a hurry or a temper.

Whisker goes straight to it, slips under, sits down in the exact middle of the floor beneath and looks up at James through the chair legs. *Here.* The smell comes over the bond, stale and sharp.

Only one man in the room looks like he slept badly: a heavy carter at the end of the long table with grey stubble and red eyes, holding his head in one hand and his spoon in the other, and not eating.

Marta comes past with a stack of bowls on her hip. She sees James and nods at the hatch. "Two sausages, under the cloth. Mam nearly gave them to Garric."

Then he asks his question, and she shifts the bowls and gives the corner table a sour look.

"That one, aye. Went on past midnight. Master Ammarin, the southern gentleman in the front room upstairs. He plays with his own cards, always does. Green ones with gold on, like you said. Garric over there sat in, and Brannoc's lad from the smithy, and a sellswordy woman passing through. Lad lost his whole week. Mam had to put them out at the end." She lowers her voice a little. "Master Ammarin was down already this morning, before you. He asked had the floor been swept yet. Mam told him not that corner. He said he'd be back down after he'd dressed."

She's already moving toward the carters with the bowls. "Sausages are going cold, Master Worgen."

---

*Out of game: your purse is all gold (350 gp, no silver), so the silver piece can't come out of it as written. I've held the tip back for now and the promise is still open. Tell me if you'd rather give her a gold piece, or ask her mother to break one at the hatch.*

James goes to the hatch first and slides a gold piece across the sill to Marta's mother.

"Morning. Could you break that for me? Silver, if you have it." When the coins come back he takes them, catches Marta as she passes back with an empty tray, and presses one into her hand. "As promised. And thank your mam for guarding the sausages from Garric. That was heroism."

He takes his bowl, the two sausages and a heel of bread, and doesn't sit at the long table. He picks a small table along the wall, close enough to the corner table to watch it, with a clear view of the stairs. He sits with his back to the wall, the way he always does, and starts eating slowly.

Whisker stays where he is under the round table for a moment. Then James clicks his tongue softly and the cat comes over to sit by his boot. James drops him a piece of sausage skin.

"Good work," he murmurs. "Now we wait for the gentleman to come and look for what you stole. Try to look innocent."

He doesn't take out the card. He keeps his eye on the stairs and on Garric, and eats.

*(Out of game: I break 1 gp into 10 sp at the hatch and give Marta 1 sp. That leaves 349 gp and 9 sp. I'm waiting for Ammarin to come down and won't approach anyone yet.)*
turns.reply:
Mistress Hollin takes the gold piece in floury fingers, turns it once to look at the stamp, and drops it into an apron pocket. A moment later ten silver pieces come back across the sill in a little white-dusted heap.

"Ten," she says. "Count 'em if you like. Garric'll live." She's already turning back to the pot before you can answer.

Marta goes past with an empty tray, and you press a silver piece into her hand. She closes her fist around it and grins. "I'll tell her it was heroism. She'll pretend she didn't hear, and then she'll tell everyone." Then she's off to the carters with the bread basket.

You take the bowl, the two sausages, which are still warm under the cloth, and a heel of bread to a small table against the wall. From there you can see the corner table on your right and the foot of the stairs straight ahead. You sit with your back to the plaster and eat slowly. Whisker stays under the round table a moment longer, as if to show he's coming because he wants to. Then he comes over, sits down by your boot and takes the sausage skin from your fingers neatly. When you tell him to look innocent, he wraps his tail around his paws, half-closes his eyes and stares at the far wall like a cat who has never seen a playing card in his life.

The carters finish one by one and go out into the yard to their teams. The journeymen leave too. Garric stays, gets about three spoonfuls into his porridge, then pushes the bowl away and sits staring at the corner table. He doesn't look like a man remembering a fun night.

The bells of Lathander have gone quiet and half the room has emptied by the time a step sounds on the stairs.

The man coming down is about fifty, lean, and dressed for a better town than Beregost. He wears a dark plum coat buttoned high to a stiff collar, and his grey beard is cut close and sharp along the jaw. There's a ring on each hand, gold on the left and a dark stone on the right. He doesn't hurry. He nods to Mistress Hollin at the hatch, says something low that you don't catch, and she points her ladle at the corner without looking up.

Master Ammarin goes to the round table. He doesn't drop to his knees at once. First he moves the crooked bench and sets it straight, as if he's tidying up. Then he crouches, one hand on the table's edge, and looks underneath. He takes his time. His eyes follow the gaps between the floorboards and the gap where the wall meets the floor, then the space under the cold hearth's lip. He slides two fingers along a crack. He checks under the tallow puddles on the tabletop as well, lifting each stub with a fingernail.

You've seen men look for a dropped card before. Most of them glance under the table, curse, and buy a new deck at the next market, because any town on the Trade Way sells cards. A man who plays with his own deck minds more than that, and a fine old deck isn't cheap. But this man is going over the floor plank by plank, and you've only ever seen that done for something that can't be bought again.

He straightens and brushes off his knees. For a moment his face is quite still. Then he smooths it back into ease, turns, and finds you looking at him. It's only a glance, polite and passing. Then his eyes go to the cat at your boot.

He crosses the room to your table and gives you a small bow from the neck, the southern way.

"Good morning, sir. Forgive me for interrupting your breakfast." His Common is careful, softened by an Amnian accent. "A foolish matter. I lost a card from my deck last night, there under the table. It's worth nothing to anyone but me. The deck was my late wife's, and it isn't the same with a card missing." He smiles at Whisker as if they've been introduced. "The lady of the house tells me the corner hasn't been swept. And cats do like to carry things off, I find. Is he yours? I don't suppose he's brought you any presents this morning?"

Garric, at the end of the long table, has lifted his head and is watching the two of you.

 *(Out of game: I didn't roll any of these four because none of them had an uncertain outcome. All four already happened in the story. Mistress Hollin broke your gold piece into ten silver, you gave Marta one, you're sitting with your back to the wall with a view of the corner table and the stairs, and Whisker took the sausage skin. You now have 349 gp and 9 sp, and your promise to Marta is settled. Master Ammarin has asked you about the cat, so it's your move.)*

Ammarin's smile doesn't move when you say "widower." He takes the bench across from you, sitting the way a man does who is used to better chairs: back straight, coat-tails flicked aside, hands folded on the table where you can see them. The gold ring is on the left hand and the dark stone on the right. He sets them on the wood without fuss.

"Of course. You are quite right to ask." The answer comes at once. "The queen of coins. The back is green, a deep green, with a border of vines in gilt, worn thin at the corners. The queen wears a high collar in the old fashion, and the coin in her hand bears a little ship." He spreads his fingers a fraction. "My wife had a fondness for ships. It must have gone under the table when the lady of the house ended our game. There was some haste at the end."

At the end of the long table, Garric has put his spoon down.

You watch the man across from you while he talks, the way you used to watch a man across the felt when the pot got big.

You get nothing. His face is pleasant and tired, the face of a man who has had a bad morning over a small thing and is too well bred to make a fuss. His hands stay still on the table, and the rings don't turn. When he talks about his wife, his voice softens about as much as a man's does, no more and no less. Maybe he buried her, or maybe he has told that story at a hundred tables. You've sat across from men who could do either, and this time you can't tell which. If the card worries him, it doesn't reach his face.

What you do know is that he got every detail right: the collar, the vines, the thin gilt at the corners, the little ship. It's his card, or he has studied it very closely.

Garric pushes himself up from the long table with both hands. He comes over slowly, the way a big man moves the morning after, and stops at the end of your table. He smells of horse and last night's wine. He doesn't look at you. He looks at Ammarin.

"Card went missing," he says. His voice is thick and slow. "From that game."

"From my deck, Master Garric. It fell at the end, I think, when we were put out."

"At the end." Garric chews on it. "Or before."

Ammarin turns his head to look up at him, polite as a priest. "I'm sorry for your losses last night. Truly. The cards were cruel to everyone but me, and I know how that looks the next morning." He turns back to you before Garric can find his next words, and opens one hand on the table, palm up. "Sir, you've been very patient with a stranger. I would be glad to pay something for your cat's honesty, if he'll accept it. Two gold? For his trouble."

The card is still in your inside right pocket. Garric stays where he is with his thumbs hooked in his belt, and he is looking at your coat now.

*(Out of game: Insight 13 against 15, a miss. James can't tell whether the widower story is true or whether the man is worried about the card. All you can be sure of is that his description matches the card exactly.)*

 James's read on Ammarin fails. He gives the man's face the same long look he once gave opponents across the table, and he can't tell whether the late wife is grief or just a good story, or whether there's any fear behind the courtesy. Ammarin's hand stays open on the table, waiting.

turns.reply:
Ammarin looks at the card under your palm, then at your face, and for a moment he says nothing. Then he laughs quietly, the laugh of a man who has been caught being too proper.

"Fifty-two. Yes, of course. You are a careful man, sir. I respect that."

Garric bends over her with both fists on the table edge, close enough that you can smell the wine on him. He keeps his thumbs to himself.

Ammarin watches the card, and then you, and he hears the remark about Athkatla. You know dealers. You sat across from them for years, and you remember what a house man does with his face when someone names his house.

You see it. It's small and quick, and you've seen it a hundred times across the felt.

Being called a dealer doesn't trouble him. When you say "Athkatla," the corner of his mouth almost lifts. A man who has worked a good house is a little proud of it, and that's what crossed his face. The backs aren't the same, and they aren't meant to be. You know what this is. You saw it in Calimport and twice in Athkatla. Once, in a game near Zazesspur, you only learned it the morning after, with empty pockets. They're called readers. The man who inked the leaves knows the map: the place of the dark leaf gives the rank, the cluster gives the suit. From across the table, in candlelight, he can tell every card before it's turned. In this deck, he could tell what was coming off the top of the deck before he dealt it.

As James straightens, the dark stone moves.

Garric's hand comes down flat on the silk.

At the hatch, Mistress Hollin has stopped stirring.

Garric doesn't look at Ammarin. He looks at you.

It isn't hiding from everyone, though. Ink like that is worked to show itself to one particular sight, the way a lock is made for one key. A house dealer near the Bridge didn't lay it. Whoever did knew real craft, wizard's or artificer's work, and took their time over every leaf of fifty-two cards. The ink alone can't tell you what key it waits for.

When James straightens up, Ammarin is looking at the candle and not at him.

For a moment the gentleman doesn't move. Then he takes hold of the ring on his right hand with his left forefinger and thumb and works it slowly over the knuckle. It sticks, like a ring that hasn't been off in years. He lays it on the table beside Garric's fist, the way James asked.

Now that the ring is off his hand you can see it properly. The band is old silver, worn thin at the back where the palm presses it. The stone is cut flat and smooth, and in the candlelight it isn't black at all. It's a deep green-black, the same flat shade as the leaf you found in the sun. On the inside of the band, where it lies tilted toward the flame, something is engraved. It's too small to read from where you sit.

Ammarin folds his bare hands on the table. When he speaks his voice is just as pleasant as before.

"The queen of coins, sir."

Garric looks at the card under James's hand, then at Ammarin, then at James. It takes him a moment, and you can see him working it through.

"The queen of coins," he says slowly. "He watched you turn her over."

Ammarin says nothing to that. He sits with his ringless hands folded and looks at James. Whisker has stood up on the bench and is staring at the ring.

---

James lifts his hand off the queen. Garric looks down at the ring lying by his knuckles as though someone has handed him a horse to hold.

"Nobody touches it," he says. He slides his fist an inch closer to it. Whisker, on the bench, pushes one paw slowly across the wood toward the silver. Garric's other forefinger comes down in front of the paw without any fuss, like a gate closing. The cat looks at the finger, then at Garric, and sits back down. He doesn't stop staring at the ring.

James draws four cards out of the spread from under the edge of the silk. He doesn't look at their faces. He lays them with the queen of cups and turns his chair a quarter turn, so his shoulder stands between Ammarin and the table.

"Eyes shut, Master Ammarin. Hands where Garric can see them."

Ammarin shuts his eyes. He folds his bare hands on the table in front of him, the pale band of skin showing on his right finger where the ring has sat for nine years. James watches his eyelids long enough to be sure they don't flicker. Then he gathers the queen of coins in with the other five and mixes them low under his palm, slowly, the old way. The cards whisper against the wood. Garric's eyes try to follow and give up after the second pass. James lays the six out in a row in the candlelight, green backs up. They're six identical backs, gilt vines catching the little flame, and there's no dark leaf on any of them that anyone at this table can see.

"Open them. No ring. Find me the queen of coins. One try."

Ammarin opens his eyes.

His eyes don't go to any one card. They go to the row. They start at the left end and move slowly along all six backs, the way a man reads a line he can't make out, then come back again. On the second pass they slow over the fourth card and the fifth, as if the candlelight might give him something, and it doesn't. You've seen that look a thousand times across the felt, on men holding nothing who have to bet anyway.

He doesn't refuse, though. He's a player, and one chance in six is better than none. After a long breath he puts out one finger and touches the fourth card.

"That one, sir."

James turns it over. It's the seven of staves, painted by the same good hand, with Amnian vines winding up the staves.

Nobody says anything for a moment. The candle gutters and steadies.

"Seven," Garric says at last. He looks at the ring by his fist, and his jaw settles. "Not the queen."

Ammarin looks at the seven of staves. Then he leans back on the bench and unfolds his hands, and the polish comes off him for a moment. He looks like a tired man of fifty who has been up too late and lost.

"No," he says quietly. "Not the queen." He glances at the pale band of skin on his finger, then back up at you. "So you have it all now. The ink waits for the stone, and without it I'm only a man with a pretty deck." He breathes out through his nose. "The man near the Bridge sold me the two together. He said they were never to be parted. He didn't say why, and nine years ago I didn't think to ask."

His eyes go to the ring by Garric's fist, and stay there just a moment too long.

"Sir. I've paid back every coin, and I've failed your test in front of this whole house. The deck is worthless to anyone but me, and you know it. But the ring..." He stops and chooses his words. "I would ask for the ring back before anything else. Whatever you decide about my queens."

Whisker hasn't taken his eyes off the silver for a moment.

"Before anything else, you said." He keeps his voice mild. "That's the first thing you've asked for this morning that you actually wanted, Master Ammarin. So it's the last thing I'll decide."

He bends close to read the engraving. Out of the corner of his eye he watches Whisker, and he reaches along the thread between them, quietly, the way he'd touch a scout's shoulder in the dark: *What is it? What do you smell?*

Without looking up from the ring, he adds:

"And while I read, tell me the name of the man near the Bridge. The house too. A man who sells a deck and a stone together and says they're never to be parted didn't think he was selling a game."

*(Out of game: I'm turning the ring with the dish, not touching it with my hands, to read the inside of the band. I'm also asking Whisker over the bond what he senses from it. My hand stays clear of the cards in the row. Roll whatever you need for either.)*
turns.reply:
James slides the edge of the tin dish under the band and nudges it. The ring rocks and turns a little. The candle flame leans. He nudges again, a quarter turn at a time. Garric's fist stays where it is, an inch away, and the carter watches the dish move as if it might bite.

On the third nudge the inside of the band comes round to the light.

James bends low. The engraving is small and the lines are fine. A thumb has polished the silver for nine years, but it never reached inside the band, and the cut is still sharp. It's a leaf, the same three-lobed vine leaf that runs along the border of every card in the deck. Inside the leaf is an eye. It's a single curved line for the lid with five tiny strokes below it for lashes, and the eye is shut.

There are no letters, no date and no name. Just the leaf and the closed eye, cut by a hand that took great care over something nobody would ever see unless the ring came off.

While he looks, he reaches along the thread to Whisker, quietly.

The answer comes back slowly, the way a cat does everything. First comes the smell of the man who wore it: skin, old sweat, pomade, the brass tang of silver. That part is plain and dull. Then the cat's attention narrows past the band to the stone, and the impression changes. The stone has no smell at all. Everything has a smell, the table and the wax and the wood and the dust, and the stone has none. To the cat it's like a hole cut in the world exactly that size. With that comes a fierce, simple wanting: to put a paw on it, to bat it off the table, to carry it away somewhere dark and sit on it. It's the same satisfaction he felt carrying the card up the stairs last night, only stronger. Then the impression thins out. Whisker hasn't moved on the bench. His eyes haven't left the ring.

Garric leans in enough to see what James is looking at.

"An eye," he says. "Shut."

Ammarin answers the question while James is still bent over the band. He doesn't haggle, and he doesn't wait to be asked twice.

"Teodor Vasse." He says the name like a man paying a debt he'd hoped to put off. "He kept the tables at a house called the Ivy Door, on the near side of the Bridge, where the moneychangers' street comes down to the river. A respectable house, as such houses go. The Council's men played there." He looks at the ring lying in the candlelight and doesn't reach for it. "He sold me the pair for four hundred gold. I paid it gladly, and I made it back inside a year. That is the whole of what I know about Teodor, except that he was a careful man and never cheated anyone in his own house. Whether he is still there, I cannot tell you. I left Athkatla six years ago and I have not been back."

He pauses.

"And that eye, sir. I have looked at it more nights than I would care to count. I asked him once what it meant. He said it was the maker's, and that the maker was not a man to go looking for. I took it for a dealer's joke." His bare hands stay folded. "I have never been sure."

Outside, a cart rolls past the window and the light on the table shifts. Ammarin glances at the window, then back at you, and keeps quiet. He has given you the name, and he's waiting.

---

*(Out of game: I didn't need to roll for any of it. With time, a candle and the ring turned to the light, nothing about reading the engraving was uncertain, and Whisker's impression comes through the bond on its own. Ammarin gave the name freely. It's about five to ten.)*

James straightens slowly and sets the tin dish back down by the candle, well away from the ring. He looks at it a while longer before he speaks.

"A maker who signs on the inside where nobody looks, and shuts the eye he signs with." He rubs his thumb along his jaw, over the nick from his shave. "That isn't a dealer's joke, Master Ammarin. That's somebody who doesn't want to be seen watching."

He glances down at Whisker. The cat is still staring at the stone as if it owes him money. James moves his boot an inch along the bench, between the cat and the table, without making anything of it.

Then he looks back at Ammarin, and his voice is quieter, meant for the three of them and not for the hatch.

"You asked for the ring before the deck, before your name, before anything. So I'll ask you one honest question about it, and then I'll decide. Nine years on your finger. Have you had it off since? An hour, a night? And when you do take it off, what happens? To you, I mean. Not to the cards."

While he waits for the answer, he keeps his hands well clear of the silver and studies the flat green-black stone in the candlelight. He isn't looking at the band now. He's looking at the stone that, to Whisker, isn't there at all.

*(Out of game: I'm asking Ammarin what the ring does to him, and in the meantime I'm having a closer look at the stone with Arcana (+3). Still not touching it, and I'm keeping my boot between Whisker and the table. The two queens stay in the row of six, face down.)*
turns.reply:
James sets the tin dish down beside the candle, a hand's width from the silver. Whisker feels the boot slide along the bench between him and the table. He turns his head and looks at it for a long moment, offended in the quiet way cats are. Then he settles down with his front paws tucked under, his eyes still on the ring over the top of the boot.

Garric hears the bit about not wanting to be seen watching. He looks at the closed eye on the band, then up at the window, as if somebody might be standing in it.

Ammarin listens to the question and doesn't answer at once. He looks at the pale band of skin on his finger and rubs it once with his left thumb, the way a man feels for a tooth that has just come out.

"Off," he says. "Once. The first winter, in Crimmor. It had begun to pinch, so I took it to a jeweller to have the band let out. He held it for perhaps an hour. Then he brought it back to me unchanged. He said he would not cut it, that it was not a band for cutting, and he wouldn't take my money for the hour." A thin smile. "After that it stopped pinching, or I stopped noticing. It has not been off since. Not to wash, not to sleep. Nine years."

He pauses and picks his next words with care, as he does with everything. This time there's less polish on them.

"What happens to me. Nothing, sir. That's the honest answer, and I have thought about it a great deal. In Crimmor I sat in a wine shop across the street for that hour and could not have told you what I drank. I was not afraid. I only could not stop thinking where it was." He glances at the candle. "And this morning, since I laid it there, I would say the candle is brighter than it was. A small thing. I'm fifty, and I was up past midnight, so likely it's nothing."

He folds his bare hands again and waits.

James bends to the stone. This time he leaves the band alone and looks only at the flat green-black face, close enough to feel the candle's warmth on his cheek again.

He looks at it the way he looked at the ink and reaches with the same sense, the part of him that feels the coin warm at his throat.

He gets nothing. The flame sits on the polished face and slides off it, and under the shine the stone is just dark. There's no coolness and no draught from a door he can't see. Whatever was laid into the ink, he can't tell whether the stone holds the same thing, or a different thing, or anything at all. The coin at his throat stays as warm as ever, which tells him nothing either. As far as his eyes can say, it's a flat dark stone in an old silver band, and he has run out of ways to look at it without picking it up.

When he straightens, his back gives a small complaint from all the bending over tables this morning.

Garric hasn't moved his fist. Whisker hasn't moved his eyes. In the yard a wagon goes by and someone shouts at a horse, and Ammarin's gaze flicks to the window and back again.

"You said one question, sir, and then you'd decide," he says quietly. "I've answered it as truly as I can."

*(Out of game: Arcana 8 against 15, a miss. James can't learn anything more about the stone by looking at it, and he still hasn't touched it. It's about ten o'clock.)*

"You have," he says. "So here's my answer, and I'll make it plain."

He taps the row of six face-down cards.

"The deck is yours. It's a pretty thing, and without that stone it's only pretty. Garric can let go of it." He nods to the carter. "But the queen of coins stays with me for now. She walked up my stairs on her own last night, more or less, and I'm superstitious about that sort of thing."

"As for the ring, I won't keep it, and I won't steal it off a man who's been honest with me for the last hour. But I won't put it back on your hand blind, either. "Those are the words of a man describing a hook, Master Ammarin, not a keepsake."

He jerks his chin toward the door and the bells that rang this morning.

"The Song of the Morning is a few streets from here. Lathander's priests look at cursed things for a living. You come with me now, the ring rides in Garric's fist or in a dish, nobody's hand on it, and a priest looks at it. If they say it's clean, it goes straight back on your finger and I'll apologise in front of the altar. If they say it isn't, then you've lost nothing but an hour you'd have spent fretting anyway." He gives a crooked smile. "And on the way back I've a smith's lad to pay."

He glances at Garric. "You're welcome to walk with us, if you'd like to see it through."

note.text:
## Player's note: James Worgen, session 1 (Beregost, one morning)

### What worked

**The scene itself was excellent.** I came in with "no quest, the day is yours," and within twenty minutes of game time a single odd card on the windowsill had grown into a proper mystery. It ran from a cheating dealer to a reader deck to enchanted ink to a keyed ring to a maker's mark. Each step was earned at the table, never handed to me.

- **It played fair.** My failures stayed failures. The natural 1 upstairs gave me nothing. The missed Insight left me unsure whether the widow was real. The missed Arcana on the stone told me nothing. Successes gave clear, usable facts. I never felt the outcome was decided before I rolled.
- **The details paid off.** Ammarin's dealer's spread, the fold of the silk, the pale band on his finger, Garric gating the cat's paw with one finger, Mistress Hollin's "on the house, if it gets him gone." The NPCs had their own wants and timing. The sellsword had already left on the north road without me, and that's the world running on its own.
- **Whisker was exactly right.** Speaking only in impressions (smell, wanting, "a hole cut in the world") is a lovely way to give a familiar a voice. It also left what the cat really is open.
- **The GM took my flags seriously.** When the deck's label leaked "marked," the GM owned it and corrected it. I appreciated that.
- **Promises came out of my own throwaway lines.** "Worth your while," the lad's wages, and the sellsword's five gold all became tracked promises. That's a great feature.

### What broke

1. **Skill modifiers on the roll card.** Intimidation and Persuasion both showed **+4** in the header and the math, while the line under them said +7. The GM acknowledged this and promised +7 "from now on." The very next Persuasion card added +4 again. I'm guessing the server takes it from the combat profile's "skill modifier" field (the sheet note says "0, or 3 if refused") plus something, not from the skill line. The bug is in the system, not the narration, and the GM can't fix it by promising.
2. **The reroll button didn't work.** I pressed "Request an allowed reroll" twice and the card came back unchanged both times. The session then ended on that unresolved roll. That's the worst possible place for it to fail, since rerolls are a stated resource ("two per session").
3. **Turns sometimes didn't go through.** If I pressed a button with an out-of-game note attached, I often got "Nothing was sent: the turn waits for the card" and had to press again. Either buttons should accept a note, or the app should say clearly that it won't.
4. **Small record issues:**
   - The queen of cups was listed as "In the camp" while she sat on the table in front of me. The label explains it, but "camp" reads as mine.
   - The smith's lad's 1 gp 5 sp went straight into my own purse (350 gp 14 sp). It's a promise to deliver and should be tracked apart from my money.
   - The records say Healing Light is up to 4 dice at once, while my sheet says 5. That's worth checking.
   - The records correctly say I'm not proficient with the rapier (+2), while my sheet says +5. Here the records are right and my sheet was wrong.

### What was missing or could be better

- **The out-of-game notes got long.** The "none of these needed a roll, here's why" lists were repetitive by the third time. One line is enough.
- **The ending was abrupt.** The session stopped mid-roll, with Ammarin's answer, the trip to the temple and the ring all hanging. A cliffhanger is fine, but not one caused by a broken button.
- **Tymora went unmentioned.** My patron is the whole premise. A queen of coins on the sill reads like her hand, and I'd guess that's intended. One small nod from the coin at my throat, warmer at the right moment, would have tied the hook to my character.

**Overall:** the storytelling was strong and the dice felt honest. Fix the skill-modifier source and the reroll button and I'd happily keep playing this exact thread.

after.text:
Yes, three of them.

**1. Touching the coin and asking Tymora.** This is the big one. When the queen turned up on my sill, and again when the ring came off, I wanted James to close his hand around the coin at his throat and quietly ask, *"Is this yours? Is this the job?"* I didn't, for two reasons:
- I didn't know how this table handles patron contact. Can I ask at all, or would I be putting words in the goddess's mouth that the GM hadn't planned for?
- It felt like asking for a hint. Everything else in the scene was earned by rolls, and I didn't want to short-circuit it.

A cue would have unlocked it, even just a line that the coin stayed warm. I'd also gladly have rolled Religion for it.

**2. Letting Whisker have the ring.** When the cat felt that "fierce, simple wanting" to bat it off the table and carry it somewhere dark, part of me wanted to let him. James has a cat whose nature is undecided, and the cat is the one who found the card in the first place. Maybe he's the goddess's hand, and maybe he knows something. I put my boot between them instead, because a soldier's caution said not to let anything touch an unknown magic object. It was the right in-character call, but I suspect it was the less interesting one. I'm still wondering what would have happened.

**3. Leaning into the cards.** When Ammarin spread that deck in one perfect arc, the honest James reaction is a flicker of hunger: wanting to pick it up, feel the weight, shuffle it once just to see. That's his stated weakness. I played him as purely professional instead. I worried that if I roleplayed the temptation myself, I'd be inviting trouble the GM hadn't set up, and that it would derail a scene that was going well. In hindsight, one line of James's fingers itching would have been free character work and cost nothing.

A smaller, practical one: I wanted to **break off and go to Brannoc's smithy** with the lad's money, or step outside to see who else was watching that window. The scene was good enough that I never left the common room, and "the day is yours" turned into "the morning at one table." I don't regret it, but I noticed it.

There's also a mechanical one: a few times I wanted to add a small action to a button press, such as a glance at Garric or a word to the cat. Because notes on button presses didn't go through, I dropped them rather than send twice.

opening.text:
Morning finds you before you find it: a thin bar of light through the shutters, the clang of the first forge hammer somewhere down the street, and the slow bronze voice of Lathander's bells rolling over the rooftops of Beregost. The room above the Lantern and Anvil smells of old timber, cold ashes and fresh bread drifting up the stairs.

Your cat sits on the windowsill, tail curled neatly around its paws, watching you with the patience of a creature that has been awake for hours. Beside it, face up on the sill, lies a playing card: the queen of coins, its edges soft with handling. Your own deck is where you left it. This card is not from it, and it was not there last night.

From the yard below comes the rattle of dice in a cup, a burst of laughter and someone cursing their luck. A knock sounds at the door, and a young woman's voice calls through it: "Master Worgen? Hot water, if you want it, and there's porridge and sausages downstairs while they last."

The purse is heavy, the day is empty, and the queen of coins looks up at you from the windowsill. What do you do?

Marta's keys jingle as the door opens. She looks him over the way she looks over everyone: boots, hands, face. Her eyes rest for a moment on the coin turning between his fingers, then on the cat.

When he holds out his hand for the silver, the purse gives him only gold. There isn't a single silver piece in it.

"Keep it till you're down," she says, waving the gold away before he can offer it. "I'll change it at the bar. I don't carry silver up the stairs, the lads at the table would have it off me." She lowers her voice and nods toward the floor.

"He's still there. He took the little table by the door and ordered tea. Who orders tea at an inn? He's been nursing it since before the bells. He's a southerner, by his voice. Thin, older than you, grey at the temples, beard trimmed close. Good boots that have done a lot of road. He wears a sword, but he keeps it the way a clerk keeps a pen, out of the way. He's got a leather case for papers on the table, and he keeps one hand on it." She thinks. "He asked polite. He asked about the cat first, then about a man. Most ask the other way round."

Behind her, down the stairwell, someone at the card table slaps down a winning hand and the room groans. Marta doesn't turn round.

"He's sat where he can see the stairs, master Worgen. If it's trouble, I'd take it kindly if it went out into the street."

On the windowsill, Jinx has stopped watching the street. The cat is looking at the floor, toward the room below.

*(Out of game: James's purse holds only gold, 350 gp and no silver, so Marta will change a gold piece when he settles at the bar. Nothing has been paid yet.)*

Breakfast noise fills the stairwell: fat spitting on the griddle, spoons on bowls, and from the corner the soft riffle of a deck being shuffled. James keeps his eyes ahead of him. Jinx walks down the steps a little in front, tail straight up.

The man at the little table by the door doesn't get up, but he's watching. He looks just as Marta described him: thin, grey at the temples, a sober coat cut for travel, and the tea in front of him long gone cold. One hand rests on the leather case. When James steps to the side of the table so the door stays in view, the man notices and gives a small nod, as if James has passed a test he wasn't told about.

Jinx goes under the table, sniffs the man's boots for a long time with great seriousness, and then sits down beside them.

"A fair introduction," the stranger says. "Please sit." His vowels are clipped short and his consonants are careful. James knows that voice from the south, from Amn and the counting-house streets of Athkatla. A man across the table at that last hand spoke the same way: Corvin Mallo, the Amnian merchant who ran out of coin before he ran out of nerve and pushed a folded, signed paper into the pot instead. The paper is still upstairs in James's pack, with his other papers.

The stranger waits for James to sit, then taps the case twice with two fingers.

"Pell Arvane. I'm a finder by trade, out of Athkatla. People engage me to recover things that have gone astray: debtors, heirs, now and then a document." He keeps his voice level and pitched under the room's noise. "I looked for the cat because a man may change his name or his coat, Master Worgen, but a grey tabby with one torn ear stays the same."

He tips his head toward Jinx's ear and gives a slight apologetic smile, as if sorry to mention it.

"I act for a gentleman who was at a table with you not long ago. In the course of the evening he parted with a paper bearing his signature and seal. He'd like it back, discreetly, and he's prepared to pay a fair sum for it. Before we discuss that sum, I need to know one thing." His fingers stay still on the case. "Do you still have it?"

Over at the bar, Marta is wiping the same stretch of counter for the third time.

Pell Arvane watches James's hands settle on the table and keeps his own where they are, one flat on the case, the other beside his cold tea. He hears the name. Something in his face shifts slightly, the look of a man crossing out a line in his head.

"You've named him, so I won't insult you by pretending otherwise." He undoes the case's buckle with two fingers and slides out a single sheet. He turns it so James can read it but keeps it on his own side of the table. It is a letter of engagement in a merchant's sloping hand, short and dry. It authorises *the bearer, Pell Arvane of Athkatla* to act on the writer's behalf "in the matter of a paper lately lost at play." It is signed *C. Mallo*, and a pressed seal of dark green wax sits under the name. "Master Mallo engaged me himself, in person, eleven days ago in Athkatla. He was very particular about the date. I've been on the road most of the time since."

He puts the letter back in the case and closes the buckle.

"Two hundred gold pieces. In coin, here, this morning, against the paper and your word that no copy was made." He says it plainly, the way a man reads a price off a list. Then, after a moment: "I'll be frank with you, Master Worgen, because I think you'd notice if I weren't. I've recovered a good many gambling markers. Most men who lose one at cards would sooner forget it than pay a finder to cross two borders after it. Master Mallo didn't want to forget this one." Two fingers tap the leather, once, twice. "He didn't tell me why. That's his right."

Under the table Jinx has stopped paying attention to the boots. The cat is sitting very upright with its eyes half closed, and through the thin thread between them James gets what the cat is noticing. The man smells of road dust, horse and cheap inn soap. Underneath that is a fainter, sharper smell of sealing wax, warm and fresh, as if a stick of it was melted recently and not eleven days ago.

At the card table someone calls for another round. Marta doesn't turn round.

Pell keeps his eyes on James's face, not his hands.

"May I ask," he says, "whether you've read it?"

The stair creaks under his weight on the third step, as it did last night. Behind him Pell Arvane inclines his head and lifts the cold cup. "Of course. Care is what I'd expect." He doesn't watch James go. He watches the cat.

The room is as he left it: the bed unmade, the shutters half open, the forge hammers keeping time down the street. The pack is on the floor by the washstand. The pay slip from Tethyr is in the inner pocket, soft as cloth from years of folding. Next to it is Mallo's paper, folded in three, with the green seal broken along one edge where James opened it that night and gave it only a glance.

He unfolds it at the window, where the light is best.

The hand is the same sloping merchant's hand as the letter downstairs, smaller and more hurried here, as if written on a tavern table. It is short.

*I, Corvin Mallo, merchant of Athkatla, do pledge to the bearer of this paper one third part of the price of lot the seventh, consigned under my mark aboard the cog* Patient Heron *now lying at Gray Harbor in Baldur's Gate. The lot is held under bond at the warehouse of Osric Vell, Lower City, until the day of sailing. The bearer shall have the right to attend the breaking of the bond and the counting of the lot, and to receive his third from the sale at Athkatla. The price agreed is four thousand gold pieces.*

Below that is Mallo's signature and his green seal, the same as on the letter of engagement. Below Mallo's seal is a second name, *O. Vell, bondholder*, in a cramped clerk's script, and beside it a second seal.

That seal is not green. It is grey wax, a thumbnail across, pressed with a closed eye inside a ring of tiny letters, so small and close-set that James can't make them into any script he reads. He brushes it with his thumb, and the wax is cold. The paper around it has warmed in his hand by the window, but the grey wax has not. It stays cool, like a stone pulled out of a stream.

On the line describing the lot, in Vell's hand, a few words have been added: *one crate, under seal, contents not declared.*

A third of four thousand is a little over thirteen hundred gold. Pell is offering two hundred.

Through the thread between them, Jinx is still sitting under the little table by the door. The cat's view is mostly boots and table legs. Pell hasn't moved from his chair. He has taken a small book bound in black cloth out of his coat and is writing in it with a stub of pencil, a short line and then another. When Marta passes with a tray he asks her something too quietly for Jinx to catch. She answers in three words and keeps walking. At the card table, one of the caravan guards calls over, cheerful and loud, asking whether the gentleman plays. Pell raises one hand without looking up, a polite no, and goes back to his little book.

No one has come in through the door. No one has gone out.

The grey seal is still cold under James's thumb.
