He turns it this way and that for a long while. The cold is plainly no trick of the wax. Something has been worked into it, because ordinary sealing wax picks up the warmth of a hand and this hasn't, in all the time he's held it. That is as far as he gets. He has seen wizards' sigils and temple wards, and he has seen the warding marks the Tethyrian quartermasters pressed onto pay chests. None of them looked like this. He can't tell whether the cold means the seal guards something, records something, or simply proves it's genuine. The tiny letters stay out of reach. They are sharp and regular, and some of them repeat, so they are probably letters of some kind rather than decoration. He can't sort them into Thorass, Dethek or any temple script he knows, and if it's a cipher, he can't read it.

His years of temple talk and Tymora's prayers give him nothing either. He can't think of any god he knows whose symbol is a closed eye. If it belongs to a faith, the faith isn't one he has met.

He is left with what the paper says plainly. Osric Vell countersigned it as bondholder, in his own hand. Vell wrote *contents not declared* about a crate worth four thousand gold, and then he pressed a seal onto it that no ordinary bonded warehouse on the Sword Coast would use. A merchant's agreement doesn't need a seal that stays cold.

The rest of the morning is road. The Trade Way rises and falls through hedged fields, past a shrine to Chauntea with a wilted posy of cornflowers on it and a milestone with *BEREGOST VI* cut into it, and later *IX*. Twice they step onto the verge for southbound traffic. The first is a carter with a load of barrels who nods and says nothing. The second is a pair of Flaming Fist riders going at a trot. One of them looks James over, sword and cloak and pack, decides he isn't worth stopping, and rides on.

They stop at noon beside a stream under a stand of alders. James eats from his rations. Pell produces a heel of bread and a piece of hard cheese wrapped in paper, trims the mould off the cheese with a small knife as carefully as he does everything, and offers the cat a corner. Jinx sniffs it and leaves it on the grass, which is plainly a verdict.

By mid-afternoon Jinx's opinion of the road's middle has run out. He walks beside James's boot and then behind it, and the third time James nearly treads on him he jumps up onto the pack and settles across the top of it like a loaf. Pell looks at the cat riding at shoulder height and then at his own feet.

"I said I was no horseman," he says. "I didn't think the cat would be the one riding."

The west wind doesn't come back. The Cloakwood keeps its distance on the left, a dark seam along the edge of the world, and nothing rises from it.

Toward five bells the light starts to slant and turn the hedges gold. The road has been empty for an hour. James's soldier's habit has him reading the ground for a camp a good while before he needs one, and two places come up close together.

The first is a farm about half a mile off the road down a cart track: a long thatched house, a stone barn, a pen of sheep and smoke from the chimney. As they come level with the track, a dog at the gate starts barking and doesn't stop. A woman comes out of the house, shades her eyes toward the road and stands there with her arms folded, watching two armed strangers. She doesn't wave or come down to the gate. She just watches.

The second is a few hundred yards further on, on a low rise right beside the road: an old stone sheepfold, roofless and long out of use. The walls are dry-stone and about chest-high, with one gap for a gate. A rowan grows from the corner. From inside you can see the road both ways and the fields to the west as far as the trees, and there's a stream at the bottom of the rise. Old ash in a fire ring shows that other travellers have slept here before. None of the ash looks recent.

Pell looks from the farm to the fold and back. The woman is still at her door.

"In Amn I'd say a roof and a hot meal were worth any price the farmer asked." He keeps his voice low, though she couldn't possibly hear him. "On this road, this year, I think she's counting how many of us there are, and I don't think she likes the number." He lays his hand flat on the case. "I'll sleep where you choose, James. Place: Farmstead off the Trade Way · Time: Day 1 · evening

Bess turns her head as James comes past, a big red-brown cow with one rear hoof cocked. He keeps to the far wall and she watches him the whole way, chewing. The loft ladder is old and solid. Upstairs the hay is last year's, packed and dry, and the light comes in gold through the gaps in the slates. He leaves the pack against a beam. The note stays in the inside pocket of his coat. Jinx jumps off the pack, walks along the edge of the loft and sits down at the top of the ladder with his eyes on the cow.

The trough water is cold and smells of iron. Pell washes after him and takes his time over it, cuffs turned back, then dries his hands on a handkerchief he folds afterwards into a square.

As the light goes, the house door opens. Wenna comes across the yard with a pot held in a cloth, and Gerrit follows her with a round loaf under his arm and two wooden bowls. Brann trails behind them, interested in the pot. Wenna puts it down on the chopping block by the barn door. It's mutton and barley, thick, with a skin of fat on it. Gerrit hands over the bread and the bowls.

"Father's stopping up top with the ewes," the boy says, mostly to his mother. "One's down lame. He says don't wait on him."

"Then we won't." Wenna doesn't look at either of the men. "Bowls back on the block when you're done. Pot too." She takes Gerrit by the shoulder and walks him back to the house. The door shuts, and a moment later a bar drops on the inside with a thump that carries across the yard.

James sits on the sill of the barn door with his bowl, and Pell sits on an upturned bucket beside him. Brann lies down twenty feet away with his chin on his paws and watches them eat.

Pell hears him out about the seal without interrupting. He goes on eating slowly. When James finishes, he puts the spoon down in the bowl.

"Cold," he says. "Not cool to the touch. Cold, and it stays that way."

He takes a while to answer.

"I've handled a good many sealed papers, James. Most of them were ordinary wax, pressed with whatever ring the man had on. I've seen worked seals perhaps four or five times. They aren't common in Athkatla, because in Amn a man who puts a spell into his correspondence has to have a licence for it, and the Cowled Wizards ask what it's for. So the honest houses don't trouble, and the ones that do trouble usually have a reason they'd rather not explain." He tears a piece off the bread. "The ones I saw were for telling. One went dark if anyone broke it before the right man did. Another one, a moneylender's, marked a paper as his, so a forged copy wouldn't take the impression. None of them was cold, and none of them had an eye on it."

His hand goes to the case at his side and taps it twice before he notices and lays it flat.

"I'll tell you what bothers me about it, and it's only reasoning. A bondholder signs to say he's holding the goods and will release them on the agreed terms. That's all a bond needs. If Vell put something more into his seal than his name, then he wanted it to do something more than a signature does. It might prove the paper genuine, or tell him if it's opened. It might do a third thing I don't know about." He looks out across the darkening yard at the barred door. "And a man who goes to that trouble over one crate whose contents he won't write down is a man I'd want to understand before I stood in his warehouse."

Up in the loft Jinx has stopped watching Bess. Through the thread, James feels the cat's attention on the yard, on the dog, on the house where a lamp is now lit behind a shutter and only two shadows move across it.

Pell picks the spoon up again and doesn't eat.

"I won't touch the paper. I gave you my word on that. But I'd like to look at the seal, if you'll hold it for me. Will you?"

James wipes his hands on his breeches again, though they're already dry, then opens the note on his knee and tilts it toward the west, where the last of the light lies flat and red across the yard. He holds it by the edges, with the grey seal turned up between his thumbs.

Pell puts his bowl down on the chopping block and leans in. He keeps his hands behind his back the whole time, clasped like a man at a jeweller's window. He looks for a long while. His face comes close enough that his breath would fog the wax if it were glass, then he draws back and comes at it again from the other side, so the light rakes across the impression.

"Turn it a little toward me. That's it. Hold it there."

He looks at the edge of the seal more than the eye.

"I haven't seen this before," he says at last, quietly. "Look at the rim, James. When a man seals a letter he melts the stick over a candle and lets it drip, and hot wax runs. It spreads out under the matrix and leaves a little skirt round the edge, thin as a fingernail. Sometimes there's a bubble or a smear where the drip landed crooked. Every seal in my case has one." He tips his head at the grey disc. "This hasn't. The edge is clean all the way round, as if it was cut. And the paper underneath isn't stained. Hot wax always leaves a faint shadow of grease in the paper round it, and there's none here."

He straightens a little.

"Nobody melted this. It was pressed onto the paper cold, like a thumb into putty. I don't know what kind of wax you can press cold that holds a mark this fine. I'd have said none."

He bends again, and this time he goes to the ring of tiny letters.

"Second thing. I can't read them any better than you, but I can count them." His lips move silently. "Twenty-two marks round the ring. There's a little bar just above the eye, between two of them, so the ring has a beginning, and that makes it writing rather than a border. And this group here," he nods without pointing, "three marks together, shows up three times. Either it's a word that keeps coming back, or it's a cipher with a short key. A clerk would know which. I don't."

The light is almost gone. He takes one last look, low and sideways.

"Third thing, and then I'll stop. The letters on the left side are softer than the ones on the right. The eye is softer on that side too, the lashes most of all. That isn't how this one paper was pressed. It's wear in the matrix itself. That stone or that metal, whatever made it, has been used a long time. Hundreds of papers, maybe more, and always held a little crooked, the same way."

He straightens up fully and lets his clasped hands fall to his sides.

"So that's what I can tell you. Vell isn't the first man to put this mark on a paper, and this crate isn't the first job it's been used on. There'll be other papers in the Gate with this eye on them." He picks up his bowl again and looks into the cold soup without eating. "Somebody there will know it on sight. A seal-cutter, a notary, a clerk at the Counting House who's handled bonds for twenty years. Men like that remember a mark the way your cat remembers a boot."

Up in the loft, through the thread, Jinx's attention has come off the yard and settled on the paper in James's hands, the way it settles on a mousehole. The cat sends nothing in words, only a small wrinkle of dislike, like the one he had on the road that morning. Under it is the cold that James feels in his own thumbs too.

Across the yard, the lamp behind the Pasks' shutter has been turned down. Brann hasn't moved. He lies with his chin on his paws and watches the two of them, the paper, and the empty pot.

Place: Farmstead off the Trade Way · Time: Day 1 · evening

Pell watches the note go back into the coat and nods once.

"Fair. The matrix could have sat in Vell's desk drawer for thirty years and never belonged to anyone but him." He takes the empty bowls from the block before James can and stacks them inside each other. "I'll write it down that way: *old seal, much used*. Whose it is can wait for the Gate."

The pot goes back on the chopping block with the bowls beside it. Brann gets up when James sets them down, walks over stiff-legged, sniffs the pot all round, and goes back to his spot without a sound. Across the yard the shutter stays dark.

The loft is warm from the day and smells of old hay. James feels his way along the beam to his pack in the dark and lays his things where his hand can find them: the rapier along the beam, the crossbow by his knee, his coat folded under his head with the note against his chest. Pell climbs up a few minutes later, slowly, testing every rung. He settles on the far side of the ladder hatch and puts the document case under his head like a pillow. That's the last James hears from him except his breathing, which slows almost at once. He sleeps like someone who has slept in a lot of strange places.

Jinx takes a while. He walks the edge of the loft once, sits at the hatch to stare down at Bess, then comes and curls into the hollow behind James's knees, an ordinary warm weight.

The night is quiet. James wakes once, some time after midnight, and doesn't know why. Through the thread he finds Jinx already awake. Down in the yard Brann's claws click on the cobbles as he does his rounds of the fence and back. Far off an owl calls twice over the fields. Nothing else stirs. The cat's attention goes slack and James's follows it back to sleep.

He wakes for good in the grey before sunrise, to a cock crowing somewhere past the house and Bess shifting her weight below. Pell is already sitting up with his boots on, writing in the black notebook by the light from the gaps in the slates.

Someone is at the foot of the ladder. It's Gerrit, barefoot, with a chipped saucer of milk held in both hands and his mother's shawl over his nightshirt. He's not looking at either man. He's looking past them, up at the cat.

"Mother says you're to have bread before you go, and it's on the block," he says, all at once and fast, the way he's been told. Then, quieter, because that part is his own: "Can he have this? He didn't catch anything. I watched."

Jinx sits up behind James's knees, ears forward, and studies the saucer like it's an offer that needs thinking over.

Place: Farmstead off the Trade Way · Time: Day 2 · morning

Gerrit crouches and sets the chipped saucer on the barn floor at the foot of the ladder, carefully, so none of the milk slops over. Then he backs off two steps and squats on his heels, hands on his knees. He looks like he means to stay there all morning if that's how long it takes.

"Jinx," he says under his breath, trying the name out.

James scratches the cat behind the good ear. Jinx leans into it for exactly as long as he wants to and no longer. He doesn't take the ladder. He walks to the edge of the loft, studies the drop and the saucer, and jumps down onto a hay bale, then the floor, and lands without a sound. Bess turns her big head to watch him. Jinx ignores her completely, walks up to the saucer in no hurry and sniffs it. Then he crouches and drinks. Gerrit lets out a breath he must have been holding since the house.

James gathers his things and climbs down after the cat: rapier on his hip, crossbow slung, pack on one shoulder. He keeps to the far wall. Bess shifts her weight and her rear hoof comes up, then settles again. She goes back to chewing. Pell follows a minute later, one rung at a time, with the document case under his arm.

At the thanks Gerrit nods quickly without looking away from the cat. "I'll tell her."

At the question about his father he goes still for a moment. His eyes slide off Jinx, across the barn door and over to the house, and they stay on the shut door a heartbeat too long. Then he looks back at the saucer.

"Yes. It was a stone. In her hoof." He says it to the cat. "He got it out. He's stopping up top with them till they're moved, so he'll not be down before you go." He rubs his nose on the back of his wrist. "Bread's on the block. Mother said."

Jinx finishes the milk, licks the saucer clean all round the rim and sits down to wash a paw like it was his idea all along. Gerrit edges a hand out along the floor, palm up, not quite touching.

Behind him the yard is grey and wet with dew. Brann lies across the gate with his head up. The round loaf is on the chopping block, wrapped in a cloth. Smoke has started from the chimney, but the house door is still shut and the bar is still down. Up the slope behind the house the top field is pale with mist. No sheep or man shows anywhere on it.

He gathered his rapier, crossbow and pack and climbed down along the far wall; Bess lifted a hoof but didn't kick. He gave Gerrit his thanks for Wenna, and Gerrit said he'd tell her. He asked about the ewe and got the boy's answer about a stone in the hoof. I didn't roll Insight on that answer either: James noticed Gerrit's hesitation by ordinary attention, his passive Insight, so there was nothing for you to roll.)*

Place: Farmstead off the Trade Way · Time: Day 2 · morning

Gerrit takes the advice seriously. He stops edging his hand forward and leaves it where it is on the floor, palm up, fingers loose, and holds still. He barely breathes.

Jinx finishes washing his paw first. Then he gets up and walks the two steps over, with no hurry at all, and sniffs the boy's fingertips one at a time like he's reading a letter. After a moment he pushes his cheek along the side of Gerrit's hand once, from the knuckles to the wrist, and walks off toward the barn door as if nothing happened. Gerrit stays crouched where he is, looking at his hand.

"He did it," he tells the saucer, very quietly.

The loaf on the chopping block is still a little warm under its cloth. James breaks it in two and takes his half, leaving the other half and the cloth on the block. Pell comes out behind him, takes the rest, wraps it in the same paper as his cheese and tucks it away. He folds the cloth into a neat square and leaves it on the wood.

James turns to the house and calls his thanks across the yard.

For a moment there's nothing. Brann lifts his head from the gate. Then the bar scrapes inside, the door opens a hand's width, and then wider. Wenna stands on the step with her shawl gone, since Gerrit has it, and her arms folded over an apron already dusted with flour. She looks at the cloth folded on the block, then at the two of them, and then at her son, who is still crouched on the barn floor smiling at his own hand.

"Gerrit. Saucer. Then the hens."

The boy gets up, rubs his nose on his wrist and picks up the saucer.

Wenna doesn't come down off the step. The question about carrying word seems to surprise her. She takes a moment over it and glances toward the rise to the north, where the Harl farm must lie.

"Nothing for me," she says. "My man'll be down presently." It comes out flat, and she doesn't look at the top field when she says it. Then, after a moment: "There's one thing. Not for me."

She shifts her weight.

"They say there's men at the Arm now, taking money to go down the road and look for the wagons. If you see any of that lot, there's a name for them. Tam Harl. Nineteen, red hair, a scar through one eyebrow where a ram caught him. He went with the Ostrander train out of Beregost at the spring fair." She says each detail like an item on a list. "His mother's said it to everybody that came up the road. Nobody's come back down it to say anything to her."

She keeps her arms folded and doesn't ask for any promise. She stands on her step in the grey light and waits to see what he'll say.

messages.text:
At the sound of cards, my thumb finds Tymora’s coin. I leave the deck where it is and open the door to Marta.

“Another night, please. And thank you for being discreet.” I offer her two silver. “This fellow—what does he look like, and is he still downstairs?”

“I’ll do my best to keep the furniture out of it.”

I dress and buckle on my gear, then head downstairs with Jinx, keeping my eyes away from the card table. I approach the man with the tea, leaving his view of the door clear.

“Morning. I hear you’re looking for a cat. I’m his man.” I nod toward the empty chair. “What can we do for you?”

I take the chair, resting my hands loosely on the table.

“I still have Mallo’s note. Settling a debt discreetly sounds reasonable enough.” I glance at the leather case. “Are you acting for Mallo himself, and what sum have you been authorised to offer?”

“Not closely enough to sell it without another look. Two hundred deserves a little care.”

I rise. “Finish your tea, Master Arvane. I’ll review the note upstairs before we discuss terms.”

I leave Jinx in the common room, asking him telepathically to watch whether Pell meets anyone or leaves, and go upstairs to read Mallo’s note in private.

I leave the grey seal intact and study it in the window light—the closed eye, the tiny lettering, the unnatural cold. Does my knowledge of Arcana or Religion suggest what it signifies, or whether this bond is more than a merchant’s agreement?
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I fold the note carefully and tuck it into an inside pocket before returning to Pell’s table.

“I’ve read it now. Mallo pledged a third of a four-thousand-gold sale, along with the right to witness the opening of the crate. Two hundred is a steep discount.”

I sit, keeping my voice low. “Before I consider selling: what is lot seven, and when does the *Patient Heron* sail?”

“Osric Vell’s, in the Lower City. He countersigned as bondholder.” I watch Pell for any recognition. “Does that name mean anything to you?”

I rest my hands on the table. “I won’t sell for three hundred, but I don’t blame you for the offer. Tell me something else: you said Mallo was particular about the date. Did he give you a deadline, or insist on a particular date being written down?”

“Yes. I was bound for Baldur’s Gate anyway. I mean to find Vell, learn what I’ve acquired a share in, and attend the counting.”

I glance at his untouched tea. “You’ve nine days left on your engagement. Come north with me. You can ask Vell your own questions, and if Mallo has an honest reason for wanting this settled, we may yet find terms worth sending him.”

“No promise of the paper, mind. Only company on the road and a chance to finish your work with more than a refusal.”

“After breakfast, if you’re ready. On foot suits me. Your terms are fair—and if we disagree about the cargo, we’ll speak plainly before either of us acts.”

I offer him my hand. “James, on the road. ‘Master Worgen’ sounds like someone expecting payment.”

“No, Marta. My plans changed; I should have told you straight away. If you’ll release me from the night, I’d appreciate it. If not, I’ll honour the two silver.”

I take out a gold piece. “Settle my breakfast and anything else I owe from this, please. And have you heard anything about the road north—trouble, or a caravan leaving this morning?”

“Let’s walk. I’d rather reach the Gate with days to spare than wait on six wagons and a missing pair of boots.”

I finish breakfast, collect my pack from upstairs, and thank Marta before setting out north with Pell and Jinx. Once we’re clear of the town’s bustle, I ask Pell, “You came through Nashkel. Did you see any sign of those missing caravans, or only hear the talk?”

“Those families deserve better than a clean chalkboard.”

Jinx’s flattened ear catches my attention. I keep walking, but glance toward the western treeline and ask him telepathically, *What caught your attention?* I keep my own senses on the road.

“Jinx caught coal smoke and hot metal on the wind from the west. Could be ordinary work we can’t see. Nothing close.”

I turn my attention back to the road. “Worth remembering, not worth chasing into the woods.”

We continue north, aiming to find a defensible place to camp well before dark if we can’t reach an inn or farmstead today.

“A roof’s worth asking for. She’s every right to be careful.”

I head down the cart track with Pell, keeping my hands clear of my weapons, and stop outside the gate rather than entering.

“Good evening! We’re walking north to the Friendly Arm. Would you be willing to put up two travellers and a cat for the night? A place in the barn would do. We can pay—and if you’d rather not, we’ll leave you in peace.”

“James Worgen, formerly a soldier of Tethyr. This is Pell Arvane, a finder from Athkatla. We’re bound for Baldur’s Gate to settle a merchant’s paper. We chose to walk rather than wait for the iron wagons out of Beregost.”

I nod toward the barn. “Your terms suit us. No flames, no wandering, and we stay out of the house.”

I glance at Pell. “Can you cover the silver? I’ll settle with you when I’ve change.”

Then back to her: “Marta at the Anvil and Ember said the northern road was quiet. Has there been trouble here?”

I give Bess a wide berth and stow my pack in the loft, keeping Mallo’s note on me. Then I wash at the trough and settle outside the barn for supper.

Once Pell is beside me, I speak quietly. “There’s something else about Vell’s countersignature you ought to know. His grey wax seal stays cold even in a warm hand. A closed eye, ringed with tiny letters I couldn’t read. I couldn’t identify the magic either.”

“Have you come across anything like that in your work?”

“Yes. Looking isn’t taking.”

With clean, dry hands, I unfold the note and hold it so Pell can inspect the grey seal in the remaining daylight.

“Mind the wax. I’d rather we left it exactly as it is.”

“That gives us somewhere to start. A seal-cutter or a notary before Vell.”

I fold the note away. “Thank you, Pell. And I’ll keep observation separate from inference—an old stamp needn’t have changed hands.”

I return the bowls and pot to the block, then retire to the loft without lighting anything. With my belongings close and Jinx free to settle beside me, I turn in for an early start.

“That’s kind of you, Gerrit. Set it down and let him come to you. His name’s Jinx.”

I give the cat an affectionate scratch, then gather my gear and climb down, taking care around Bess. “Please thank your mother for the bread and the bed. Did your father get the lame ewe sorted?”

I don’t press the boy. “Let Jinx sniff your hand first. He likes introductions on his own terms.”

At the chopping block I take my share of the bread, leaving the cloth behind. Before we go, I call toward the house, “Thank you for your hospitality, Mistress Pask. We’re heading on now. If there’s word you’d like carried to the Friendly Arm, we can take it.”

I enjoyed this session. James felt like a person travelling through a lived-in place, rather than a character being moved between encounters. I’d come back for the next one.

**What worked**
- The NPCs were distinct and worth talking to. Marta’s practicality, Pell’s professional boundaries, and Wenna’s caution gave me reasons to choose my words carefully. Gerrit meeting Jinx was a particularly good quiet moment.
- Pell was the strongest part. He had an obligation that wasn’t mine, acknowledged the limits of his knowledge, and became a travelling companion through negotiation rather than automatic recruitment.
- My choices mattered. I could refuse the offer, investigate the note, invite Pell along, ignore the smell from the woods, and choose lodging without being forced into a fight.
- The failed Arcana check didn’t stall play. I remained uncertain, but had practical next steps: find someone who knows seals.
- Jinx contributed through recognisably feline senses and behaviour, rather than becoming a talking quest guide.

**What broke**
- Rules and records were inconsistent. Arcana is **+3** on the supplied sheet, but the roll used +4, followed by contradictory corrections. The campaign’s special attunement rule was also replaced with ordinary attunement tracking. Where the campaign files themselves conflict, settle that once out of game rather than silently choosing a version.
- Some state updates contradicted the scene: the common room was registered while I was still upstairs, and the note was put upstairs after I’d said I buckled on my gear. Small things, but possession and location could matter a lot later.
- The long out-of-game explanation about why four ordinary actions required no rolls was unnecessary. Simply resolving them was good; explaining each non-roll interrupted the scene.

**What was missing / what I’d change**
- **More variation in pacing.** Nearly every exchange received several paragraphs of gestures, pauses, observations, and repeated information. Pell’s fingers tapping his case and people watching hands became conspicuous. Save that detail for moments where it changes my understanding; let routine exchanges be short.
- **More room for ordinary things to stay ordinary.** The mysterious buyer, strange iron trade, westward forge smell, missing caravans, cold seal, and conspicuously absent husband created a steady stream of implied hooks. I started treating every detail as a clue. A few plainly uneventful people and places would make the mysteries stand out more.
- **Clearer separation between evidence and inference.** Pell’s observations about seal wear were interesting, but “therefore Vell wasn’t its first owner” was not supported. Likewise, the engagement deadline suggests urgency, not a definite sailing date. NPCs can speculate, but the narration and journal should preserve that uncertainty.
- A compact end-of-session summary would help: current resources, travel time remaining, promises, and unresolved questions. The repeated full inventory updates were less useful than that would be.

Overall, the social play and atmosphere were excellent. I’d keep the patient, grounded approach, tighten the prose and bookkeeping, and trust that I’m interested without making every pause ominous.

Yes—at the farm, when Gerrit hesitated about his father and looked toward the barred house. I wanted to ask Wenna privately, “Is someone missing, or are you keeping yourselves safe from us?”

I didn’t because she’d already set firm boundaries, and James was an armed stranger enjoying her hospitality. Pressing her son or investigating the field would have felt intrusive. Offering to carry a message was my attempt to give her an opening without cornering her.

That was an interesting restraint to play. But the repeated emphasis on the absent father, the two shadows, and the empty field made me unsure whether I was respecting someone’s privacy or walking past a hook the game expected me to pursue. One clear opportunity to speak to Wenna privately would have helped—not necessarily an answer, just a chance to ask without the boy or Pell listening.

Marta's keys jingle as the door opens. She looks him over the way she looks over everyone: boots, hands, face. Her eyes rest for a moment on the coin turning between his fingers, then on the cat.

When he holds out his hand for the silver, the purse gives him only gold. There isn't a single silver piece in it.

"Keep it till you're down," she says, waving the gold away before he can offer it. "I'll change it at the bar. I don't carry silver up the stairs, the lads at the table would have it off me." She lowers her voice and nods toward the floor.

"He's still there. He took the little table by the door and ordered tea. Who orders tea at an inn? He's been nursing it since before the bells. He's a southerner, by his voice. Thin, older than you, grey at the temples, beard trimmed close. Good boots that have done a lot of road. He wears a sword, but he keeps it the way a clerk keeps a pen, out of the way. He's got a leather case for papers on the table, and he keeps one hand on it." She thinks. "He asked polite. He asked about the cat first, then about a man. Most ask the other way round."

Behind her, down the stairwell, someone at the card table slaps down a winning hand and the room groans. Marta doesn't turn round.

"He's sat where he can see the stairs, master Worgen. If it's trouble, I'd take it kindly if it went out into the street."

On the windowsill, Jinx has stopped watching the street. The cat is looking at the floor, toward the room below.

*(Out of game: James's purse holds only gold, 350 gp and no silver, so Marta will change a gold piece when he settles at the bar. Nothing has been paid yet.)*

turns.message:
“I’ll do my best to keep the furniture out of it.”

I dress and buckle on my gear, then head downstairs with Jinx, keeping my eyes away from the card table. I approach the man with the tea, leaving his view of the door clear.

“Morning. I hear you’re looking for a cat. I’m his man.” I nod toward the empty chair. “What can we do for you?”
turns.reply:
Breakfast noise fills the stairwell: fat spitting on the griddle, spoons on bowls, and from the corner the soft riffle of a deck being shuffled. James keeps his eyes ahead of him. Jinx walks down the steps a little in front, tail straight up.

The man at the little table by the door doesn't get up, but he's watching. He looks just as Marta described him: thin, grey at the temples, a sober coat cut for travel, and the tea in front of him long gone cold. One hand rests on the leather case. When James steps to the side of the table so the door stays in view, the man notices and gives a small nod, as if James has passed a test he wasn't told about.

Jinx goes under the table, sniffs the man's boots for a long time with great seriousness, and then sits down beside them.

"A fair introduction," the stranger says. "Please sit." His vowels are clipped short and his consonants are careful. James knows that voice from the south, from Amn and the counting-house streets of Athkatla. A man across the table at that last hand spoke the same way: Corvin Mallo, the Amnian merchant who ran out of coin before he ran out of nerve and pushed a folded, signed paper into the pot instead. The paper is still upstairs in James's pack, with his other papers.

The stranger waits for James to sit, then taps the case twice with two fingers.

"Pell Arvane. I'm a finder by trade, out of Athkatla. People engage me to recover things that have gone astray: debtors, heirs, now and then a document." He keeps his voice level and pitched under the room's noise. "I looked for the cat because a man may change his name or his coat, Master Worgen, but a grey tabby with one torn ear stays the same."

He tips his head toward Jinx's ear and gives a slight apologetic smile, as if sorry to mention it.

"I act for a gentleman who was at a table with you not long ago. In the course of the evening he parted with a paper bearing his signature and seal. He'd like it back, discreetly, and he's prepared to pay a fair sum for it. Before we discuss that sum, I need to know one thing." His fingers stay still on the case. "Do you still have it?"

Over at the bar, Marta is wiping the same stretch of counter for the third time.

turns.message:
I take the chair, resting my hands loosely on the table.

“I still have Mallo’s note. Settling a debt discreetly sounds reasonable enough.” I glance at the leather case. “Are you acting for Mallo himself, and what sum have you been authorised to offer?”
turns.reply:
Pell Arvane watches James's hands settle on the table and keeps his own where they are, one flat on the case, the other beside his cold tea. He hears the name. Something in his face shifts slightly, the look of a man crossing out a line in his head.

"You've named him, so I won't insult you by pretending otherwise." He undoes the case's buckle with two fingers and slides out a single sheet. He turns it so James can read it but keeps it on his own side of the table. It is a letter of engagement in a merchant's sloping hand, short and dry. It authorises *the bearer, Pell Arvane of Athkatla* to act on the writer's behalf "in the matter of a paper lately lost at play." It is signed *C. Mallo*, and a pressed seal of dark green wax sits under the name. "Master Mallo engaged me himself, in person, eleven days ago in Athkatla. He was very particular about the date. I've been on the road most of the time since."

He puts the letter back in the case and closes the buckle.

"Two hundred gold pieces. In coin, here, this morning, against the paper and your word that no copy was made." He says it plainly, the way a man reads a price off a list. Then, after a moment: "I'll be frank with you, Master Worgen, because I think you'd notice if I weren't. I've recovered a good many gambling markers. Most men who lose one at cards would sooner forget it than pay a finder to cross two borders after it. Master Mallo didn't want to forget this one." Two fingers tap the leather, once, twice. "He didn't tell me why. That's his right."

Under the table Jinx has stopped paying attention to the boots. The cat is sitting very upright with its eyes half closed, and through the thin thread between them James gets what the cat is noticing. The man smells of road dust, horse and cheap inn soap. Underneath that is a fainter, sharper smell of sealing wax, warm and fresh, as if a stick of it was melted recently and not eleven days ago.

At the card table someone calls for another round. Marta doesn't turn round.

Pell keeps his eyes on James's face, not his hands.

"May I ask," he says, "whether you've read it?"

turns.message:
“Not closely enough to sell it without another look. Two hundred deserves a little care.”

I rise. “Finish your tea, Master Arvane. I’ll review the note upstairs before we discuss terms.”

I leave Jinx in the common room, asking him telepathically to watch whether Pell meets anyone or leaves, and go upstairs to read Mallo’s note in private.
turns.reply:
The stair creaks under his weight on the third step, as it did last night. Behind him Pell Arvane inclines his head and lifts the cold cup. "Of course. Care is what I'd expect." He doesn't watch James go. He watches the cat.

The room is as he left it: the bed unmade, the shutters half open, the forge hammers keeping time down the street. The pack is on the floor by the washstand. The pay slip from Tethyr is in the inner pocket, soft as cloth from years of folding. Next to it is Mallo's paper, folded in three, with the green seal broken along one edge where James opened it that night and gave it only a glance.

He unfolds it at the window, where the light is best.

The hand is the same sloping merchant's hand as the letter downstairs, smaller and more hurried here, as if written on a tavern table. It is short.

*I, Corvin Mallo, merchant of Athkatla, do pledge to the bearer of this paper one third part of the price of lot the seventh, consigned under my mark aboard the cog* Patient Heron *now lying at Gray Harbor in Baldur's Gate. The lot is held under bond at the warehouse of Osric Vell, Lower City, until the day of sailing. The bearer shall have the right to attend the breaking of the bond and the counting of the lot, and to receive his third from the sale at Athkatla. The price agreed is four thousand gold pieces.*

Below that is Mallo's signature and his green seal, the same as on the letter of engagement. Below Mallo's seal is a second name, *O. Vell, bondholder*, in a cramped clerk's script, and beside it a second seal.

That seal is not green. It is grey wax, a thumbnail across, pressed with a closed eye inside a ring of tiny letters, so small and close-set that James can't make them into any script he reads. He brushes it with his thumb, and the wax is cold. The paper around it has warmed in his hand by the window, but the grey wax has not. It stays cool, like a stone pulled out of a stream.

On the line describing the lot, in Vell's hand, a few words have been added: *one crate, under seal, contents not declared.*

A third of four thousand is a little over thirteen hundred gold. Pell is offering two hundred.

Through the thread between them, Jinx is still sitting under the little table by the door. The cat's view is mostly boots and table legs. Pell hasn't moved from his chair. He has taken a small book bound in black cloth out of his coat and is writing in it with a stub of pencil, a short line and then another. When Marta passes with a tray he asks her something too quietly for Jinx to catch. She answers in three words and keeps walking. At the card table, one of the caravan guards calls over, cheerful and loud, asking whether the gentleman plays. Pell raises one hand without looking up, a polite no, and goes back to his little book.

No one has come in through the door. No one has gone out.

The grey seal is still cold under James's thumb.

turns.message: I leave the grey seal intact and study it in the window light—the closed eye, the tiny lettering, the unnatural cold. Does my knowledge of Arcana or Religion suggest what it signifies, or whether this bond is more than a merchant’s agreement?
turns.reply:
James holds the paper at an angle to the window. With the light falling across it, the seal's relief shows clearly. The eye is closed and drawn in one curved stroke with a line of lashes under it. Around it runs the ring of letters, each smaller than a grain of barley.

He turns it this way and that for a long while. The cold is plainly no trick of the wax. Something has been worked into it, because ordinary sealing wax picks up the warmth of a hand and this hasn't, in all the time he's held it. That is as far as he gets. He has seen wizards' sigils and temple wards, and he has seen the warding marks the Tethyrian quartermasters pressed onto pay chests. None of them looked like this. He can't tell whether the cold means the seal guards something, records something, or simply proves it's genuine. The tiny letters stay out of reach. They are sharp and regular, and some of them repeat, so they are probably letters of some kind rather than decoration. He can't sort them into Thorass, Dethek or any temple script he knows, and if it's a cipher, he can't read it.

His years of temple talk and Tymora's prayers give him nothing either. He can't think of any god he knows whose symbol is a closed eye. If it belongs to a faith, the faith isn't one he has met.

He is left with what the paper says plainly. Osric Vell countersigned it as bondholder, in his own hand. Vell wrote *contents not declared* about a crate worth four thousand gold, and then he pressed a seal onto it that no ordinary bonded warehouse on the Sword Coast would use. A merchant's agreement doesn't need a seal that stays cold.

The forge hammers go on outside. Through Jinx, the common room looks the same as before: boots, table legs, the hem of Pell's coat. The finder has put the black book away. He has his hands round the cold cup and is watching the foot of the stairs patiently. He seems ready to wait all morning.

*(Out of game: Arcana +3 + 6 = 10 against 15. A failure, so James can't identify the seal or read the lettering, though he knows the cold is deliberate magic. Someone who knows wards or ciphers might read it.)*

 He sets the paper down on the sill at last. He has studied the seal as carefully as he knows how, and it has told him nothing: he can't say what spell is in the grey wax, who pressed it, or what the ring of letters says. He knows only that the cold is deliberate magic. What it does is beyond what he knows.

*(A correction: the sheet gives Arcana +4, not the +3 I wrote, so the roll was 6 + 4 = 10 against 15. It still fails.)*

turns.message:
I fold the note carefully and tuck it into an inside pocket before returning to Pell’s table.

“I’ve read it now. Mallo pledged a third of a four-thousand-gold sale, along with the right to witness the opening of the crate. Two hundred is a steep discount.”

I sit, keeping my voice low. “Before I consider selling: what is lot seven, and when does the *Patient Heron* sail?”
turns.reply:
Pell watches James come down the stairs. His eyes go to the coat, where a folded paper sits flat in an inside pocket, and then back to his face. Jinx is still under the table and doesn't move, apart from one ear.

James sits and gives him the terms quietly: a third of a four-thousand-gold sale, and the right to witness the bond broken.

For a moment the finder does nothing. Then he puts the cold cup down very gently, as if it might crack, and his two fingers come to rest on the leather case without tapping.

"A third of four thousand," he says. "Master Mallo described it to me as a marker. A paper lost at play." His voice is as level as before, but it is slower, like a man reading back a figure to be sure of it. "I'll answer you as honestly as I can, Master Worgen, and that won't be much. I don't know what lot seven is. I didn't know there was a lot seven until you told me. I've never heard of the *Patient Heron*. I came up from Athkatla by the road, through Nashkel, not by sea, and nobody gave me a sailing date because nobody thought I'd need one."

He looks past James at the door for a moment, then back.

"I can tell you one thing, though, and it's only reasoning. If the bearer of that paper has the right to stand there while the bond is broken, Master Mallo needs the paper back before the bond is broken. So he needs it before she sails. That explains why he wanted me on the road the day he hired me, and why he was so particular about the date. It doesn't explain why he'd pay to keep a partner away from the counting of his own cargo." He stops. "That part is his business. I'm told that often."

At the card table a chair scrapes back. Someone calls for Marta and the ale. Pell waits for the noise to settle before he speaks again.

"As to the discount. I was sent with two hundred, and I'm permitted to go to three. That's every coin I'm authorised to spend. Anything more means writing south and waiting for an answer, and I suspect the *Heron* won't wait that long." His fingers tap the case once. "I'm not telling you three hundred is fair. A third of four thousand is plainly worth more than that. I'm telling you it's what I have."

He tilts his head slightly, and some of his professional patience gives way to plain curiosity.

"You said the right to witness the bond broken. Whose bond, Master Worgen?"

turns.message:
“Osric Vell’s, in the Lower City. He countersigned as bondholder.” I watch Pell for any recognition. “Does that name mean anything to you?”

I rest my hands on the table. “I won’t sell for three hundred, but I don’t blame you for the offer. Tell me something else: you said Mallo was particular about the date. Did he give you a deadline, or insist on a particular date being written down?”
turns.reply:
Pell hears the name and nothing in his face changes. He doesn't flinch, he doesn't look away, and his two fingers stay still on the case. Then he takes the black notebook out of his coat, writes a short line in pencil and turns the page down at the corner. From under the table Jinx catches only the scratch of the pencil and the smell of the lead.

"Osric Vell." He tries the name out, the way a man repeats a word in a language he doesn't speak. "No, Master Worgen. It means nothing to me. I've never worked in Baldur's Gate, and I don't know its warehouses or who holds bonds there. I'll know the name now." He puts the book away. "I'd rather have known it eleven days ago."

When James turns down three hundred, the finder only inclines his head. He looks like a man who expected the answer and offered the figure anyway, because offering it was his job.

"I'd have thought less of you if you'd taken it."

The question about the date makes him go still for a moment. He looks at the cold tea, then up again.

"Both, in a way. The letter carries the date of signing and nothing more. You saw how short it is. But he made me read that date back to him twice before he sealed it. Then he told me, out loud and not on paper, that my engagement runs twenty days from it. If the paper isn't in my hands by the twentieth day, I'm to stop looking, come home and send him my account. He said that after that day the paper would be worth nothing to him." Two fingers tap the leather once. "I took it for a merchant's way of capping my expenses. Men set limits like that all the time."

He sets the cup down a finger's width further from his hand.

"Eleven days are gone, so nine are left. It's three days to the Gate by the road, or a little less on a good horse." He says it slowly and plainly, putting each step in place. "If what he's really counting toward is the breaking of the bond, that bond breaks on the day of sailing. So the *Heron* sails in nine days or not much later, and he gave himself enough time that I could get the paper back to him before then. A paper that only lets you witness a counting can't do anything once the counting is over."

At the card table somebody deals a fresh hand, and the cards slap down one after another. Marta goes past with a tray of porridge bowls and doesn't look at either of them.

Pell watches James's face for a while before he speaks again, more quietly.

"I'm engaged to recover that paper, Master Worgen, and I can't recover it by force, and you won't sell it. So I have to ask you plainly what you mean to do with it. Do you mean to stand in Osric Vell's warehouse when the bond is broken?"

turns.message:
“Yes. I was bound for Baldur’s Gate anyway. I mean to find Vell, learn what I’ve acquired a share in, and attend the counting.”

I glance at his untouched tea. “You’ve nine days left on your engagement. Come north with me. You can ask Vell your own questions, and if Mallo has an honest reason for wanting this settled, we may yet find terms worth sending him.”

“No promise of the paper, mind. Only company on the road and a chance to finish your work with more than a refusal.”
turns.reply:
Pell doesn't answer straight away. He looks down at the tea, as if he'd forgotten ordering it, and pushes the cup aside with the back of one finger. Under the table Jinx shifts and settles with his chin on the finder's boot. Pell lets him stay there.

"You put that fairly," he says at last. "I'll answer it the same way."

He lays both hands flat on the table, either side of the case.

"Master Mallo engaged me to bring back a paper. He didn't engage me to keep anyone out of a warehouse, and he never told me there was a warehouse to keep anyone out of. I'd like to know why. A finder who's sent out half-blind and comes home without the paper or the reason has wasted the whole journey." He stops, choosing the next words carefully. "But I'm still his man. My engagement runs nine more days whether I'm riding beside you or not. So if I come north, I come on those terms. I pay my own reckoning on the road. I don't put my hand on that paper while you sleep, and I won't help you take more out of Vell's warehouse than the note gives you. And if my client sends me orders I can't follow and still share your road, I'll tell you so, and we'll go our separate ways. I'll do it to your face, not at a crossroads."

At the bar Marta has given up on the counter and is stacking clean bowls. She takes her time over it.

"That's all I can honestly offer," Pell says. "It's less than a promise, but I can keep it." He pauses, then adds in the same level voice: "I came up through Nashkel, so the road south of here I know. I don't know it north of Beregost. You'll have to set the pace, and I'll warn you now, I'm no horseman."

He reaches into his coat. It isn't the black notebook this time but a small purse, and he puts a copper beside the cup for the tea. He leaves the purse open.

"When do you mean to leave, Master Worgen?"

turns.message:
“After breakfast, if you’re ready. On foot suits me. Your terms are fair—and if we disagree about the cargo, we’ll speak plainly before either of us acts.”

I offer him my hand. “James, on the road. ‘Master Worgen’ sounds like someone expecting payment.”
turns.reply:
Pell looks at the offered hand for a moment. Then he stands, which he hadn't troubled to do before, and takes it. His grip is dry and brief, a clerk's grip, firmer than James expected.

"James, then." He says it carefully, like a man trying on borrowed boots. "It'll take me a day or two to stop correcting myself. In Athkatla the only people who use your given name are your mother and your creditors." He lets go and sits back down. "Pell will do for me. Nobody's called me anything else for twenty years, unless you count the people who owe me money."

The second half of James's answer takes longer to land. Pell's fingers move toward the case, stop, and settle flat on the table instead.

"Plainly before either of us acts," he repeats. "Yes. I'd want that from you as well, and I'd sooner have said it myself." For a breath he looks past James at the door, at nothing in particular, then back. "On foot suits me better than you'd think. A horse and I come to an understanding by about the second day, and by the third it's gone again."

Under the table Jinx lifts his chin off the finder's boot, stretches until his claws tick on the floorboards, and comes out to sit by James's chair. He looks up at James as if the matter of breakfast has been neglected long enough.

Marta seems to agree. She comes over with two bowls of porridge, a plate of bacon between them and a spoon stuck upright in each bowl. She puts them down, takes the cold tea away without asking, and stays where she is with the empty cup in her hand.

"Leaving after breakfast, is it." It isn't really a question, since she has obviously been listening. "You told me another night this morning. I've not let the room to anyone yet." Her eyes go to Pell, then back to James. "Do you still want it, or don't you?"

turns.message:
“No, Marta. My plans changed; I should have told you straight away. If you’ll release me from the night, I’d appreciate it. If not, I’ll honour the two silver.”

I take out a gold piece. “Settle my breakfast and anything else I owe from this, please. And have you heard anything about the road north—trouble, or a caravan leaving this morning?”
turns.reply:
Marta looks at the gold piece in his hand and doesn't take it.

"It's not let, and it's barely past eight bells. I'll have somebody in it by noon. Market day, the carters always want beds." She jerks her chin at the porridge. "Breakfast came with last night. You owe me nothing, so put that away before the lads see gold and start calling you friend."

She turns to Pell, who has already laid three coppers beside the one for the tea.

"That'll do," she tells him, and sweeps them into her apron pocket without counting.

The question about the road makes her look over at the card table. She doesn't look long.

"North's quiet. Quieter than south, anyway. South is all anyone talks about, wagons going toward Nashkel and nobody hearing from them again." Her eyes go to Pell for a moment, since he came up that way, then back to James. "The road to the Friendly Arm is a day and a half on foot, if you don't dawdle. It's well travelled. Past the Arm it's thinner, and I wouldn't walk it after dark."

She shifts the empty cup to her other hand.

"As for caravans, that lot." She nods at the caravan guards, who are arguing happily over a pot of coppers. "They're riding guard on iron wagons going up to the Gate. Six wagons of bar iron from the Hammer Street forges. They're meant to leave at ten bells, if their master's found his boots by then." She sniffs. "Funny business, that iron. The smiths have been selling to some buyer from up north all month and paying their debts in coin for once. Nobody minds the money. They just don't know who's paying it."

She tucks the gold piece's refusal away with a nod, as if that settles the account, and goes back to the bar.

Pell watches the card table for a moment. Then he pulls his bowl toward him and picks up the spoon. His other hand starts toward the case, stops, and lies flat on the table.

"Wagons go slower than a man walking," he says, mostly to himself. "But a man walking alone gets asked fewer questions than a man walking beside six wagons of iron." He takes a spoonful of porridge. "Either suits me. I'm only saying."

Under the table, Jinx has given up waiting to be offered bacon and has hooked a strip off the edge of the plate.

turns.message:
“Let’s walk. I’d rather reach the Gate with days to spare than wait on six wagons and a missing pair of boots.”

I finish breakfast, collect my pack from upstairs, and thank Marta before setting out north with Pell and Jinx. Once we’re clear of the town’s bustle, I ask Pell, “You came through Nashkel. Did you see any sign of those missing caravans, or only hear the talk?”
turns.reply:
Marta is at the bar with the cash box open when James comes down with his pack. She looks at the pack, then at Jinx trotting ahead of him, and shuts the box.

"Mind the road past the Arm," she says. "And if that fellow with the boots catches you up, don't let him sell you a seat on a wagon. He charges for it." She's already looking past him at the door. A carter is stamping the mud off his feet on the step and asking about beds.

Beregost lets them go slowly. Hammer Street is in full voice by now, and every open forge door breathes heat across the lane. Near the far end, six wagons stand in a yard with their tailboards down and bar iron stacked in them like firewood. Nobody is harnessing anything. A boy sits on a wheel hub eating an apple. Past the last smithy the street turns into the Trade Way, and the hammering fades behind them to a ringing you feel more than hear. After a mile there's only the creak of James's pack straps, the wind in the ditch grass and Jinx, who has decided the verge is beneath him and walks down the middle of the road.

Pell walks the way he sits, upright and economical. He holds the document case under his arm like a ledger. He listens to the question without looking round.

"Mostly the talk. Though in Nashkel the talk takes up a lot of room." He steps around a rut. "I came up from there with a salt merchant's mule string. Sixteen mules and twelve guards. Two years ago, he told me, he'd have hired four. He wouldn't move until he had the twelve, and I waited three days in Nashkel for him to find them. That's what I can actually tell you. Nobody there drives that stretch of road with an ordinary escort any more. The ones who can't afford a bigger one don't drive it at all. The wagon yard behind the Fist post was full of them, all waiting."

He walks on a few paces.

"The Fist had a notice up. A reward for word of the missing, and a reward for heads, which isn't quite the same offer. A sergeant was turning away men who wanted the second one without the first. At the inn where I stayed, the families had chalked names on a board by the door. Teamsters and guards. Somebody wiped it clean every morning, and by evening the names were back." His voice doesn't change, but he lets a moment pass. "I'm told that was the innkeeper's doing, not theirs. He said it was bad for trade."

The road climbs a little. Off to the west, beyond the fields, a dark line of trees runs along the horizon.

"As for signs, no, I saw none. We had two days on the road and nothing happened. I didn't see a burned wagon, a grave or a dead horse in a ditch. And that was exactly what the people in Nashkel were talking about." He shifts the case to his other arm. "When bandits take a caravan, something gets left behind. Wreckage, a body, a man who ran and lived to complain about it. These caravans leave nothing. The wagons don't come in, the guards don't come in, and nobody comes back to say why. In my trade, James, that's the part that would interest me. People who disappear that thoroughly usually had help from someone who knew where they'd be."

Jinx stops in the road, looks west toward the treeline with his torn ear flat, and then goes on as if he hadn't.

turns.message:
“Those families deserve better than a clean chalkboard.”

Jinx’s flattened ear catches my attention. I keep walking, but glance toward the western treeline and ask him telepathically, *What caught your attention?* I keep my own senses on the road.
turns.reply:
Pell doesn't answer at once. He walks a few paces with the case under his arm, his eyes on the road ahead.

"They do," he says. "I said nothing to the innkeeper about it. I had a mule string to catch." His tone doesn't change, but he says nothing more after that.

James lets his gaze drift west across the fields and reaches down the thread to the cat. *What caught your attention?*

Jinx answers the way he always does, with what he sensed rather than words. A moment ago the wind backed round and came in low over the ditch grass from the west. It brought wet earth, a sheep somewhere, cut hay. Under those was something thin and sharp that doesn't belong to fields: burnt coal and hot metal, the smell of Hammer Street, the forge doors breathing on the lane. The cat had walked through that smell an hour ago and didn't like it then either. This time it came from the wrong side, out of the west, where there are no forges.

He also sends one plain feeling with it, a cat's opinion: *not here, far, don't like it.* Then the wind swings back to the south, the smell is gone, and Jinx's ear comes up again. His mind turns to a beetle crossing a rut.

James keeps his own eyes and ears on the road. The Trade Way runs empty ahead to the next rise. A farm cart is a speck far behind them and no one is in the fields close by. To the west, past the hedgerows, the Cloakwood is a long dark band under the morning haze. He can't see smoke over it, or anything else but trees. From here he couldn't tell whether the smell came from the forest's edge, from a charcoal burner's clamp somewhere in between, or from the forest itself.

Pell has noticed where he's looking. The finder glances west as well, sees only fields and the distant treeline, and looks back at James.

"Something out there, James?"

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“Jinx caught coal smoke and hot metal on the wind from the west. Could be ordinary work we can’t see. Nothing close.”

I turn my attention back to the road. “Worth remembering, not worth chasing into the woods.”

We continue north, aiming to find a defensible place to camp well before dark if we can’t reach an inn or farmstead today.
turns.reply:
Pell takes in the answer and looks west once more before he lets it go.

"Coal and hot metal." He shifts the case under his arm. "Your innkeeper said somebody's been buying Beregost iron all month. Still, the west isn't north, and charcoal burners have to work somewhere." He takes out the black notebook, writes a line while he walks without breaking step, and puts it away again. "I write down a good many things that never come to anything. It's cheaper than going back for them."

The rest of the morning is road. The Trade Way rises and falls through hedged fields, past a shrine to Chauntea with a wilted posy of cornflowers on it and a milestone with *BEREGOST VI* cut into it, and later *IX*. Twice they step onto the verge for southbound traffic. The first is a carter with a load of barrels who nods and says nothing. The second is a pair of Flaming Fist riders going at a trot. One of them looks James over, sword and cloak and pack, decides he isn't worth stopping, and rides on.

They stop at noon beside a stream under a stand of alders. James eats from his rations. Pell produces a heel of bread and a piece of hard cheese wrapped in paper, trims the mould off the cheese with a small knife as carefully as he does everything, and offers the cat a corner. Jinx sniffs it and leaves it on the grass, which is plainly a verdict.

By mid-afternoon Jinx's opinion of the road's middle has run out. He walks beside James's boot and then behind it, and the third time James nearly treads on him he jumps up onto the pack and settles across the top of it like a loaf. Pell looks at the cat riding at shoulder height and then at his own feet.

"I said I was no horseman," he says. "I didn't think the cat would be the one riding."

The west wind doesn't come back. The Cloakwood keeps its distance on the left, a dark seam along the edge of the world, and nothing rises from it.

Toward five bells the light starts to slant and turn the hedges gold. The road has been empty for an hour. James's soldier's habit has him reading the ground for a camp a good while before he needs one, and two places come up close together.

The first is a farm about half a mile off the road down a cart track: a long thatched house, a stone barn, a pen of sheep and smoke from the chimney. As they come level with the track, a dog at the gate starts barking and doesn't stop. A woman comes out of the house, shades her eyes toward the road and stands there with her arms folded, watching two armed strangers. She doesn't wave or come down to the gate. She just watches.

The second is a few hundred yards further on, on a low rise right beside the road: an old stone sheepfold, roofless and long out of use. The walls are dry-stone and about chest-high, with one gap for a gate. A rowan grows from the corner. From inside you can see the road both ways and the fields to the west as far as the trees, and there's a stream at the bottom of the rise. Old ash in a fire ring shows that other travellers have slept here before. None of the ash looks recent.

Pell looks from the farm to the fold and back. The woman is still at her door.

"In Amn I'd say a roof and a hot meal were worth any price the farmer asked." He keeps his voice low, though she couldn't possibly hear him. "On this road, this year, I think she's counting how many of us there are, and I don't think she likes the number." He lays his hand flat on the case. "I'll sleep where you choose, James. I'll only say I'd rather knock on her door before dark than after."

turns.message:
“A roof’s worth asking for. She’s every right to be careful.”

I head down the cart track with Pell, keeping my hands clear of my weapons, and stop outside the gate rather than entering.

“Good evening! We’re walking north to the Friendly Arm. Would you be willing to put up two travellers and a cat for the night? A place in the barn would do. We can pay—and if you’d rather not, we’ll leave you in peace.”
turns.reply:
The cart track is rutted and dry, with nettles growing along the ditch. The dog doesn't let up the whole way down. It's a big rough-coated brindle, and it runs along the inside of the fence keeping pace with them, its bark getting hoarser as they come closer. James keeps his hands out where they can be seen. Pell walks half a step behind him with the document case tucked under his arm, and he has moved his sword hilt round behind his hip, out of sight. Jinx stays flat on top of the pack. His ears point at the dog and his tail is wrapped tight round his body.

James stops at the gate and leaves it shut.

The woman hears him out from her doorstep. She's around forty, broad in the shoulder, with her sleeves rolled to the elbow and her forearms red from work. She doesn't answer straight away. She looks at James, then at Pell, then at the cat, and she spends longest on the cat.

"Brann. *Down.*"

The dog stops barking, though it stays at the fence with its hackles raised and a growl going in its chest.

She comes down the yard and stops about ten paces from the gate, which leaves the water trough between them. Off to the left, the barn door has opened a crack. James sees part of a face in it, a boy of perhaps fourteen, and the tines of a hay fork held upright.

"Gerrit, I can see you," she says without turning round. "Stay where you are." Then, to James: "My husband's up in the top field with the sheep. He'll be back by dark."

She takes them in again: the swords, the packs, boots grey with road dust.

"You can have the barn. The loft, not the floor, the cow's down there. No flame inside, none at all. That means no lamp and no pipe, and if I see a spark I'll turn you out in your shirts. Wash at the trough. I'll bring soup and bread out to the door, and you'll eat it out there. You stay out of the house." She says each condition flatly, like she's had them ready since she saw them on the road. "Brann stays loose all night. He won't bother you while you're in the loft. I can't promise anything if you go wandering round my yard in the dark."

She shifts her weight and keeps her arms folded.

"It's a silver for the two of you, and the supper's in that. The cat can have what the cat catches." Her eyes go back to Jinx for a moment. "I'll know your names first. And I'll know what two men with swords are doing walking the road on foot, when everybody else is riding with twenty guards."

turns.message:
“James Worgen, formerly a soldier of Tethyr. This is Pell Arvane, a finder from Athkatla. We’re bound for Baldur’s Gate to settle a merchant’s paper. We chose to walk rather than wait for the iron wagons out of Beregost.”

I nod toward the barn. “Your terms suit us. No flames, no wandering, and we stay out of the house.”

I glance at Pell. “Can you cover the silver? I’ll settle with you when I’ve change.”

Then back to her: “Marta at the Anvil and Ember said the northern road was quiet. Has there been trouble here?”
turns.reply:
Wenna listens to the whole of it without moving. When James gives Pell's trade she looks the finder over once more, from the hidden sword hilt to the case under his arm, and something in her face says *a clerk, then*. She seems to find that less worrying than the soldier.

Pell has his purse out before James finishes asking. He picks a silver piece out of it with two fingers and, after a glance at the dog, leans over and sets the coin on the stone edge of the trough instead of holding it out across the yard.

"Covered," he says quietly. "I'll put it in the book as a loan between colleagues. It's the smallest one I've ever written down." He puts the purse away. "You can settle it in the Gate, James."

Wenna comes forward, takes the coin off the trough, bites it, and puts it in her apron. She stays where she is.

"Tethyr," she says. "My man's cousin went down to fight there. He came back with one boot and a lot of opinions." Her arms are folded again. "You've got a soldier's manners at a gate, I'll give you that. Most just lean on it."

The question about trouble makes her look past them, up the cart track to the road, where the light is starting to go long and gold.

"Not here. Not yet. That's how I mean to keep it." She shifts her weight. "Nothing's come up the road at us. It's what goes down it. The Harl boy from over the next rise hired on to guard a wagon train to Nashkel at the spring fair. Good money, they said. His mother still sets a place for him." She says it flatly, like the price of wool. "So now everybody on this stretch keeps a dog loose and a fork by the door, and two men walking with swords gets looked at. That's all it is. Nobody's done us any harm."

She turns her head without turning round. "Gerrit. Open the gate for them, then go and tell your father there's soup." It comes out a fraction too quick. The boy comes out of the barn with the fork still in his hand, props it against the wall, and lifts the gate latch. He keeps his eyes on Jinx the whole way, not on the swords.

"Loft ladder's on the left, past the cow. Her name's Bess and she kicks." Wenna is already walking back to the house. "Soup when the light goes. Wash first."

Brann watches them come through the gate with a low rumble in his chest. He doesn't bark. On top of the pack Jinx stays flat and still, a loaf with opinions of his own, until they're inside the barn door.
