turns.message:
I give Bess a wide berth and stow my pack in the loft, keeping Mallo’s note on me. Then I wash at the trough and settle outside the barn for supper.

Once Pell is beside me, I speak quietly. “There’s something else about Vell’s countersignature you ought to know. His grey wax seal stays cold even in a warm hand. A closed eye, ringed with tiny letters I couldn’t read. I couldn’t identify the magic either.”

“Have you come across anything like that in your work?”
turns.reply:
Bess turns her head as James comes past, a big red-brown cow with one rear hoof cocked. He keeps to the far wall and she watches him the whole way, chewing. The loft ladder is old and solid. Upstairs the hay is last year's, packed and dry, and the light comes in gold through the gaps in the slates. He leaves the pack against a beam. The note stays in the inside pocket of his coat. Jinx jumps off the pack, walks along the edge of the loft and sits down at the top of the ladder with his eyes on the cow.

The trough water is cold and smells of iron. Pell washes after him and takes his time over it, cuffs turned back, then dries his hands on a handkerchief he folds afterwards into a square.

As the light goes, the house door opens. Wenna comes across the yard with a pot held in a cloth, and Gerrit follows her with a round loaf under his arm and two wooden bowls. Brann trails behind them, interested in the pot. Wenna puts it down on the chopping block by the barn door. It's mutton and barley, thick, with a skin of fat on it. Gerrit hands over the bread and the bowls.

"Father's stopping up top with the ewes," the boy says, mostly to his mother. "One's down lame. He says don't wait on him."

"Then we won't." Wenna doesn't look at either of the men. "Bowls back on the block when you're done. Pot too." She takes Gerrit by the shoulder and walks him back to the house. The door shuts, and a moment later a bar drops on the inside with a thump that carries across the yard.

James sits on the sill of the barn door with his bowl, and Pell sits on an upturned bucket beside him. Brann lies down twenty feet away with his chin on his paws and watches them eat.

Pell hears him out about the seal without interrupting. He goes on eating slowly. When James finishes, he puts the spoon down in the bowl.

"Cold," he says. "Not cool to the touch. Cold, and it stays that way."

He takes a while to answer.

"I've handled a good many sealed papers, James. Most of them were ordinary wax, pressed with whatever ring the man had on. I've seen worked seals perhaps four or five times. They aren't common in Athkatla, because in Amn a man who puts a spell into his correspondence has to have a licence for it, and the Cowled Wizards ask what it's for. So the honest houses don't trouble, and the ones that do trouble usually have a reason they'd rather not explain." He tears a piece off the bread. "The ones I saw were for telling. One went dark if anyone broke it before the right man did. Another one, a moneylender's, marked a paper as his, so a forged copy wouldn't take the impression. None of them was cold, and none of them had an eye on it."

His hand goes to the case at his side and taps it twice before he notices and lays it flat.

"I'll tell you what bothers me about it, and it's only reasoning. A bondholder signs to say he's holding the goods and will release them on the agreed terms. That's all a bond needs. If Vell put something more into his seal than his name, then he wanted it to do something more than a signature does. It might prove the paper genuine, or tell him if it's opened. It might do a third thing I don't know about." He looks out across the darkening yard at the barred door. "And a man who goes to that trouble over one crate whose contents he won't write down is a man I'd want to understand before I stood in his warehouse."

Up in the loft Jinx has stopped watching Bess. Through the thread, James feels the cat's attention on the yard, on the dog, on the house where a lamp is now lit behind a shutter and only two shadows move across it.

Pell picks the spoon up again and doesn't eat.

"I won't touch the paper. I gave you my word on that. But I'd like to look at the seal, if you'll hold it for me. Will you?"

changes.summary: Time passes: 1 hour 20 minutes
Journal: “The man asking after a man with a cat” updated

place.name: Farmstead off the Trade Way

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“Yes. Looking isn’t taking.”

With clean, dry hands, I unfold the note and hold it so Pell can inspect the grey seal in the remaining daylight.

“Mind the wax. I’d rather we left it exactly as it is.”
turns.reply:
James wipes his hands on his breeches again, though they're already dry, then opens the note on his knee and tilts it toward the west, where the last of the light lies flat and red across the yard. He holds it by the edges, with the grey seal turned up between his thumbs.

Pell puts his bowl down on the chopping block and leans in. He keeps his hands behind his back the whole time, clasped like a man at a jeweller's window. He looks for a long while. His face comes close enough that his breath would fog the wax if it were glass, then he draws back and comes at it again from the other side, so the light rakes across the impression.

"Turn it a little toward me. That's it. Hold it there."

He looks at the edge of the seal more than the eye.

"I haven't seen this before," he says at last, quietly. "Look at the rim, James. When a man seals a letter he melts the stick over a candle and lets it drip, and hot wax runs. It spreads out under the matrix and leaves a little skirt round the edge, thin as a fingernail. Sometimes there's a bubble or a smear where the drip landed crooked. Every seal in my case has one." He tips his head at the grey disc. "This hasn't. The edge is clean all the way round, as if it was cut. And the paper underneath isn't stained. Hot wax always leaves a faint shadow of grease in the paper round it, and there's none here."

He straightens a little.

"Nobody melted this. It was pressed onto the paper cold, like a thumb into putty. I don't know what kind of wax you can press cold that holds a mark this fine. I'd have said none."

He bends again, and this time he goes to the ring of tiny letters.

"Second thing. I can't read them any better than you, but I can count them." His lips move silently. "Twenty-two marks round the ring. There's a little bar just above the eye, between two of them, so the ring has a beginning, and that makes it writing rather than a border. And this group here," he nods without pointing, "three marks together, shows up three times. Either it's a word that keeps coming back, or it's a cipher with a short key. A clerk would know which. I don't."

The light is almost gone. He takes one last look, low and sideways.

"Third thing, and then I'll stop. The letters on the left side are softer than the ones on the right. The eye is softer on that side too, the lashes most of all. That isn't how this one paper was pressed. It's wear in the matrix itself. That stone or that metal, whatever made it, has been used a long time. Hundreds of papers, maybe more, and always held a little crooked, the same way."

He straightens up fully and lets his clasped hands fall to his sides.

"So that's what I can tell you. Vell isn't the first man to put this mark on a paper, and this crate isn't the first job it's been used on. There'll be other papers in the Gate with this eye on them." He picks up his bowl again and looks into the cold soup without eating. "Somebody there will know it on sight. A seal-cutter, a notary, a clerk at the Counting House who's handled bonds for twenty years. Men like that remember a mark the way your cat remembers a boot."

Up in the loft, through the thread, Jinx's attention has come off the yard and settled on the paper in James's hands, the way it settles on a mousehole. The cat sends nothing in words, only a small wrinkle of dislike, like the one he had on the road that morning. Under it is the cold that James feels in his own thumbs too.

Across the yard, the lamp behind the Pasks' shutter has been turned down. Brann hasn't moved. He lies with his chin on his paws and watches the two of them, the paper, and the empty pot.

turns.message:
“That gives us somewhere to start. A seal-cutter or a notary before Vell.”

I fold the note away. “Thank you, Pell. And I’ll keep observation separate from inference—an old stamp needn’t have changed hands.”

I return the bowls and pot to the block, then retire to the loft without lighting anything. With my belongings close and Jinx free to settle beside me, I turn in for an early start.
turns.reply:
Pell watches the note go back into the coat and nods once.

"Fair. The matrix could have sat in Vell's desk drawer for thirty years and never belonged to anyone but him." He takes the empty bowls from the block before James can and stacks them inside each other. "I'll write it down that way: *old seal, much used*. Whose it is can wait for the Gate."

The pot goes back on the chopping block with the bowls beside it. Brann gets up when James sets them down, walks over stiff-legged, sniffs the pot all round, and goes back to his spot without a sound. Across the yard the shutter stays dark.

The loft is warm from the day and smells of old hay. James feels his way along the beam to his pack in the dark and lays his things where his hand can find them: the rapier along the beam, the crossbow by his knee, his coat folded under his head with the note against his chest. Pell climbs up a few minutes later, slowly, testing every rung. He settles on the far side of the ladder hatch and puts the document case under his head like a pillow. That's the last James hears from him except his breathing, which slows almost at once. He sleeps like someone who has slept in a lot of strange places.

Jinx takes a while. He walks the edge of the loft once, sits at the hatch to stare down at Bess, then comes and curls into the hollow behind James's knees, an ordinary warm weight.

The night is quiet. James wakes once, some time after midnight, and doesn't know why. Through the thread he finds Jinx already awake. Down in the yard Brann's claws click on the cobbles as he does his rounds of the fence and back. Far off an owl calls twice over the fields. Nothing else stirs. The cat's attention goes slack and James's follows it back to sleep.

He wakes for good in the grey before sunrise, to a cock crowing somewhere past the house and Bess shifting her weight below. Pell is already sitting up with his boots on, writing in the black notebook by the light from the gaps in the slates.

Someone is at the foot of the ladder. It's Gerrit, barefoot, with a chipped saucer of milk held in both hands and his mother's shawl over his nightshirt. He's not looking at either man. He's looking past them, up at the cat.

"Mother says you're to have bread before you go, and it's on the block," he says, all at once and fast, the way he's been told. Then, quieter, because that part is his own: "Can he have this? He didn't catch anything. I watched."

Jinx sits up behind James's knees, ears forward, and studies the saucer like it's an offer that needs thinking over.

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
“That’s kind of you, Gerrit. Set it down and let him come to you. His name’s Jinx.”

I give the cat an affectionate scratch, then gather my gear and climb down, taking care around Bess. “Please thank your mother for the bread and the bed. Did your father get the lame ewe sorted?”
turns.reply:
Gerrit crouches and sets the chipped saucer on the barn floor at the foot of the ladder, carefully, so none of the milk slops over. Then he backs off two steps and squats on his heels, hands on his knees. He looks like he means to stay there all morning if that's how long it takes.

"Jinx," he says under his breath, trying the name out.

James scratches the cat behind the good ear. Jinx leans into it for exactly as long as he wants to and no longer. He doesn't take the ladder. He walks to the edge of the loft, studies the drop and the saucer, and jumps down onto a hay bale, then the floor, and lands without a sound. Bess turns her big head to watch him. Jinx ignores her completely, walks up to the saucer in no hurry and sniffs it. Then he crouches and drinks. Gerrit lets out a breath he must have been holding since the house.

James gathers his things and climbs down after the cat: rapier on his hip, crossbow slung, pack on one shoulder. He keeps to the far wall. Bess shifts her weight and her rear hoof comes up, then settles again. She goes back to chewing. Pell follows a minute later, one rung at a time, with the document case under his arm.

At the thanks Gerrit nods quickly without looking away from the cat. "I'll tell her."

At the question about his father he goes still for a moment. His eyes slide off Jinx, across the barn door and over to the house, and they stay on the shut door a heartbeat too long. Then he looks back at the saucer.

"Yes. It was a stone. In her hoof." He says it to the cat. "He got it out. He's stopping up top with them till they're moved, so he'll not be down before you go." He rubs his nose on the back of his wrist. "Bread's on the block. Mother said."

Jinx finishes the milk, licks the saucer clean all round the rim and sits down to wash a paw like it was his idea all along. Gerrit edges a hand out along the floor, palm up, not quite touching.

Behind him the yard is grey and wet with dew. Brann lies across the gate with his head up. The round loaf is on the chopping block, wrapped in a cloth. Smoke has started from the chimney, but the house door is still shut and the bar is still down. Up the slope behind the house the top field is pale with mist. No sheep or man shows anywhere on it.

 *(Out of game: I didn't roll any of the four because none of them needed it. Nothing was uncertain and nothing turned on failing, so James simply did each one, and they're all in the narration above. He scratched Jinx behind the good ear. He gathered his rapier, crossbow and pack and climbed down along the far wall; Bess lifted a hoof but didn't kick. He gave Gerrit his thanks for Wenna, and Gerrit said he'd tell her. He asked about the ewe and got the boy's answer about a stone in the hoof. I didn't roll Insight on that answer either: James noticed Gerrit's hesitation by ordinary attention, his passive Insight, so there was nothing for you to roll.)*

changes.summary: Time passes: 10 minutes

place.name: Farmstead off the Trade Way

stats.depthReason: DM hint: calm; the base of the range (deep only for «важный ход» or a combat climax)

turns.message:
I don’t press the boy. “Let Jinx sniff your hand first. He likes introductions on his own terms.”

At the chopping block I take my share of the bread, leaving the cloth behind. Before we go, I call toward the house, “Thank you for your hospitality, Mistress Pask. We’re heading on now. If there’s word you’d like carried to the Friendly Arm, we can take it.”
turns.reply:
Gerrit takes the advice seriously. He stops edging his hand forward and leaves it where it is on the floor, palm up, fingers loose, and holds still. He barely breathes.

Jinx finishes washing his paw first. Then he gets up and walks the two steps over, with no hurry at all, and sniffs the boy's fingertips one at a time like he's reading a letter. After a moment he pushes his cheek along the side of Gerrit's hand once, from the knuckles to the wrist, and walks off toward the barn door as if nothing happened. Gerrit stays crouched where he is, looking at his hand.

"He did it," he tells the saucer, very quietly.

The loaf on the chopping block is still a little warm under its cloth. James breaks it in two and takes his half, leaving the other half and the cloth on the block. Pell comes out behind him, takes the rest, wraps it in the same paper as his cheese and tucks it away. He folds the cloth into a neat square and leaves it on the wood.

James turns to the house and calls his thanks across the yard.

For a moment there's nothing. Brann lifts his head from the gate. Then the bar scrapes inside, the door opens a hand's width, and then wider. Wenna stands on the step with her shawl gone, since Gerrit has it, and her arms folded over an apron already dusted with flour. She looks at the cloth folded on the block, then at the two of them, and then at her son, who is still crouched on the barn floor smiling at his own hand.

"Gerrit. Saucer. Then the hens."

The boy gets up, rubs his nose on his wrist and picks up the saucer.

Wenna doesn't come down off the step. The question about carrying word seems to surprise her. She takes a moment over it and glances toward the rise to the north, where the Harl farm must lie.

"Nothing for me," she says. "My man'll be down presently." It comes out flat, and she doesn't look at the top field when she says it. Then, after a moment: "There's one thing. Not for me."

She shifts her weight.

"They say there's men at the Arm now, taking money to go down the road and look for the wagons. If you see any of that lot, there's a name for them. Tam Harl. Nineteen, red hair, a scar through one eyebrow where a ram caught him. He went with the Ostrander train out of Beregost at the spring fair." She says each detail like an item on a list. "His mother's said it to everybody that came up the road. Nobody's come back down it to say anything to her."

She keeps her arms folded and doesn't ask for any promise. She stands on her step in the grey light and waits to see what he'll say.

note.text:
I enjoyed this session. James felt like a person travelling through a lived-in place, rather than a character being moved between encounters. I’d come back for the next one.

**What worked**
- The NPCs were distinct and worth talking to. Marta’s practicality, Pell’s professional boundaries, and Wenna’s caution gave me reasons to choose my words carefully. Gerrit meeting Jinx was a particularly good quiet moment.
- Pell was the strongest part. He had an obligation that wasn’t mine, acknowledged the limits of his knowledge, and became a travelling companion through negotiation rather than automatic recruitment.
- My choices mattered. I could refuse the offer, investigate the note, invite Pell along, ignore the smell from the woods, and choose lodging without being forced into a fight.
- The failed Arcana check didn’t stall play. I remained uncertain, but had practical next steps: find someone who knows seals.
- Jinx contributed through recognisably feline senses and behaviour, rather than becoming a talking quest guide.

**What broke**
- Rules and records were inconsistent. Arcana is **+3** on the supplied sheet, but the roll used +4, followed by contradictory corrections. The campaign’s special attunement rule was also replaced with ordinary attunement tracking. Where the campaign files themselves conflict, settle that once out of game rather than silently choosing a version.
- Some state updates contradicted the scene: the common room was registered while I was still upstairs, and the note was put upstairs after I’d said I buckled on my gear. Small things, but possession and location could matter a lot later.
- The long out-of-game explanation about why four ordinary actions required no rolls was unnecessary. Simply resolving them was good; explaining each non-roll interrupted the scene.

**What was missing / what I’d change**
- **More variation in pacing.** Nearly every exchange received several paragraphs of gestures, pauses, observations, and repeated information. Pell’s fingers tapping his case and people watching hands became conspicuous. Save that detail for moments where it changes my understanding; let routine exchanges be short.
- **More room for ordinary things to stay ordinary.** The mysterious buyer, strange iron trade, westward forge smell, missing caravans, cold seal, and conspicuously absent husband created a steady stream of implied hooks. I started treating every detail as a clue. A few plainly uneventful people and places would make the mysteries stand out more.
- **Clearer separation between evidence and inference.** Pell’s observations about seal wear were interesting, but “therefore Vell wasn’t its first owner” was not supported. Likewise, the engagement deadline suggests urgency, not a definite sailing date. NPCs can speculate, but the narration and journal should preserve that uncertainty.
- A compact end-of-session summary would help: current resources, travel time remaining, promises, and unresolved questions. The repeated full inventory updates were less useful than that would be.

Overall, the social play and atmosphere were excellent. I’d keep the patient, grounded approach, tighten the prose and bookkeeping, and trust that I’m interested without making every pause ominous.

after.text:
Yes—at the farm, when Gerrit hesitated about his father and looked toward the barred house. I wanted to ask Wenna privately, “Is someone missing, or are you keeping yourselves safe from us?”

I didn’t because she’d already set firm boundaries, and James was an armed stranger enjoying her hospitality. Pressing her son or investigating the field would have felt intrusive. Offering to carry a message was my attempt to give her an opening without cornering her.

That was an interesting restraint to play. But the repeated emphasis on the absent father, the two shadows, and the empty field made me unsure whether I was respecting someone’s privacy or walking past a hook the game expected me to pursue. One clear opportunity to speak to Wenna privately would have helped—not necessarily an answer, just a chance to ask without the boy or Pell listening.

opening.text:
Grey light slips through the shutters. Down the street a forge hammer strikes, then another, until Beregost has its morning rhythm. Bells sound from the temple of Lathander. The cat is already up, sitting on the windowsill with its tail curled, watching the street as if it owns it. The purse on the chair is heavy: about three hundred and fifty gold, all that is left of the last hand.

Someone knocks three times, brisk and practised. "Morning, master Worgen," calls Marta Holloway, the innkeeper, through the door. "Breakfast's on below, porridge and bacon. Will you be keeping the room another night? Two silver, same as before." She pauses. "And a fellow at the bar was asking whether a man with a cat was stopping here. Didn't give a name. I didn't give him yours."

Through the floorboards come the rattle and slap of a game being dealt, and a burst of laughter from the caravan guards. On the sill, the cat's ears turn toward the door.
